quiz.explain: Air in the balloon sits in a steep susceptibility gradient right against the posterior peripheral zone, and echo-planar DWI is the sequence least able to tolerate field inhomogeneity, which is why the T2W images survive and the diffusion images do not. The distortion grows with field strength, so 3T is where it bites hardest. PI-RADS v2.1 answers this directly: expel the air and distend the balloon with a liquid such as perfluorocarbon or barium suspension, or use a rigid coil that needs no balloon. 'Rescan at 1.5T, where the same balloon causes less trouble' would indeed shrink the distortion, and dropping field strength is the right move when the source of inhomogeneity cannot be removed, as with a metal prosthesis; here it can be removed, so 1.5T surrenders the signal-to-noise and resolution a staging study was booked for in order to solve a problem a syringe of barium solves. Raising the b-value lowers signal-to-noise without touching the inhomogeneity, and dropping the coil throws away the resolution the staging question depends on.
choices: Repeat the diffusion sequence after raising the b-value further
Re-inflate the balloon with a liquid such as barium suspension
Remove the coil and accept the lower-resolution T2W images
Rescan at 1.5T, where the same balloon causes less trouble

nodes.title: What Each Modality Detects
nodes.goal: Choose the modality whose physics can answer the clinical question in front of you, and say why the others cannot.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain and tenderness an hour after fatty meals. The overnight team ordered a contrast CT of the abdomen, which is reported as showing no stones, and the referrer now considers the gallbladder cleared. What is the strongest objection to that conclusion?
choices: Many gallstones match bile in attenuation on CT
The gallbladder empties before a CT is acquired
Contrast in the wall hides stones in the lumen
Stones under one centimetre fall below CT resolution
quiz.answer: Many gallstones match bile in attenuation on CT
quiz.explain: CT forms its image from differences in X-ray attenuation, and a cholesterol stone sitting in bile often has almost the same attenuation as the bile around it, so a substantial minority of gallstones are invisible on CT however good the scanner. Ultrasound does not measure attenuation at all: it listens for sound reflected at boundaries where acoustic impedance changes, and the step from bile to a stone is large enough to send back a bright arc with a clean shadow behind it, moving as the patient rolls. Ultrasound also delivers the rest of the answer in the same minute, with wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign obtained under the probe. The resolution option inverts the physics: CT resolves well under a millimetre, and ultrasound routinely shows 2 mm stones, so what CT lacks here is contrast, not detail.

quiz.prompt: An ultrasound machine assumes a speed of sound in soft tissue of 1540 metres per second. A pulse leaves the transducer and its echo returns 130 microseconds later. At what depth does the machine place that reflector? Answer in centimetres to the nearest whole number, with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The pulse travels to the reflector and back, so the depth is half the round trip: 1540 multiplied by 130 microseconds is 0.2002 metres of travel, and half of that is 0.100 metres, or 10 cm. Two things follow. First, the machine is assuming 1540 m/s for every tissue, and where sound actually travels more slowly, through fat at roughly 1450 m/s, the echo is placed too deep, which is one origin of the duplication and refraction artefacts seen at fat interfaces. Second, depth costs time, because the machine has to wait for the deepest echo before firing again; imaging deeper therefore lowers the frame rate, and that is why a cardiac study narrows its sector to keep the images moving.

quiz.prompt: A 16-year-old presents three hours after sudden severe left testicular pain, with a high-riding tender testis. The on-call team debates imaging. Which property of ultrasound makes it the test that settles this question fastest?
choices: It shows blood flow in real time at the bedside
It penetrates gas and bone better than CT does
It measures tissue attenuation in absolute units
It separates tissues by their water content alone
quiz.answer: It shows blood flow in real time at the bedside
quiz.explain: Torsion is a perfusion question, and the finding that answers it is absent or asymmetrically reduced flow inside the testis, which Doppler shows in minutes at the bedside while the greyscale changes of infarction are still hours away. The other three describe things ultrasound does badly or not at all: gas and bone reflect almost the whole beam rather than transmitting it, absolute attenuation in calibrated units is what CT measures, and separating tissues by their water and fat content is the business of MRI. The clinical rider matters as much as the physics: where the diagnosis is clinically obvious, imaging must not delay exploration, because the salvage rate falls steeply with each hour of ischaemia, and normal Doppler flow does not exclude intermittent torsion in a convincing history.

quiz.prompt: A bedside ultrasound in a large-bodied patient with abdominal pain returns 'pancreas not visualised, obscured by bowel gas'. The requesting doctor asks why the same gas that hides the pancreas from ultrasound does nothing to a CT taken minutes later. Answer in terms of what each machine detects.
quiz.answer: Ultrasound builds its image from sound reflected at boundaries between tissues of differing acoustic impedance, and the impedance step from soft tissue to gas is so large that almost the entire pulse is reflected at the first bowel surface it meets. Nothing is left to travel deeper, so the pancreas behind the gas returns no signal at all, and the thick body wall attenuates the beam further, forcing a lower frequency and coarser resolution. CT does not listen for echoes: it measures how much of a transmitted X-ray beam is absorbed along each path through the body, and gas absorbs very little, so a gas-filled loop is simply a low-attenuation structure that is imaged rather than a barrier standing in front of everything behind it. Body habitus costs CT noise for a given dose rather than access, which is why the retroperitoneum is CT territory and the gallbladder, thyroid and testis are ultrasound territory.
quiz.explain: The two machines fail in different ways because they detect different things. Ultrasound is a reflection technique and therefore has a hard geometric requirement: an unobstructed acoustic window. Anything with an impedance far from soft tissue, meaning gas or bone, reflects the pulse almost totally and casts a shadow behind it, which is why the lungs, the bowel and the adult skull are barriers. CT is a transmission technique, so it does not need a window, and a structure that transmits nearly everything is imaged as a very low number rather than as an obstacle. This is also why the same physics that defeats ultrasound in the abdomen makes it excellent at the pleural surface, where the barrier itself is the finding.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old has anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand. Radiographs at presentation and again at ten days are normal, and the wrist is still painful. MRI is chosen ahead of CT. What does MRI show that makes it the better test here?
choices: Marrow oedema at the fracture, before any displacement
Finer bone detail than CT achieves in the same wrist
The scapholunate ligament, which fractures alongside
Cortical breaks that radiographs are too coarse to show
quiz.answer: Marrow oedema at the fracture, before any displacement
quiz.explain: An undisplaced trabecular fracture need not alter the cortical outline at all, which is why the radiographs are normal and why a repeat film ten days later can stay normal. What changes immediately is the marrow, which bleeds and swells: water content rises, so the site becomes bright on fluid-sensitive sequences and dark against normal fatty marrow on T1. MRI is treated as the reference standard for the occult scaphoid fracture for exactly that reason, and it shows the differential in the same acquisition, including bone bruise, ligament injury and a distal radial fracture. The second option is backwards, since CT resolves cortical and trabecular bone better than MRI does, and the fourth describes what CT is good at, which is the fracture that MRI is being called in to find when CT has nothing to show.

quiz.prompt: Plain radiographic interpretation rests on a small number of basic densities. Put these five in order of increasing X-ray attenuation, from the one that appears blackest on the image to the one that appears whitest.
quiz.answer: air fat soft-tissue bone metal
quiz.explain: Attenuation rises with physical density and, in the energy range used for imaging, very steeply with effective atomic number, because photoelectric absorption depends on it. Air is thin and light and removes almost nothing from the beam, so it blackens the image; fat is slightly less attenuating than the water-like soft tissues around it, which is what makes fat planes visible at all; muscle, blood, solid organs and fluid all cluster together as one soft-tissue density, which is precisely why a radiograph cannot separate them; calcium-rich bone removes far more; and metal removes almost everything. Every plain film sign is a consequence of this ladder, from the silhouette sign, where two structures of the same density in contact lose their border, to the visibility of a pneumothorax, which exists because air has been placed next to soft tissue. CT keeps the same ordering but assigns each tissue a number instead of a shade.

quiz.prompt: Take soft tissue to attenuate ultrasound by 0.5 decibels per centimetre per megahertz, in one direction. A 5 MHz probe images a structure 8 cm deep. Counting the outward path and the return path together, how many decibels has the echo lost by the time it arrives back at the transducer? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The path length is 8 cm out and 8 cm back, so 16 cm in total; 0.5 dB per centimetre per megahertz at 5 MHz is 2.5 dB per centimetre, and 16 centimetres of that is 40 dB, a fall in intensity by a factor of ten thousand. This one line of arithmetic governs probe selection. Doubling the frequency to 10 MHz doubles the loss to 80 dB, which no amount of receiver gain recovers without amplifying noise as well, so high frequencies are confined to superficial work. Frequency is also what sets resolution, since a shorter pulse resolves two reflectors closer together, so every ultrasound examination trades resolution against depth: 3 to 5 MHz for an abdomen, 12 to 15 MHz for a thyroid or a testis, and a large body habitus forces the operator further down that scale exactly when the anatomy is deepest.

quiz.prompt: A supine trauma patient is hypotensive. The portable anteroposterior chest radiograph is read as normal. Bedside ultrasound of the anterior chest is then performed and lung sliding is absent on the left. Why did the radiograph miss what ultrasound found?
choices: Free air collects anteriorly in a patient lying supine
Portable radiographs are exposed at too low a voltage
The pleural line lies outside the radiographic field
Air in the pleural space attenuates as much as lung
quiz.answer: Free air collects anteriorly in a patient lying supine
quiz.explain: On an upright film pleural air rises to the apex and outlines a visceral pleural line against the chest wall. Supine, it collects anteriorly and basally instead, where it is projected through aerated lung and produces only indirect signs such as a deep lateral sulcus or an unusually crisp cardiac border. Ultrasound looks at the pleural interface itself rather than through the chest: air in the pleural space stops the beam at that surface, so the shimmering movement of the two pleural layers against one another is lost, and the point where sliding returns marks the edge of the pneumothorax. Absent sliding is sensitive but not specific, since pleurodesis, dense consolidation, apnoea and a main-stem intubation abolish it too, so the finding is read alongside the clinical picture. The fourth option inverts the physics, because pleural air attenuates the X-ray beam far less than lung tissue does.

quiz.prompt: A junior notices that on MRI the cortex of the femur is a black line while the marrow inside it is bright, and that on the plain radiograph of the same femur the cortex is the whitest structure in the image. Explain both appearances from what the two machines detect.
quiz.answer: MRI detects a radiofrequency signal from hydrogen nuclei that are mobile enough to precess freely and still be giving signal when the sequence reads out, so brightness tracks the mobile water and fat in a voxel. Cortical bone is dense mineral with very few mobile protons and an extremely short T2, so its signal has decayed to nothing before a conventional readout and it appears as a signal void; the marrow inside it is fat and water and is therefore bright. A radiograph detects the transmitted X-ray beam, and attenuation rises with physical density and steeply with effective atomic number, so the calcium-rich cortex removes far more photons than the fatty marrow beside it and leaves that part of the detector unexposed, which prints white. The two machines are answering different questions about the same bone: the radiograph maps mineral, MRI maps the water and fat around it, which is why a fracture invisible on the radiograph can be obvious as marrow oedema on MRI, and why a lytic lesion must destroy a substantial fraction of the cortex before a radiograph shows it.
quiz.explain: The general rule is worth carrying: X-ray-based imaging sees electron density and atomic number, so it sees mineral and iodine well and water badly; MRI sees mobile hydrogen and its chemical environment, so it sees water, fat and marrow well and mineral not at all. Both statements are two sides of one fact. It also explains their blind spots. MRI is poor at cortical detail and at calcification, which is why a suspected fracture line or a calcified matrix goes to CT, and why lung parenchyma, being mostly air, is difficult on MRI. X-ray imaging is poor at separating soft tissues that differ only in water content, which is why iodinated contrast exists.

quiz.prompt: A 71-year-old is brought in 40 minutes after sudden dense right hemiparesis and aphasia. Non-contrast CT of the head is obtained immediately and is normal. The team proceeds to thrombolysis. What was the CT for?
choices: To exclude haemorrhage before a thrombolytic is given
To confirm the infarct that the deficit already suggests
To measure the volume of tissue already infarcted
To grade the collateral supply to the affected side
quiz.answer: To exclude haemorrhage before a thrombolytic is given
quiz.explain: At 40 minutes an ischaemic infarct is usually invisible on CT, and a normal scan is the expected result rather than evidence against the diagnosis. What CT does deliver within minutes, anywhere, in a patient who may be restless and vomiting, is the one finding that turns a life-saving treatment into a lethal one: intracranial haemorrhage. It also excludes some structural mimics. Measuring infarct core and grading collaterals are real tasks with real consequences for thrombectomy selection, but they belong to CT perfusion and CT angiography acquired in the same visit, after the haemorrhage question is settled. Diffusion-weighted MRI would show the infarct within minutes, and where it is available immediately it is used, but availability and speed decide this at 40 minutes.

quiz.prompt: A metal fabricator is booked for a lumbar spine MRI. Screening reveals that a fragment was removed from his eye at work some years ago, with no imaging performed at the time. He has no ocular symptoms now. What should happen before he enters the scan room?
choices: Orbital radiographs to look for a retained fragment
A slit-lamp examination on the morning of the scan
A written declaration that his vision is normal now
A reduced specific absorption rate for the study
quiz.answer: Orbital radiographs to look for a retained fragment
quiz.explain: A ferromagnetic intraocular foreign body is one of the few hard exclusions in MRI screening, because the static field can rotate or translate a fragment lying against the retina and cause blindness in a patient who came in for a back problem. Two plain radiographs of the orbits, or CT where radiography is equivocal, are the accepted screen, and a negative screen clears the patient. Symptoms and visual acuity do not settle it, since a small retained intraocular or intraorbital fragment is often asymptomatic, and a self-reported history of an injury years ago is exactly the situation the screen exists for. Specific absorption rate governs radiofrequency heating of tissue and is the wrong lever here, since the hazard is mechanical force from the static field, which is present from the moment he walks through the door.

nodes.title: Radiation Safety
nodes.goal: Justify and optimise an exposure, name who carries most of the risk from it, and say which examinations carry none.

quiz.prompt: A patient is transferred with abdominal pain and brings a disc containing a CT of the abdomen performed at the referring hospital two days ago. The images are awkward to import, and the receiving team asks for the scan to be repeated so that it sits on the local system. What is the correct response?
choices: Import the outside study rather than repeat the scan
Repeat the scan, since local images are read faster
Repeat it with a lower dose protocol to compensate
Repeat the single phase that the local team wants
quiz.answer: Import the outside study rather than repeat the scan
quiz.explain: Justification asks whether this exposure will change what happens to this patient. An exposure that duplicates a diagnostic study performed two days ago delivers the whole of the risk and almost none of the information, and avoidable repeat imaging is a recognised source of population dose that departments are expected to design against. Optimisation is the answer to a different question, namely how to keep the dose as low as reasonably achievable once an examination has been justified, and a lower-dose protocol cannot rescue an exposure that failed the prior test of whether to expose at all. Repeating a single phase is the same argument in a smaller package. The right work here is administrative rather than radiological: import the disc, or ask the referring department to push the study, and escalate the interoperability problem so that it stops generating exposures.

quiz.prompt: During a fluoroscopically guided procedure the scattered dose rate one metre from the patient is 360 microsieverts per hour. Scatter falls with the square of the distance from the patient. What is the dose rate three metres from the patient, in microsieverts per hour? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three times the distance means a ninth of the rate, so 360 becomes 40 microsieverts per hour. The patient is the source as far as staff are concerned, because the scattered beam coming off the irradiated tissue, not the primary beam, is what reaches the room. Distance is therefore the cheapest protection available: it costs nothing, needs no equipment, protects the eyes and the hands as well as the trunk, and it does not alter the patient's dose by a microsievert. Lead of 0.35 to 0.5 mm equivalent attenuates most of the scattered beam but protects only what it covers and is worn all day, and the other classical levers are time, meaning short fluoroscopy runs at low pulse rates, and shielding, meaning ceiling-suspended screens and table drapes.

quiz.prompt: Your department is asked why a 4-year-old having a CT of the abdomen is not simply scanned on the adult protocol with the milliampere setting turned down. Give the reasons that make dose in a child a separate problem, covering both how much dose the child receives and what that dose then does.
quiz.answer: Two separate things are at stake. First, the delivered dose differs: a small body attenuates far less of the beam, so an adult technique deposits a substantially higher absorbed dose in a child's organs, and those organs sit closer together and closer to the surface, so more of them lie within the primary beam and fewer are spared by depth. A paediatric protocol therefore changes tube current and tube potential together, restricts the scan length to the anatomy the question needs, drops phases that add nothing, and adapts to the size of the child rather than to the age on the request card. Second, the same absorbed dose carries more risk: growing tissues divide rapidly and are more radiosensitive, and a young child has many more years ahead in which a stochastic effect such as a radiation-induced cancer can appear. Justification therefore bites harder in children, which is why ultrasound and MRI are preferred wherever they can answer the same question.
quiz.explain: Turning one dial down is not a paediatric protocol, and the reason is that two independent multipliers are working against the child at once. The physical one is attenuation: less tissue means more of the beam reaching the far side, and a lower fraction absorbed does not translate into a lower dose when the same output is used. The biological one is radiosensitivity multiplied by remaining lifespan, which is why the risk per millisievert is estimated to be several times higher in early childhood than in late adulthood. The practical corollary is the one to remember at the request stage: the single largest dose reduction available in a child is usually the scan that is not performed, followed by the modality that uses no ionising radiation at all.

quiz.prompt: Effective dose weights the absorbed dose to each organ by a tissue weighting factor before summing. Put these four tissues in order of increasing ICRP 103 tissue weighting factor, from the smallest weight to the largest.
quiz.answer: skin thyroid gonads breast
quiz.explain: ICRP Publication 103 assigns skin 0.01, thyroid 0.04, the gonads 0.08 and breast 0.12, the last shared with red bone marrow, colon, lung and stomach. The ordering carries a practical message: a scan that puts the breast in the primary beam, such as a chest CT in a young woman, spends its dose on heavily weighted tissue, which is one argument behind breast shielding debates, behind organ-based tube current modulation, and behind preferring perfusion scintigraphy to CT in some pregnant patients. Two cautions belong with the numbers. Effective dose is a protection quantity, averaged across both sexes and all ages, designed for setting standards and comparing protocols rather than for estimating the risk to the individual in front of you. And the weights are for stochastic risk, so they say nothing about tissue reactions such as skin injury, where the absorbed dose to the skin itself is what counts.

quiz.prompt: A 28-year-old at nine weeks of pregnancy has pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and hypoxia. Leg ultrasound shows no thrombus. The team is reluctant to expose the fetus and proposes treating on suspicion alone. What is the better course?
choices: Image the chest and let the result direct treatment
Anticoagulate for six months without any imaging
Defer chest imaging until the second trimester
Repeat the leg ultrasound daily for three days
quiz.answer: Image the chest and let the result direct treatment
quiz.explain: The fetal dose from CT pulmonary angiography, and from perfusion scintigraphy, is far below the levels at which fetal harm has been demonstrated, and both examinations are accepted in pregnancy. What is not acceptable is committing a young woman to months of anticoagulation, to the bleeding risk around delivery and to the label in every future pregnancy, on suspicion alone, when untreated pulmonary embolism remains a leading cause of maternal death. A negative leg ultrasound reduces the probability but does not exclude embolism, since the clot may have embolised entirely. Choosing between CT angiography and perfusion scintigraphy turns on the chest radiograph and on which dose is being minimised, because CT delivers more to the maternal breast and scintigraphy a little more to the fetus, and both are small; the conversation with the patient about that trade is part of the examination.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old with ileal Crohn disease will need repeated assessment of disease activity over decades. The team asks for CT enterography each time, because it is quicker to schedule. What is the better standing arrangement?
choices: MR enterography for the repeated assessments
CT enterography with a reduced-dose protocol
Abdominal radiographs between the CT studies
CT enterography at half the usual scan length
quiz.answer: MR enterography for the repeated assessments
quiz.explain: The decision that matters here is not made scan by scan but over a lifetime: a relapsing disease diagnosed at 22 means decades of repeat imaging, and cumulative exposure in inflammatory bowel disease is a recognised problem concentrated in the young patients who are scanned most often. MR enterography answers the same questions, being mural thickening, mural enhancement, strictures, fistulae and collections, with no ionising radiation, and it adds a cine assessment of peristalsis that CT cannot give. Bowel ultrasound is increasingly used in the same surveillance role and is quicker still. Optimising the CT protocol is worth doing and buys a real reduction, but it still spends dose at every visit, and shortening the scan length sacrifices the anatomy the question needs. CT keeps its place for the acute complication, where speed and the search for free air or an abscess decide.

quiz.prompt: Take the effective dose of a posteroanterior chest radiograph as 0.02 mSv and that of a CT of the abdomen and pelvis as 10 mSv. How many chest radiographs deliver the same effective dose as one such CT? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Ten divided by 0.02 is 500. The arithmetic is trivial and the scale is the point: the two examinations sit orders of magnitude apart, so the mental habit of treating any imaging as roughly equivalent breaks down immediately. Natural background is a few millisieverts a year in most countries, which puts a chest radiograph at a few days of background and an abdominal CT at a few years of it, and those comparisons are useful for a conversation with a patient. Use them to inform rather than to reassure, for two reasons: effective dose is a protection quantity averaged over a reference population rather than a personal risk figure, and the actual dose of a given CT varies severalfold with the patient's size, the protocol and the number of phases, so the 10 mSv in the question is a typical value and not a constant.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after a long fluoroscopically guided embolisation, a patient reports a well-demarcated red patch of skin on the back, roughly square and about the size of the image field. What does this represent?
choices: A tissue reaction from skin dose above a threshold
A delayed allergic response to the iodinated agent
A stochastic effect of the radiation on skin cells
A pressure injury from lying still on a hard table
quiz.answer: A tissue reaction from skin dose above a threshold
quiz.explain: The shape gives it away: a sharply squared patch matching the collimated field is a dose map, not a disease. Skin injury is a deterministic effect, or tissue reaction, with a threshold in the region of 2 Gy for transient erythema, above which severity rises with dose through epilation and desquamation to dermal necrosis, and the latency lengthens as the severity increases. That is why long interventional procedures track cumulative skin dose, vary the beam angulation to spread the entrance point, set notification levels and arrange follow-up above them. A stochastic effect has no threshold and rises in probability rather than severity with dose, appearing as a cancer years later rather than as a field-shaped patch at three weeks. A contrast reaction does not respect the edges of a collimated field, and a pressure injury sits over a bony prominence rather than in a rectangle.

quiz.prompt: A general practitioner requests lumbar spine radiographs for six weeks of non-specific low back pain in a 35-year-old with no red flags. Draft the substance of your reply, using justification and optimisation as two separate ideas.
quiz.answer: The request fails justification, which is the prior question of whether this exposure will change what happens to this patient. In non-specific back pain without red flags the radiographs will either be normal or show degenerative change that is common in people of the same age who have no pain at all, so management is unchanged either way while the patient acquires a label and a reason to believe the spine is damaged. The dose is not trivial either, because a lumbar spine series delivers an effective dose many times that of a chest radiograph, to the abdomen and gonads. Optimisation is a separate idea and comes second: it asks how to keep the dose as low as reasonably achievable once an examination has been justified, through collimation, projection choice, exposure factors, shielding where it helps and avoiding repeat exposures. A well-optimised examination that should not have happened is still an unjustified exposure, so the reply should offer what does change management: conservative treatment with review, and imaging reserved for red flags, for failure to improve, or for a planned intervention.
quiz.explain: The two principles are ordered, and the order is what trainees most often lose. Justification is a judgement about this patient and this question, made jointly by the referrer and the practitioner who authorises the exposure, and it can only be answered yes or no. Optimisation is an engineering exercise applied afterwards, and it is continuous rather than binary. Running them together produces the two characteristic errors: agreeing to an unhelpful examination because the dose is small, and refusing a helpful one because the dose is large. The third principle, dose limitation, does not enter at all here, because dose limits do not apply to the medical exposure of patients.

quiz.prompt: A radiographer refuses a third CT this year in a patient with metastatic disease, saying that the patient has used up the annual dose limit. How should this be answered?
choices: Dose limits are set for staff and the public, not patients
The limit resets on the anniversary of the first study
The limit applies once three studies have been done
The limit is set per organ, so the chest is exempt
quiz.answer: Dose limits are set for staff and the public, not patients
quiz.explain: The system of radiological protection applies dose limits to occupational and public exposure, where the person exposed receives no direct benefit from the exposure. Medical exposure of a patient is controlled differently, through justification for that patient and optimisation of that examination, with diagnostic reference levels as the audit tool for the department rather than a cap on the individual. There is therefore no annual patient allowance to exhaust, and inventing one would deny imaging to precisely the patients whose illness makes imaging most valuable, which in this case is a patient whose treatment decisions depend on measuring the disease. The radiographer's instinct is still worth having and should be spent on the questions that do apply: will this scan change management, has the interval since the last one been long enough to show a change, and could a shorter or lower-dose protocol answer it.

quiz.prompt: An operator wants to cut personal dose on a busy fluoroscopy list. Which single change lowers the operator's dose while leaving the dose to the patient exactly as it was?
choices: Standing a metre further back during acquisitions
Pulsing the fluoroscopy at half the frame rate
Collimating tightly to the region of interest
Removing the anti-scatter grid for small patients
quiz.answer: Standing a metre further back during acquisitions
quiz.explain: The operator is irradiated by scatter from the patient, so distance acts on the operator alone: the rate falls with the square of the separation, and a single step back is worth more than most equipment. The other three are all good practice, and all of them work by making less radiation in the first place, so each reduces the patient's dose as well and therefore does not answer the question as put. Halving the pulse rate roughly halves the fluoroscopic dose, tight collimation reduces both the irradiated volume and the scatter it produces, and removing the grid in a small patient lowers the entrance dose needed for the same image. The other protections that spare the operator without touching the patient are the ceiling-suspended screen, the table drape, lead glasses and, where geometry allows, keeping the tube under the table so that the densest scatter goes downwards.

nodes.title: Reading the CT Image
nodes.goal: Read a CT slice as measured numbers on a chosen display: use Hounsfield units and windows deliberately, and name the artefact in front of you.

quiz.prompt: At the effective energy of a scan, water has a linear attenuation coefficient of 0.180 per centimetre and one voxel measures 0.207 per centimetre. The CT number is a thousand times the voxel's difference from water, divided by that of water. What is the CT number of the voxel, in Hounsfield units? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A thousand times 0.027 divided by 0.180 is 150 HU. The scale is anchored at two fixed points, water at 0 and air at minus 1000, and that anchoring is what makes a CT number a measurement rather than a shade of grey: the same tissue should return the same number on a different scanner on a different day, which is why attenuation can be quoted in a report and compared between studies. Two caveats travel with it. The number is an average over the whole voxel, so a small structure is diluted by whatever shares its voxel, and the beam is polychromatic rather than monoenergetic, so the effective energy shifts as the beam passes through dense tissue and the same material can measure differently in different surroundings.

quiz.prompt: A CT is displayed at a window level of 40 HU with a window width of 400 HU. At and above which CT number does everything appear the same pure white? Answer in Hounsfield units, with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The displayed range runs from the level minus half the width to the level plus half the width, so 40 plus or minus 200 gives minus 160 to plus 240. Everything at or above 240 saturates to white, everything at or below minus 160 to black, and the entire grey scale is spent on the 400 HU in between. That is why cortical bone at around a thousand, a surgical clip at several thousand and a densely calcified plaque all look identical on a soft-tissue window, and why fat at minus 100 and lung at minus 800 do not look identical there but a pneumothorax at minus 1000 and the lung next to it both vanish into black. Narrowing the width raises contrast per Hounsfield unit and magnifies noise with it; widening it shows everything faintly.

quiz.prompt: A chest CT has been reviewed on soft-tissue settings only and reported as normal. The clinical team, still suspecting a pneumothorax, asks the radiographer to bring the patient back and scan the chest again on lung settings. What should the radiographer say?
choices: The stored numbers can be redisplayed without rescanning
A lung acquisition needs a different tube potential
The lung study must be acquired in full inspiration
Lung images require a separate low-dose acquisition
quiz.answer: The stored numbers can be redisplayed without rescanning
quiz.explain: Windowing is a display transformation applied to CT numbers that are already stored, so the lung information is in the dataset whether or not anybody looked at it, and re-scanning to change a window is a pure dose penalty for nothing. The lesson underneath is the one that caused the miss: a window discards all contrast outside its range, so a chest CT is scrolled at least three times, on lung, mediastinal and bone settings, and a small anterior pneumothorax, subtle emphysema or a rib fracture lives on only one of them. One related operation genuinely is not a display change: the reconstruction kernel is applied when the images are made from the raw projection data, so a sharp lung kernel has to be reconstructed rather than windowed, but that too is done from data the scanner already holds, still without exposing the patient again.

quiz.prompt: Different review tasks on the same CT dataset call for different window widths. Put these four review windows in order of increasing window width, from the narrowest to the widest.
quiz.answer: brain soft-tissue lung bone
quiz.explain: A brain window runs about 80 HU wide, because the whole diagnostic task lives in the few tens of units separating grey matter, white matter, oedema and acute blood, and a wider setting would render all of them the same grey. Soft tissue is about 350 to 400 wide, enough to separate fat, fluid, nodes and enhancing vessels. Lung is about 1500, spanning aerated parenchyma near minus 900 up to vessels near zero. Bone is 2000 or more, since cortex and trabeculae differ by hundreds of units and fine detail matters more there than subtle contrast. Narrow windows amplify noise along with contrast, which is why a low-dose head CT looks so much worse than a low-dose abdomen. Task-specific variants exist for exactly this reason, such as the wider subdural window that separates a thin extra-axial collection from the bright skull beside it.

quiz.prompt: On a head CT, a dark band runs across the pons between the two petrous temporal bones, sitting in the same place on consecutive slices, with no mass effect and nothing in the examination to match it. What is it?
choices: Beam hardening between the dense petrous bones
An acute infarct in the basilar artery territory
A ring artefact from a miscalibrated detector
Motion during the acquisition of those slices
quiz.answer: Beam hardening between the dense petrous bones
quiz.explain: A polychromatic beam loses its lower-energy photons preferentially as it passes through dense bone, so the beam emerging is harder and is attenuated less than the reconstruction algorithm assumes. The algorithm compensates by assigning numbers that are too low along that path, producing the classic dark band between two dense structures with brighter streaks nearby. Three clues separate it from disease: it is bounded by bone rather than by a vascular territory, it lies in the same plane on every slice because the geometry that causes it does not change, and it exerts no mass effect. Higher tube potential, bow-tie filtration, correction algorithms and dual-energy reconstruction all reduce it, and posterior fossa protocols are built around it. A ring artefact is a circle centred on the isocentre, and motion smears the whole image rather than one band.

quiz.prompt: A 2 cm renal lesion measures 34 HU before contrast and 46 HU on the nephrographic phase, with the same size of region of interest placed in the same part of the lesion. How should this be reported?
choices: Indeterminate: the rise is too small to call enhancement
Enhancing, and therefore a solid mass until disproved
A simple cyst, since the rise stays under twenty units
Artefactual, since a cyst is stable between the phases
quiz.answer: Indeterminate: the rise is too small to call enhancement
quiz.explain: The convention in wide use is that a rise of 20 HU or more counts as enhancement, a rise of 10 HU or less does not, and the band between the two is indeterminate, because pseudo-enhancement of a small lesion surrounded by dense cortex, beam hardening, partial volume and imperfect region-of-interest placement can each shift a measurement by that much. A rise of 12 HU sits in the middle of that band and is a reason to keep looking rather than a verdict. Note also that the unenhanced value of 34 HU already places this above the simple-cyst range, so the lesion needed characterising regardless: the next step is a dedicated renal protocol with matched measurements, or MRI, which separates the same lesions by signal characteristics and subtraction and does not suffer pseudo-enhancement. Reporting it as a simple cyst discards exactly the caution the indeterminate band exists to enforce.

quiz.prompt: A coronal reformat of an abdominal CT comes back blurred and stepped, although the axial images look sharp. The axial series was reconstructed at 5 mm. Explain the appearance, and say what can be done about it without bringing the patient back.
quiz.answer: A reformat can only be as good as the thinnest data it is built from. A 5 mm axial series has voxels that are far longer through the plane than they are wide, so a plane reformatted along that long axis has to interpolate between widely spaced samples, which produces stair-step edges and through-plane blur, while the same data looks sharp displayed in the plane in which it was sampled. The remedy is to reconstruct thin sections, of the order of a millimetre with some overlap, from the raw projection data that the scanner still holds; that gives near-isotropic voxels which reformat in any plane, and in three dimensions, without loss. It requires no new exposure, because the photons were already collected and the slice thickness is a reconstruction choice rather than an acquisition one on a modern multidetector scanner. The practical catch is that the raw data is deleted after a set period, so the request has to be made early, which is why departments routinely archive a thin series alongside the thicker one used for reading.
quiz.explain: The distinction worth fixing here is between what the scanner acquired and what somebody chose to reconstruct. Detector collimation sets the thinnest section that can ever be made; everything at or above that is a choice made afterwards from the same projections. Thick sections are chosen deliberately, because averaging more photons per voxel lowers noise and there are fewer images to read, and they are perfectly adequate for viewing in the acquired plane. What they cannot do is support reformatting, three-dimensional rendering or the measurement of small structures. Hence the standard compromise of reading a thicker series while archiving a thin one, and hence the urgency of asking before the raw data window closes.

quiz.prompt: A 4 mm rounded focus in the liver measures 45 HU on the 5 mm series and 9 HU on the 1 mm series reconstructed from the same acquisition, with the region of interest placed carefully both times. What accounts for the difference?
choices: The thick slice averaged the focus with the liver around it
The thin series was reconstructed at a lower energy
Noise in the thin series pulled the mean value down
The focus enhanced between the two reconstructions
quiz.answer: The thick slice averaged the focus with the liver around it
quiz.explain: Each voxel returns one number, the average attenuation of everything inside it. A 4 mm object cannot fill a 5 mm slice, so the number reported there is a blend of the low-attenuation focus and the roughly 60 HU liver above and below it, pulled upward. Reconstructing thinner reduces the blend and reveals the true value of 9 HU, a simple cyst. This is why small structures must be measured on the thinnest series available, and why so many tiny liver and renal lesions that appear to be in the soft-tissue range on thick sections turn out to be cysts. Partial volume averaging works in both directions and also dilutes small dense objects, so a punctate calcification or a small stone can vanish on thick slices. Noise widens the spread of values without shifting the mean, and both series were reconstructed from the same photons at the same energy.

quiz.prompt: A pelvic CT in a patient with bilateral hip replacements is degraded by dark and bright streaks across the bladder and rectum, and the study must be repeated to assess the pelvic organs. Which change to the acquisition helps most?
choices: Raise the tube potential and apply metal correction
Lower the tube potential to boost iodine contrast
Increase the pitch so the tube passes through faster
Reconstruct with a sharper kernel and thin slices
quiz.answer: Raise the tube potential and apply metal correction
quiz.explain: Streaks around metal come from three overlapping causes: photon starvation along paths that pass through the prosthesis, beam hardening, and scatter. A higher tube potential produces a beam that penetrates the metal, so fewer projections are starved of photons, and raising the tube current-time product helps for the same reason. Dedicated metal artefact reduction reconstruction, or high-keV virtual monoenergetic images from a dual-energy acquisition, correct much of what survives. Lowering the potential does raise the attenuation of iodine, which is why it flatters ordinary angiography, but it raises the attenuation of metal too and worsens the artefact. Increasing pitch collects fewer projections through the same anatomy. A sharper kernel accentuates the streaks rather than suppressing them, though thin sections do reduce the through-plane component.

quiz.prompt: A student watching you report a chest CT asks why you scroll through the same slices three separate times. Explain what each pass is for, and give a finding that would be lost if the mediastinal window alone were used.
quiz.answer: The three passes look at the same stored Hounsfield numbers through three different display ranges. The lung window is wide and centred far into the negative numbers, so contrast is spread across aerated lung, and it shows nodules, emphysema, interstitial change, airways and the pleural line. The mediastinal or soft-tissue window is narrow and centred near zero, so it separates tissues differing by only tens of units, distinguishing nodes from fat and vessels, fluid from soft tissue, and it is the window on which attenuation is measured. The bone window is very wide and centred high, so cortex, trabeculae and lytic or sclerotic lesions are visible without the saturation that hides them elsewhere. Anything whose numbers fall outside the displayed range saturates to white or black and becomes invisible, so on the mediastinal window alone a small anterior pneumothorax is lost, along with a subtle nodule, early interstitial change and a rib or vertebral lesion.
quiz.explain: The habit of scrolling several times is a direct consequence of what a window is: a linear map from a range of Hounsfield units onto the shades of grey a display can show, throwing away everything outside that range. The eye can only distinguish a few tens of grey levels, so no single window can serve tissues spanning four thousand units. That fact also explains a class of reporting error that has nothing to do with knowledge: the finding was in the data, was correctly reconstructed, and was displayed as uniform white or uniform black at the moment the reader passed over it. It is the reason review protocols specify windows, why comparison with a prior study should be made on matched settings, and why a report that says the lungs are clear should mean somebody looked at them on a lung window.

quiz.prompt: Every image in a CT series carries a faint circle of the same radius, centred at the same point in the field of view, unchanged as you scroll through the stack. What has gone wrong?
choices: A detector channel is out of calibration
The patient moved during the acquisition
The couch advanced unevenly through the bore
The bolus arrived before the scan started
quiz.answer: A detector channel is out of calibration
quiz.explain: In a third-generation scanner the detector array rotates with the tube, so a channel that reads consistently high or low contributes an erroneous value at one fixed distance from the centre of rotation on every projection, and reconstruction turns that into a ring or partial ring of the same radius on every image, centred on the isocentre. It is a machine fault rather than a patient problem, so the response is recalibration or a service call, not a repeat scan that spends dose to reproduce the same circle. Recognising it matters clinically, because a ring passing through the posterior fossa, the liver or a kidney can be read as a genuine low-attenuation lesion, and because its position at the isocentre means it often falls exactly where the patient was centred. Motion smears structures and throws streaks off high-contrast edges, and neither motion nor a couch fault produces an identical circle slice after slice.

nodes.title: Telling MRI Sequences Apart
nodes.goal: Name the sequence in front of you from how fluid and fat appear on it, and say which question each one was acquired to answer.

quiz.prompt: An unlabelled brain image is handed to you. The ventricles are dark, the subcutaneous fat of the scalp is bright, and white matter is slightly brighter than the overlying cortex. Which weighting is this?
choices: T1-weighted, where fluid is dark and fat bright
T2-weighted, where fluid and fat are both bright
FLAIR, a T2 image with the fluid signal nulled
Diffusion-weighted, acquired at a high b-value
quiz.answer: T1-weighted, where fluid is dark and fat bright
quiz.explain: The fastest check is the ventricles: cerebrospinal fluid dark means T1 or FLAIR, and bright means T2. The tie-break is grey-white contrast, and it is decisive. On T1 the lipid of myelin shortens the relaxation time of white matter, so white matter is brighter than cortex; on any T2-based image, FLAIR included, cortex is brighter than white matter because it holds more water. Scalp fat is bright on T1 and also fairly bright on the fast spin echo T2 sequences used in practice, so fat alone does not separate them, which is a common source of error for readers taught the older rule from conventional spin echo. Diffusion-weighted images announce themselves differently, by coarse resolution, geometric distortion and susceptibility drop-out rather than by anatomical contrast.

quiz.prompt: An inversion recovery sequence nulls a tissue when the inversion time equals the natural logarithm of two multiplied by that tissue's T1. Taking the T1 of fat at 1.5 T as 250 ms, what inversion time nulls fat? Answer in milliseconds to the nearest whole number, with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 0.693 multiplied by 250 is 173 ms, which is why short tau inversion recovery on a 1.5 T scanner uses an inversion time in the 150 to 170 ms region. Fat's T1 lengthens as field strength rises, so a 3 T scanner needs a longer value, and a protocol carried across from one magnet to another without adjustment suppresses imperfectly. The same arithmetic applied to cerebrospinal fluid, whose T1 at 1.5 T is of the order of four seconds, gives an inversion time of a few thousand milliseconds, which is exactly what FLAIR uses to null CSF. One formula therefore generates two of the most useful sequences in the department, and it also generates their shared weakness: inversion recovery nulls by T1 alone, so it nulls anything whose T1 happens to match the chosen value.

quiz.prompt: At 1.5 T, take fat and water protons to precess 220 Hz apart. How long after the excitation pulse are they first exactly out of phase with one another? Answer in milliseconds to one decimal place, with the number alone.
quiz.explain: They accumulate a full cycle of phase difference every 1 divided by 220 seconds, so they are opposed at half of that, 2.27 ms, which rounds to 2.3. This is the opposed-phase echo time used at 1.5 T, with the in-phase echo at about 4.5 ms; at 3 T the frequency separation doubles and both times halve, to roughly 1.1 and 2.3 ms. A voxel containing both fat and water loses signal at the opposed-phase echo, which is how an adrenal adenoma and a fatty liver are diagnosed, since the diagnosis is made by comparing the two echoes rather than by any absolute value. The same effect draws the black India-ink outline around every organ where fat abuts water, and its absence in a fatty mass distinguishes bulk fat, which suppresses, from intravoxel fat, which drops out.

quiz.prompt: A brain lesion is bright on the diffusion-weighted images, and the registrar calls it an acute infarct. On the ADC map the same lesion is also bright. What does that combination mean?
choices: High signal carried over from a long T2, not restriction
Restricted diffusion, confirming a hyperacute infarct
A calculation error, as ADC follows the b-zero image
Restricted diffusion in a lesion of low cellularity
quiz.answer: High signal carried over from a long T2, not restriction
quiz.explain: A diffusion-weighted image retains T2 weighting, so anything with a long T2 is bright on it whether or not water movement is impeded; this is T2 shine-through. The ADC map removes that term, because it is calculated from the rate at which signal falls as the b-value rises rather than from the signal itself, so it is the image that decides. Genuinely restricted diffusion is bright on the diffusion images with a matching dark ADC, and that pairing is what allows an infarct to be called within minutes of onset. Bright on both means a long T2 without restriction, seen in subacute and chronic infarct, vasogenic oedema and cysts, and reading it as acute is how an old stroke is reported as a new one. The mirror image, dark on both, is T2 blackout from haemorrhage or dense mineralisation.

quiz.prompt: A fluid-sensitive fat-suppressed sequence covering both shoulders in one large field of view suppresses fat well in the centre of the image and poorly at both edges. No contrast has been given, and the patient cannot be scanned one side at a time. What is the practical fix?
choices: Repeat it with inversion recovery fat nulling
Increase the receiver bandwidth for the repeat
Give a half dose of gadolinium and repeat it
Lengthen the echo time on the repeat acquisition
quiz.answer: Repeat it with inversion recovery fat nulling
quiz.explain: Spectral fat saturation places a radiofrequency pulse at the resonant frequency of fat and spoils the signal before the sequence begins. That depends on fat resonating where the scanner expects it, which requires a uniform main field; at the edges of a large field of view, well off isocentre, near air-tissue boundaries and around metal, the field is inhomogeneous, fat's frequency drifts out of the saturation band and suppression fails, sometimes suppressing water instead and producing a bright region that looks like disease. Inversion recovery nulls by T1 recovery instead, and T1 does not care where the resonance sits, so STIR is the robust choice for large fields of view, off-centre extremities and metalwork, at the price of a lower signal-to-noise ratio and a longer acquisition. Bandwidth is the lever for chemical shift and metal displacement, not for failed saturation.

quiz.prompt: Having been rescued once by a STIR sequence, a trainee proposes using STIR for the post-gadolinium fat-suppressed series as well. Explain why that is a mistake, and give the alternatives that survive an inhomogeneous field after contrast.
quiz.answer: Inversion recovery nulls tissue by its T1: the inversion time is chosen so that fat, whose T1 is short, is crossing through zero at the moment of readout. Gadolinium works by shortening the T1 of whatever it reaches, so enhancing tissue can be dragged down into the same short-T1 range as fat and nulled along with it, which means the enhancement the series was acquired to demonstrate may be erased, and what survives is reduced in conspicuity. Post-contrast fat suppression should therefore be frequency-selective, or better still obtained with a Dixon technique, which separates water from fat by their phase difference at two echo times rather than by resonance position or by T1, tolerates an inhomogeneous field, and yields in-phase, opposed-phase, water-only and fat-only images from one acquisition. Where neither is available, subtracting the unenhanced T1 images from the enhanced ones displays enhancement with no fat suppression at all, provided the patient did not move between the two.
quiz.explain: The trap is that STIR and spectral saturation both produce an image with dark fat, so they look interchangeable until contrast is given, at which point the mechanism starts to matter. Suppression by frequency asks where a proton resonates and is defeated by field inhomogeneity; suppression by T1 asks how quickly it recovers and is defeated by anything that shortens T1, gadolinium above all, but also methaemoglobin, melanin and proteinaceous fluid, each of which can be nulled on a STIR image and disappear. Dixon methods avoid both failure modes by using the phase relationship between fat and water, which is why they have steadily displaced the older techniques in post-contrast, large-field-of-view and near-metal imaging.

quiz.prompt: On a T1-weighted image, signal falls as a tissue's T1 relaxation time lengthens. Put these four tissues in the order they appear on such an image, from the darkest to the brightest.
quiz.answer: CSF muscle white-matter fat
quiz.explain: At 1.5 T fat has a T1 of roughly a quarter of a second and has recovered almost fully by the next excitation, so it is the brightest thing in most T1 images. White matter follows, its lipid-rich myelin shortening T1 below that of grey matter and of muscle. Muscle is intermediate, and cerebrospinal fluid, at some four seconds, has barely begun to recover and is close to black. This ladder is what makes T1 the sequence for anatomy and for marrow, and it is also the reason a bright signal on T1 is such a useful alarm: the short list of things that shorten T1 is fat, methaemoglobin, melanin, highly proteinaceous fluid, some mineral deposition, and gadolinium. Relaxation times lengthen at 3 T, which is why sequence parameters cannot simply be carried across field strengths.

quiz.prompt: Gadolinium has been given for a suspected meningioma, and the post-contrast series is acquired with a long repetition time and a long echo time. No enhancement is seen anywhere. What has gone wrong?
choices: The contrast effect is looked for on T1-weighted images
The dose was too small for a lesion of that size
Enhancement takes about twenty minutes to appear
The agent needs a fat-suppressed series to be seen
quiz.answer: The contrast effect is looked for on T1-weighted images
quiz.explain: Gadolinium is paramagnetic, and its dominant effect at clinical concentration is to shorten the T1 of nearby water, so tissue that takes it up brightens on a T1-weighted sequence. A long repetition time with a long echo time is T2 weighting, where gadolinium's effect on the image is small and, at high local concentration, is to shorten T2 and darken rather than brighten. A meningioma enhances immediately and intensely, so the sequence rather than the dose or the timing is the problem here. Fat suppression is added to post-contrast T1 imaging in the orbit, neck, spine and musculoskeletal system, where bright fat competes with bright enhancement, but it is not what makes enhancement visible in the first place. The instructive exception is post-contrast FLAIR, which is used for leptomeningeal disease and works because FLAIR carries T1 weighting through its inversion pulse.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old with optic neuritis has ovoid lesions abutting the lateral ventricles. They are conspicuous on FLAIR and much harder to see on the conventional T2 series. Why?
choices: The bright fluid beside them has been nulled on FLAIR
FLAIR resolves finer detail than the T2 series does
The lesions are bright on FLAIR and dark on T2 images
FLAIR is acquired after contrast, and they enhance
quiz.answer: The bright fluid beside them has been nulled on FLAIR
quiz.explain: A demyelinating plaque is bright on T2 because it holds more water than the white matter around it; so is the cerebrospinal fluid a millimetre away, and against that background a periventricular lesion has no contrast to be seen by. FLAIR is a T2-weighted acquisition with an inversion pulse timed to null CSF, so the ventricle goes black while the lesion keeps its signal, which is the whole of the difference. The lesion is bright on both sequences, FLAIR does not resolve better, and no contrast has been given. The same trick makes cortical and juxtacortical lesions visible, and it turns failure of the CSF to null into a finding in its own right, seen with subarachnoid blood, meningitis, high protein, and also as a benign artefact from supplemental oxygen or from pulsatile flow in the basal cisterns and fourth ventricle.

quiz.prompt: A patient wakes with hemiparesis and cannot say when it began, though he was well when he went to bed eight hours earlier. MRI shows a cortical lesion bright on diffusion with a dark ADC, and the FLAIR images look normal at that site. What does that pattern tell the stroke team?
choices: The infarct is likely to be under about four hours old
The infarct is older than the eight hours in question
The diffusion finding is an artefact of the sequence
The lesion is a tumour rather than an acute infarct
quiz.answer: The infarct is likely to be under about four hours old
quiz.explain: Diffusion restriction appears within minutes of arterial occlusion, because cytotoxic oedema shifts water into cells almost immediately, whereas the net increase in tissue water that FLAIR detects takes hours to become visible. A lesion that is positive on diffusion and still negative on FLAIR therefore dates the infarct to roughly the first four and a half hours, and that mismatch was used to select patients with stroke of unknown onset for thrombolysis in the WAKE-UP trial. It is the reason a wake-up stroke is imaged rather than turned away on the clock alone, since the time of onset and the time last seen well are different quantities. Once FLAIR turns positive the mismatch is gone and the window has probably closed, which is also why the finding is read as a marker of tissue age rather than as a substitute for clinical assessment.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have a ring-enhancing lesion at the grey-white junction. One is a pyogenic abscess and the other a necrotic metastasis. Say what the diffusion and ADC images show in each, and why the underlying physics differs.
quiz.answer: The abscess cavity is bright on the diffusion-weighted images with a matching low value on the ADC map, because pus is a thick suspension of inflammatory cells, bacteria, protein and debris in which water molecules are physically impeded, so their apparent diffusion really is restricted. The necrotic centre of a metastasis is liquefied tissue with few intact cells and little structure, so water moves freely there: the core is usually not bright on diffusion and the ADC is high, often higher than normal brain. The distinction is mechanical, about how much structure the fluid contains, and it is independent of enhancement, since both lesions enhance in a ring and the enhancing rim tells you only that the blood-brain barrier is broken. The sign is powerful but not infallible, because haemorrhagic or highly cellular tumour and a treated or partly drained abscess can both mislead, so it is weighed together with the thickness and regularity of the rim, the clinical picture, and perfusion or spectroscopy where available.
quiz.explain: This is the clearest example of diffusion imaging answering a question that contrast enhancement cannot. Enhancement reports on vascular permeability, and a rim of granulation tissue and a rim of viable tumour are both permeable, so the two lesions look alike on post-contrast T1. Diffusion reports on the microscopic environment of water, and pus and liquefactive necrosis differ there completely. The same reasoning generalises: restricted diffusion marks tissue that is densely cellular or viscous, which is why it flags a hypercellular tumour, an epidermoid cyst, and an acutely infarcted brain, and why the ADC value has become a semi-quantitative measure of cellularity in oncological imaging.

quiz.prompt: A lumbar MRI for back pain shows a well-defined focus in the L3 vertebral body that is bright on T1, bright on T2, and loses its signal on the fat-suppressed series. Say what this is, why the three appearances together settle it, and what a worrying vertebral lesion would have looked like instead.
quiz.answer: Bright on T1, bright on T2 and suppressing on the fat-suppressed sequence is fat, and in a vertebral body that means either a focal island of normal fatty marrow or, when the coarse vertical trabeculae and mixed vascular signal are present, a vertebral haemangioma. The T1 image carries most of the weight: normal adult vertebral marrow is fatty and therefore bright on T1, and almost everything that matters clinically, including metastasis, myeloma, infection and an acute fracture, replaces or displaces that fat and so appears darker than the adjacent intervertebral disc or paraspinal muscle on T1, with high signal on fluid-sensitive or STIR images from the water that comes with it. The fat-suppressed series turns a guess into an answer, because fat loses signal there while water does not, which is exactly what separates a haemangioma from an infiltrative lesion. So a lesion bright on T1 is reassuring, while one dark on T1 and bright on STIR earns further work, including a look at the posterior elements, the cortical margins and any soft-tissue component.
quiz.explain: Marrow reading is the clearest case of using a sequence for what it detects rather than for what it is called. The useful internal reference standards are on every image: normal marrow should be brighter than the intervertebral disc and brighter than muscle on T1, and a body that fails that test in an adult is abnormal. Red marrow reconversion, which is common in smokers, the obese, athletes and the anaemic, is the main benign cause of dark T1 marrow, and it is distinguished by being symmetric, patchy, sparing the marrow around vessels, and never darker than the disc. Fat suppression settles the other direction, and chemical shift imaging with in-phase and opposed-phase echoes adds a further test, since benign marrow retains microscopic fat and drops signal on the opposed-phase echo while replaced marrow does not.

nodes.title: Contrast Agents and Their Risks
nodes.goal: Decide when contrast changes the answer, choose the agent for the question and the patient, and manage the reaction and the kidney.

quiz.prompt: Two minutes after an intravenous iodinated injection a 55-year-old is pale and sweating. The blood pressure is 72 over 40 and the pulse is 44. There is no rash, no wheeze and no swelling. What is the first treatment?
choices: Raise the legs and run intravenous fluid
Intramuscular adrenaline into the thigh
An intravenous antihistamine, then observe
A nebulised beta-2 agonist and oxygen
quiz.answer: Raise the legs and run intravenous fluid
quiz.explain: The discriminator is the pulse. A vagal reaction produces hypotension with bradycardia, while anaphylaxis produces hypotension with tachycardia, usually accompanied by urticaria, wheeze or angio-oedema. This patient has the vagal pattern and no allergic features, and the treatment is to lie flat with the legs elevated, give oxygen and run isotonic fluid; if the bradycardia and hypotension persist, atropine is the drug that fits the physiology. Reaching for adrenaline here treats the wrong mechanism and is not harmless in a patient with coronary disease. Two riders keep this safe: the pattern is a strong guide rather than an infallible rule, since bradycardia can appear late in a severe reaction, and the patient stays monitored until the observations have recovered rather than being sent back to the ward on the strength of a diagnosis made in the first minute.

quiz.prompt: A patient develops urticaria, wheeze, a blood pressure of 70 systolic and a pulse of 130 immediately after contrast. A colleague draws up adrenaline at 1 in 1000 and reaches for the intravenous cannula. What should you say?
choices: That strength is meant for the intramuscular route
That strength should be given by nebulised route
Adrenaline is withheld until the wheeze settles
The cannula must be resited before any drug is given
quiz.answer: That strength is meant for the intramuscular route
quiz.explain: This is anaphylaxis, recognised by hypotension with tachycardia together with mucocutaneous and respiratory features, and adrenaline is the treatment, given early and intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh, where absorption is rapid and the dose is forgiving. The 1 in 1000 concentration is the intramuscular preparation; given undiluted intravenously it risks arrhythmia and a hypertensive crisis, and the intravenous route belongs in a monitored setting, at a much greater dilution, titrated in small increments by someone equipped to manage the consequences. Exact doses differ between national resuscitation guidelines, so use the one your institution follows; what does not differ is that adrenaline goes in early, intramuscularly, alongside oxygen, fluid, and a call for help. Antihistamines and corticosteroids treat skin and may reduce late symptoms, and they do nothing for the airway or the circulation.

quiz.prompt: A patient booked for a contrast-enhanced CT reports a severe allergy to prawns. The nurse proposes cancelling the injection, and asks whether steroid cover is required instead. What is the right answer?
choices: Proceed; a seafood allergy does not predict this
Cancel; the iodine in seafood cross-reacts here
Premedicate; atopy of any kind doubles the risk
Substitute gadolinium and scan the same region
quiz.answer: Proceed; a seafood allergy does not predict this
quiz.explain: The belief that shellfish allergy predicts a contrast reaction is a durable myth with no mechanism behind it. Allergy to seafood is directed at muscle proteins such as tropomyosin, not at iodine, which is an element present in the thyroid hormones of every patient in the department and is not itself an allergen. Any atopic history raises the risk of a contrast reaction modestly, and a seafood allergy raises it no more than an allergy to anything else does. The history that actually matters is a previous reaction to iodinated contrast, which is the strongest single predictor and the trigger for reconsidering the agent, the necessity of the study and the case for premedication. Gadolinium is not a substitute here: it is an MRI agent, would show nothing useful on CT at the doses given, and carries risks of its own.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old taking metformin, with an eGFR of 52 and no acute illness, is booked for a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen. The ward asks how long the metformin should be stopped for. Give your answer and the reasoning behind it.
quiz.answer: At this level of renal function metformin does not need to be stopped at all, either before or after the injection. Metformin is not nephrotoxic; the concern is indirect, that if contrast were to precipitate an acute kidney injury the drug would accumulate and cause lactic acidosis. Current guidance therefore ties the decision to renal function and to acute illness rather than to the injection in itself: with an eGFR at or above about 30 and no evidence of acute kidney injury, metformin continues uninterrupted. Where the eGFR is below 30, where there is acute kidney injury or an illness likely to cause one, or where contrast is injected into an artery so that it reaches the renal arteries at high concentration, metformin is withheld from the time of the study and renal function is rechecked before restarting, conventionally after about 48 hours. The trap is the patient whose recorded eGFR is respectable but who is septic or volume-depleted on the day, because the acute picture decides, not the number on the last clinic letter.
quiz.explain: This question is worth getting right because the reflex answer, that metformin is always held for 48 hours, comes from older guidance and still causes avoidable harm: diabetic control deteriorates, patients are told to stop a drug and never restart it, and scans are delayed while somebody arranges a stop that was not needed. Understanding the mechanism makes the rule easy to reconstruct rather than memorise. Metformin is cleared by the kidney and does not damage it; contrast may, rarely, damage the kidney; only when both happen at once does lactic acidosis become a risk. So the decision reduces to how likely an acute kidney injury is in this patient, which is what the eGFR threshold and the acute illness question are asking.

quiz.prompt: An MRI of the liver with contrast is needed in a patient on maintenance haemodialysis. The team asks whether gadolinium can be given at all. What is the appropriate plan?
choices: Use a macrocyclic agent at the lowest useful dose
Use a linear agent, which clears through the liver
Give it and bring the dialysis session forward
Withhold it and accept an unenhanced examination
quiz.answer: Use a macrocyclic agent at the lowest useful dose
quiz.explain: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is the reason for the question. Nearly all confirmed cases followed high or repeated doses of the older linear agents in patients with severe renal impairment, in whom the agent dwells long enough for free gadolinium to be released. Macrocyclic agents hold the ion in a cage that releases far less of it, and the observed risk with them is very low or not demonstrable, so guidance permits their use in severe renal impairment when the examination is needed, at the smallest dose that answers the question, with the exposure documented. Some linear agents do have partial hepatobiliary excretion, which is what makes the second option tempting, but the route of clearance is not what determines the risk and does not make a linear agent the safe choice here. Dialysis clears gadolinium efficiently and scheduling a session soon afterwards is reasonable, though it has not been shown to prevent the disease, so it does not license the wrong agent. Withholding contrast has its own cost, since an unenhanced liver MRI answers far fewer questions.

quiz.prompt: A CT angiogram is injected with a contrast medium containing 350 mg of iodine per millilitre, at a rate of 5 millilitres per second. What iodine delivery rate does that give, in grams of iodine per second? Answer to two decimal places, with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 350 mg per millilitre multiplied by 5 millilitres per second is 1750 mg per second, or 1.75 g per second. Arterial enhancement tracks the iodine delivery rate rather than the total volume injected, which is why the same peak opacification can be reached with a more concentrated agent injected more slowly or a weaker one injected faster, and why a small or poorly sited cannula that caps the achievable rate degrades an angiogram even when the whole volume goes in. Total volume governs something different, namely how long the plateau of enhancement lasts, which matters for a long scan or a slow circulation. Tube potential is the third lever: lowering it moves the beam closer to the K-edge of iodine at about 33 keV and raises iodine attenuation, so a low-kV protocol reaches the same opacification with less iodine delivered.

quiz.prompt: A multiphase abdominal CT samples the same anatomy at several times after the injection begins. Put these four phases in the order in which they occur after an intravenous bolus.
quiz.answer: arterial portal-venous nephrographic excretory
quiz.explain: The arterial phase falls roughly 25 to 40 seconds after the injection starts and shows the arteries and hypervascular lesions. The portal venous phase at roughly 60 to 80 seconds is the workhorse for liver, bowel and solid organs. The nephrographic phase at around 100 seconds fills the renal parenchyma uniformly and is where renal masses are best detected. The excretory phase, several minutes later, opacifies the collecting systems and ureters and is what a CT urogram requires. Each phase costs dose, so phases are chosen for the question rather than acquired out of habit: hepatocellular carcinoma needs a late arterial phase and a delayed phase to demonstrate washout, an adrenal nodule needs an unenhanced series and a delayed one for the washout calculation, and a suspected gastrointestinal bleed needs an unenhanced series so that pre-existing dense material is not mistaken for extravasated contrast.

quiz.prompt: A CT of the abdomen requested for painless haematuria is acquired in the portal venous phase alone. A 3 cm renal lesion measures 62 HU. Explain why it cannot be characterised, and describe the study that should have been performed.
quiz.answer: Enhancement is a change, so it cannot be judged from a single phase with no unenhanced baseline to compare against. A homogeneous lesion measuring 62 HU may be a haemorrhagic or proteinaceous cyst that measured 62 HU before any contrast arrived and has not enhanced at all, or a solid tumour that measured 30 HU beforehand and has enhanced substantially, and the single number cannot separate them. What was needed is a dedicated renal protocol including an unenhanced series, with a region of interest of matched size and position on each phase, in which a rise of 20 HU or more counts as enhancement, a rise of 10 HU or less does not, and the band between is indeterminate. A nephrographic phase is included because it detects and characterises renal masses better than the portal venous phase does, and an excretory phase is included when the indication is haematuria, since the urothelium of the collecting systems and ureters has to be seen as well. Where iodinated contrast cannot be given, or where the CT remains indeterminate, MRI answers the same question through signal characteristics, chemical shift and subtraction.
quiz.explain: The general principle is that contrast studies are comparisons, and a comparison needs both terms. The most common version of this error is measuring a lesion on the only phase that happens to exist and reporting the number as though attenuation alone were diagnostic. It recurs across the body: an adrenal nodule cannot be called a lipid-poor adenoma without an unenhanced measurement and a washout calculation, active bleeding cannot be distinguished from pre-existing dense material without an unenhanced series, and a lesion in the liver cannot be characterised from one phase because the diagnosis lies in the pattern of enhancement over time. The corollary at the request stage is that the protocol has to be chosen from the clinical question, which is why a request that says only abdominal pain often produces a study that cannot answer the question that was really being asked.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old has sudden left loin-to-groin pain and microscopic haematuria. The registrar orders a CT of the urinary tract with intravenous contrast in the portal venous phase. Why should the protocol be changed?
choices: Opacified urine can conceal a stone in the ureter
Contrast in the ureter improves stone conspicuity
Stones are best measured on the excretory phase
Iodine raises the attenuation of a calcified stone
quiz.answer: Opacified urine can conceal a stone in the ureter
