quiz.explain: A stone is dense, and so is contrast-opacified urine; once the collecting system fills with material of similar or greater attenuation, the stone stops standing out from the urine around it and a small ureteric calculus can be lost entirely. The examination for suspected renal colic is therefore unenhanced, and it can be low dose, since stones of essentially every composition apart from the rare indinavir stone are conspicuous against unenhanced urine, and the same study shows obstruction, perinephric stranding and most of the common alternative diagnoses. Contrast is added afterwards where the unenhanced study raises a further question, or where the indication was really haematuria rather than colic. The wider lesson is that contrast conceals as well as reveals: acute intracranial haemorrhage, small calcifications and the very densities that mark bleeding are all read on unenhanced images.

quiz.prompt: A patient who had urticaria and wheeze after iodinated contrast three years ago now needs an immediate CT angiogram for suspected aortic dissection. The team asks you to arrange the standard oral steroid preparation first. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: The elective preparation is incompatible with this indication. Oral corticosteroid regimens are begun many hours before the injection, the usual schedules starting about twelve to thirteen hours ahead, and a suspected type A dissection cannot wait that long, so insisting on premedication would in effect deny the study. The weighing is between the risk of an untreated dissection, which kills at a rate measured in hours, and the risk of repeating a reaction that was moderate and treatable. So the study proceeds now, in a room with resuscitation equipment and drugs immediately to hand, with the patient cannulated, an experienced clinician present, and a period of observation afterwards; using a different iodinated agent from the one implicated three years ago is common practice. Premedication should not be treated as a guarantee in any case, since breakthrough reactions occur despite it, and where an accelerated intravenous steroid and antihistamine regimen is given for urgency it is given without delaying the scan. The one alternative worth a moment's thought is whether another test answers the question in time, such as transoesophageal echocardiography in a patient too unstable to move.
quiz.explain: Two things are being confused when a team asks for premedication in an emergency. The first is what premedication achieves: the evidence supports a reduction in mild reactions, while its effect on severe reactions is far weaker than its reputation suggests, and breakthrough reactions do occur, usually resembling the original one in severity. The second is what delay costs, which depends entirely on the diagnosis being pursued and is catastrophic in dissection, in major trauma and in suspected mesenteric ischaemia. Preparation that takes half a day is a tool for elective imaging in a previous reactor, and the emergency equivalent is not a drug at all but a plan: the right room, the right people, an alternative agent, and observation afterwards.

quiz.prompt: The injector alarms at 60 mL and the antecubital fossa is swollen, tense and painful. The hand is warm with a normal radial pulse and normal sensation. What is the immediate management?
choices: Stop, elevate the arm and apply a cold compress
Warm the arm and complete the injection slowly
Aspirate the fluid through a wide-bore needle
Refer for fasciotomy on the injected volume alone
quiz.answer: Stop, elevate the arm and apply a cold compress
quiz.explain: Most extravasations, including large-volume ones, settle with the injection stopped, the limb elevated above the level of the heart and cold compresses applied, together with an explanation to the patient, documentation, and arrangements for review. What matters is identifying the small minority that threaten the limb: pain out of proportion and increasing, tense swelling with skin blistering or ulceration, altered sensation, weak pulses or delayed capillary refill. Those warrant urgent surgical or plastics assessment for compartment syndrome or skin necrosis, and that decision rests on the examination rather than on the volume, since compartment syndrome has followed small volumes and has failed to follow large ones. Aspiration through a needle achieves little once the fluid has dispersed into the tissues and adds injury, and warming the limb and continuing the injection makes matters worse. Prevention is the better lever: a well-sited cannula in a vein that can take the flow rate, tested before the injector starts.

quiz.prompt: A patient with an eGFR of 28 has abdominal pain, a raised lactate and a clinical suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia. The medical team asks for the CT to be done without contrast in order to protect the kidneys. Set out your position.
quiz.answer: An unenhanced CT will not answer this question. The diagnosis rests on the mesenteric arteries and veins, on the presence or absence of bowel wall enhancement, and on the pattern of mural and mesenteric change, and none of that survives without contrast, so withholding it substitutes a non-diagnostic study for a diagnostic one in a condition with very high mortality in which time is the dominant variable. The risk being avoided has also been overstated: much of what older uncontrolled series attributed to contrast was the underlying illness, and controlled comparisons show a far smaller effect, with the residual concern concentrated below an eGFR of about 30. The plan is therefore to give contrast, with intravenous isotonic saline where time permits, stopping other nephrotoxic drugs, correcting volume depletion, and monitoring renal function afterwards. N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate have not been shown to help and should not be used to buy comfort. The conversation to have with the team is about which of the two risks is larger, not about whether the renal risk exists at all.
quiz.explain: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury has been one of the most instructive corrections in radiology. Early studies compared patients who received contrast against patients who did not, without accounting for the fact that the sicker patients, and those with sepsis, hypotension or nephrotoxic drugs on board, were the ones being scanned; controlled comparisons that match for those factors find a much smaller effect, and one that is concentrated in severe pre-existing impairment. The practical result is a shift in the question asked, from whether contrast is dangerous to whether the unenhanced study can answer the clinical question at all. Where it can, as in suspected renal colic, contrast is omitted for that reason and not out of renal caution. Where it cannot, as here, the harm of the non-diagnostic scan dominates the arithmetic.

nodes.title: The Chest Radiograph
nodes.goal: Read a chest radiograph to a fixed search pattern, localise disease by the silhouette sign, and separate a technically poor film from a diseased one.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with cough and fever has a PA chest radiograph. The right heart border can no longer be traced against the adjacent lung, while the right hemidiaphragm stays sharp along its whole length. On the lateral there is a wedge of increased density overlying the heart, bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the front half of the oblique fissure. Where does the disease sit?
choices: The right middle lobe
The right lower lobe
The anterior mediastinum
The lingular segments
quiz.answer: The right middle lobe
quiz.explain: A border is drawn on a radiograph wherever soft tissue meets air-filled lung along the beam. The right middle lobe is the only lung that touches the right heart border, so consolidation there erases it, and the two fissures that bound the wedge on the lateral are the middle lobe's own boundaries. The right lower lobe sits posteriorly against the diaphragm: it would rub out the hemidiaphragm and leave the heart border intact, which is the reverse of what is described, and it is the commonest wrong answer because both lobes project over the lower zone on the frontal film. The lingula does the same job on the left, so it erases the left heart border. An anterior mediastinal mass does obscure the right heart border, but it displaces structures rather than filling a fissure-bounded wedge, and on the lateral it fills the retrosternal clear space instead of overlying the heart.

quiz.prompt: A supine AP radiograph of an intensive care patient shows the left hemithorax uniformly greyer than the right. Pulmonary vessels can still be traced through the grey to the periphery, there are no air bronchograms, the left hemidiaphragm is indistinct and the mediastinum is central. What accounts for it?
choices: Pleural fluid layering behind the lung
Consolidation of the whole left lung
Collapse of the left lower lobe
Air trapped anterior to the lung
quiz.answer: Pleural fluid layering behind the lung
quiz.explain: Supine, fluid runs to the dependent posterior pleural space and spreads as a sheet behind the whole lung, so the beam passes through fluid and aerated lung in series. The result is a veil of increased density with the vascular markings preserved through it, because the lung behind the veil still contains air. Consolidation replaces that air, so it obscures the vessels and usually shows air bronchograms. Lobar collapse loses volume, and the mediastinum and hilum would shift toward the opacity rather than staying central. Anterior air makes a hemithorax blacker, not greyer. The point that survives the case is that a supine film hides an effusion in plain sight: what would be a meniscus on an erect film becomes a whole-lung haze, and an erect or decubitus view, or five seconds of ultrasound, settles it.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient becomes suddenly hypotensive as airway pressures rise. The supine AP film shows the left costophrenic sulcus extending abnormally low and lucent towards the flank, an unusually crisp left heart border and pericardial fat pad, and no visible pleural line anywhere.
choices: Air in the pleural space anteriorly
Emphysema of the left lower lobe
A left-sided diaphragmatic rupture
Loculated fluid in the left fissure
quiz.answer: Air in the pleural space anteriorly
quiz.explain: In a supine patient the least dependent part of the pleural space is anterior and basal, not apical, so pneumothorax collects in front of the lung and runs down into the costophrenic sulcus. That gives the deep sulcus sign, a hyperlucent upper abdominal quadrant, and mediastinal and diaphragmatic borders that look sharper than they should because air rather than lung now abuts them. The absent pleural line is the trap: the visceral edge is only seen where the beam runs tangential to it, and here it does not, so waiting for a white line means missing a tension pneumothorax in a patient whose blood pressure is already falling. Lower lobe emphysema does not appear in minutes, a ruptured hemidiaphragm displaces abdominal contents into the chest, and loculated fluid is dense rather than lucent.

quiz.prompt: A ward PA film reported quickly is described as showing a widened upper mediastinum and a prominent right hilum, and a CT is requested on that basis. Reviewing the film, the spinous processes at T3 lie far closer to the medial end of the right clavicle than to the left, and the posterior ribs are noticeably longer on one side. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Repeat the radiograph with the patient square
Proceed to contrast CT of the mediastinum
Add a lateral to confirm the hilar mass
Arrange a follow-up radiograph in six weeks
quiz.answer: Repeat the radiograph with the patient square
quiz.explain: The spinous processes should sit midway between the medial ends of the clavicles; when they do not, the patient is rotated and the mediastinum is being projected obliquely. An obliqued mediastinum casts a wider shadow, and one hilum is thrown clear of the spine while the other is buried in it, so both of the reported abnormalities are manufactured by geometry. A repeat film costs one exposure and a minute, and it either removes the finding or confirms it. The discipline generalises: technique is assessed before findings, because every technical fault has a disease that it imitates. The one qualification worth carrying is that rotation is an explanation, not an excuse. In a patient after significant trauma, a mediastinum that still looks wide clinically goes to CT whatever the rotation.

quiz.prompt: A frontal radiograph shows a smooth ovoid opacity in the right superior mediastinum. Its lateral margin stays crisply outlined against aerated lung as it is traced upward, remaining sharp well above the level of the clavicles. What does that tell you, and where should the next examination look?
choices: It lies posteriorly, so image the neural foramina
It lies anteriorly, so assess the thymic bed
It lies within the neck, so scan the thyroid
It lies in the middle mediastinum, near the trachea
quiz.answer: It lies posteriorly, so image the neural foramina
quiz.explain: The anterior lung stops at the clavicles, while the posterior pleural apex extends several centimetres higher into the thoracic inlet. A mass in the anterior mediastinum therefore runs out of adjacent lung at the clavicle and its border dissolves there, meeting the soft tissues of the neck; a mass sitting posteriorly still has aerated lung beside it above the clavicle and keeps a sharp edge. That is the cervicothoracic sign, and it is a depth judgement made from a single projection. The reading changes what is looked for: a posterior mediastinal mass in this position is most often neurogenic, so the follow-up study is directed at the neural exit foramina and the cord, which usually means MRI. A retrosternal goitre, the classic anterior candidate, loses its border at the clavicle and is traced up into the neck instead.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with night sweats has a PA film in which the cardiac silhouette looks grossly enlarged. Both hilar vascular shadows are still clearly visible, roughly 2 cm inside the lateral border of the enlarged shadow, and the left heart border is sharp. What does that tell you?
choices: The enlarged shadow is not the heart itself
The left atrium is enlarged behind the heart
There is a large pericardial effusion present
The pulmonary arteries are dilated centrally
quiz.answer: The enlarged shadow is not the heart itself
quiz.explain: This is the hilum overlay sign, and it is the silhouette sign used in reverse. Structures that touch each other efface each other; structures separated in depth are simply superimposed, and both are still seen. Hilar vessels visible well inside the border of a large central opacity therefore mean the opacity is not in contact with them, so it lies in front of or behind the hilum rather than arising from it. A genuinely enlarged heart, and a pericardial effusion filling the same outline, would abut the hila and push them laterally rather than leaving them projected within the shadow. In a young adult with night sweats the anterior mediastinum is where the answer lies, and the film has already told you to look there rather than at the heart.

quiz.prompt: A febrile patient's frontal film looks unremarkable. On the lateral view the thoracic vertebral bodies become progressively denser and whiter as they are followed downward towards the diaphragm, rather than progressively darker.
choices: Consolidation in a lower lobe
Consolidation of the lingula
A large anterior mediastinal mass
Air trapping in both lower lobes
quiz.answer: Consolidation in a lower lobe
quiz.explain: Descending the thoracic spine on a lateral film, there is progressively less shoulder girdle and soft tissue in the beam, so the vertebrae normally look blacker the further down you go. Anything that adds density in front of the lower spine reverses that gradient, and lower lobe consolidation is the usual cause: the spine sign. It matters because the lower lobes hide behind the heart and the diaphragm on the frontal view, which is exactly why the retrocardiac zone is a named review area and why the lateral is worth its dose. Lingular consolidation is anterior and would erase the left heart border instead. An anterior mediastinal mass fills the retrosternal clear space at the other end of the film. Air trapping makes lung blacker, not whiter.

quiz.prompt: An erect PA chest radiograph taken at full inspiration shows a maximum transverse cardiac diameter of 16.4 cm and a maximum internal transverse thoracic diameter, measured at the level of the domes of the diaphragm, of 29.8 cm. What is the cardiothoracic ratio? Give it to two decimal places. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 16.4 divided by 29.8 is 0.5503, so 0.55, and a ratio above 0.50 on a film of this kind is cardiomegaly. Each qualifier in the question is load-bearing. Erect, because supine increases pulmonary blood volume and widens the mediastinum. PA, because in an AP projection the heart lies far from the detector and is magnified. Full inspiration, because a shallow film raises the diaphragm and splays the heart transversely, which can add several centimetres of apparent width to a normal heart. And the ratio only measures a transverse shadow: concentric hypertrophy can leave it normal, a pericardial effusion can raise it with a structurally normal heart, so it is a screening observation rather than a diagnosis, and echocardiography is what settles the question.

quiz.prompt: A portable AP film is exposed with the x-ray source 100 cm from the detector, and the centre of the heart lies 20 cm in front of the detector. Treating the heart as a point object on the central ray, by what factor is its width magnified compared with an object lying against the detector? Give the factor to two decimal places. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Magnification is the source-to-detector distance divided by the source-to-object distance, that is 100 divided by 80, which is 1.25. The heart on this film is a quarter wider than it truly is, which is why a cardiothoracic ratio measured from a portable AP study routinely overcalls cardiomegaly and should not be quoted as one. Compare a departmental erect PA at 180 cm with the heart almost against the detector, perhaps 7 cm away: 180 divided by 173 is about 1.04, a four per cent magnification that the 0.50 threshold was built to tolerate. Two variables drive the difference, the shorter distance and the reversed geometry, and both are properties of the portable machine rather than of the patient.

quiz.prompt: A left lower lobe consolidation lies directly behind the heart, yet the left heart border stays sharp; a lingular consolidation of the same size erases it. Explain the physical rule that produces this difference, and state the one thing the sign gives you that a single frontal projection otherwise cannot.
quiz.answer: A border appears on a radiograph only where two tissues of different attenuation lie in contact along the path of the beam, and in the chest that means soft tissue against aerated lung. Consolidated lung has essentially the attenuation of soft tissue, so where it touches the heart the interface vanishes and the border is lost. The lingula lies immediately lateral to and in contact with the left heart border, so lingular consolidation effaces it. The left lower lobe lies posterior to the heart, and aerated lung still intervenes at the border itself, so the outline survives even though solid lung lies behind it. The sign therefore supplies depth: it localises disease to the lobe or segment that touches the effaced structure, which is anatomical information a single frontal projection has no other way to give.
quiz.explain: The rule is about contact, not about superimposition, and that is the whole of it. Disease behind a structure is superimposed on it and adds density without removing the edge; disease against a structure removes the edge. Run the map in both directions and it becomes a localiser: right heart border to middle lobe, left heart border to lingula, right hemidiaphragm to right lower lobe, left hemidiaphragm to left lower lobe, ascending aorta and superior vena cava to the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, aortic knuckle to the apicoposterior segment on the left. The same logic warns you off the two failure modes: a border that is lost because the film is rotated or under-inspired rather than because lung is diseased, and a normal variant in which a hemidiaphragm border is faint because of an interposed colon.

quiz.prompt: A portable AP film in a septic 70-year-old is reported as showing cardiomegaly with bibasal pulmonary oedema. Before accepting that report, name four technical features of the film you would assess, and for each say how it can manufacture that appearance in a normal chest.
quiz.answer: Projection: an AP portable film magnifies the anteriorly placed heart by around a fifth to a quarter, so the cardiothoracic ratio is not valid and a normal heart looks big. Inspiration: a shallow film, with fewer than five to six anterior or nine to ten posterior ribs above the hemidiaphragm, raises the diaphragms, crowds the lower zone vessels into apparent basal shadowing and splays the heart transversely. Position: supine, blood redistributes to the upper zones and mimics the upper lobe diversion of cardiac failure, and any pleural fluid layers posteriorly as a diffuse haze rather than as a meniscus. Rotation: an obliqued mediastinum looks wide and one hilum looks prominent. Exposure and penetration: an underexposed film makes lungs look uniformly opaque and adds interstitial markings that are not there, and an overexposed one erases them. The remedy is to compare with a previous film of comparable technique, and to state the technical limitation in the report rather than to report through it.
quiz.explain: Every technical fault on a chest radiograph has a disease it imitates, which is why technique is assessed first and not as a courtesy at the end. The four faults here converge on one clinical picture, and a single film carrying all four will show a big heart, upper zone vessels, hazy bases and a wide mediastinum in a patient with normal lungs. Reading in the other direction is just as important: the same faults hide disease, since a shallow film buries a lower lobe behind the diaphragm and an overexposed one erases a fine reticular pattern. What makes the report defensible is the comparison. Serial portable films in the same patient are read as a series against each other, and a change in technique between two of them is the commonest reason a chest appears to have changed overnight.

quiz.prompt: A chest radiograph reported as normal is shown three months later to have contained a 2 cm cancer. Name four review areas where an overlying structure hides lung, and for each give one finding it characteristically conceals.
quiz.answer: The apices, where the clavicles, the first ribs and the overlying soft tissues obscure lung: an apical tumour or a small pneumothorax hides here. The retrocardiac region, where the heart overlies the left lower lobe: consolidation, a collapsed left lower lobe behind the heart, and a hiatus hernia are missed here, and the lateral view rescues them. Below the diaphragms, which are part of the film: free subphrenic gas, a raised hemidiaphragm and basal disease projected below the domes. The hila, where normal vessels are dense enough to hide a nodal mass or a central tumour, and where comparison of size, density and position between the two sides is the only defence. Beyond those four, the bones and soft tissues carry rib and shoulder lesions, absent breast shadows and surgical emphysema, and the lung periphery beyond the lung markings carries the pleural line of a small pneumothorax. The common feature is that all of them are looked at after the reader believes they have finished.
quiz.explain: Satisfaction of search is the real mechanism behind most missed lesions, and a fixed review sequence is the only reliable countermeasure, because it runs whether or not the reader has already found something. The areas are not arbitrary. They are precisely the places where a dense structure is superimposed on lung, so that a lesion has to be more conspicuous than usual to be seen. Two practical additions make the sequence work: comparing the two sides directly, since the chest is nearly symmetrical and asymmetry is easier to see than abnormality, and always comparing with the oldest available previous film rather than only the most recent, since a nodule that grew slowly is invisible against yesterday and obvious against three years ago.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral chest radiograph, at the level of the mid-heart, put these structures in order from the most anterior to the most posterior.
quiz.answer: sternum right-ventricle left-atrium descending-aorta vertebral-body
quiz.explain: The lateral view exists to supply the depth the frontal view cannot. Behind the sternum lies the retrosternal clear space, which should be dark down to the level where the right ventricle meets the anterior chest wall; a filled retrosternal space is an anterior mediastinal mass until proven otherwise. The right ventricle forms the anterior cardiac border, the left atrium the posterosuperior one, and behind them the descending aorta runs down in front of the spine, with the retrocardiac clear space between the posterior heart border and the spine. That anterior-to-posterior sequence is what turns a lateral into a localiser: an opacity that overlies the vertebral bodies and stops them darkening downward is posterior, one that fills the space behind the sternum is anterior, and one that does neither but obscures the heart border is beside the heart.

nodes.title: HRCT of the Lung
nodes.goal: Name the elementary HRCT patterns from the images, use nodule distribution and an expiratory series to narrow the cause, and place a fibrotic scan into the UIP categories.

quiz.prompt: On a 1 mm axial section the right upper lobe is uniformly hazier than the left. Pulmonary vessels and the walls of the segmental bronchi are still visible running through the haze, no bronchus is outlined by surrounding density, and the appearance persists unchanged on a prone series. Which reading follows?
choices: Ground-glass opacity, not consolidation
Consolidation with air bronchograms
Dependent atelectasis of the segment
Volume averaging from a thick slice
quiz.answer: Ground-glass opacity, not consolidation
quiz.explain: The distinction is made on what survives the haze. Ground glass raises attenuation without replacing the air, so vessels and bronchial walls are still traced through it; consolidation replaces the air, obliterates the vessels, and reveals bronchi as air bronchograms precisely because everything around them is now dense. The other two options are the technical mimics that the vignette has already excluded. Dependent atelectasis is common in the posterior basal lung, looks exactly like ground glass, and disappears when the patient turns over, which is the whole reason for the prone series. Partial volume averaging in a thick section blurs fine reticulation into apparent haze, and is excluded by the 1 mm reconstruction. Ground glass itself is not a diagnosis: it can be infiltration, oedema, haemorrhage, or fine fibrosis below the resolution of the scan, and its company decides which.

quiz.prompt: Inspiratory HRCT shows sharply demarcated geographic regions of low and high attenuation. On the expiratory series the darker regions do not change in attenuation or volume, while the denser regions become denser still and shrink. The vessels running through the darker regions are smaller than those elsewhere. What has the expiratory series established?
choices: Air trapping from small airways disease
Infiltrative ground-glass in the dense areas
Reduced perfusion from chronic thromboembolism
Motion artefact between the two acquisitions
quiz.answer: Air trapping from small airways disease
quiz.explain: Lung that behaves normally empties on expiration: it loses volume and rises in attenuation. Lobules whose supplying bronchioles are obstructed cannot empty, so they stay dark and stay the same size, and that fixed attenuation is the definition of air trapping. The vessel calibre had already told you which lung was abnormal. In small airways disease the lucent regions are the diseased ones and their vessels are narrowed by hypoxic vasoconstriction, whereas in infiltrative disease the dense regions are the diseased ones and vessel calibre is equal in both. Mosaic perfusion in chronic thromboembolic disease also shows lucent regions with small vessels, which is why the inspiratory scan alone cannot separate the two, and it is the expiratory series that does: perfused-but-ventilated lung still empties normally. In that direction, look also for an enlarged central pulmonary artery, mural thrombus and dilated bronchial arteries.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old with a dry cough and no occupational dust exposure has HRCT showing small nodules strung along the fissures, the subpleural surfaces and the bronchovascular bundles, most numerous in the upper and mid zones, together with symmetrical hilar and right paratracheal nodal enlargement. Which diagnosis does that combination favour?
choices: Sarcoidosis of the lung
Miliary tuberculosis
Lymphangitic carcinoma
Silicosis of the lung
quiz.answer: Sarcoidosis of the lung
quiz.explain: Nodules that follow the fissures, the pleural surface and the bronchovascular bundles are perilymphatic, because those are where the lung's lymphatics run, and that distribution narrows the field to sarcoidosis, silicosis and coal worker's disease, and lymphangitic spread of carcinoma. Upper and mid zone predominance with symmetrical hilar and paratracheal nodal enlargement in a young adult is sarcoidosis. Silicosis produces an almost identical perilymphatic upper zone picture and can calcify its nodes in an eggshell pattern, so the discriminator is the occupational history the vignette explicitly removes, which is worth remembering as the reason that history must be asked for. Lymphangitic carcinoma thickens the interlobular septa nodularly, is often basal and asymmetrical, and comes with a known primary. Miliary tuberculosis is random rather than perilymphatic: uniform 1 to 3 mm nodules scattered without regard to lobular anatomy, some abutting the pleura and some in the middle of a lobule.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old pigeon fancier has HRCT showing profuse ill-defined ground-glass nodules a few millimetres across, sitting in the centres of the secondary lobules and sparing the pleural and fissural surfaces, with patchy lobular areas of low attenuation that persist on expiration. Which reading fits?
choices: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Perilymphatic sarcoid nodules
Haematogenous lung metastases
Endobronchial spread of TB
quiz.answer: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
quiz.explain: Centrilobular nodules sit a few millimetres away from the pleura, the fissures and the interlobular septa, because the structure at the centre of the secondary lobule is the terminal bronchiole with its accompanying arteriole. Anything arriving by air lands there. Ill-defined ground-glass centrilobular nodules combined with lobular air trapping, in a person with an inhaled antigen exposure, is the classic non-fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis picture: cellular bronchiolitis fills the lobular centres and partial bronchiolar obstruction traps air in whole lobules. Sarcoid nodules are perilymphatic and would sit on the fissures the vignette says are spared. Haematogenous metastases arrive by blood, so they are random and favour the lung bases where perfusion is greatest. Endobronchial tuberculosis is also centrilobular, but it is dense and branching, the tree-in-bud of impacted bronchioles, rather than ground-glass, and it usually comes with cavitation elsewhere.

quiz.prompt: A fibrotic CT shows, in the upper lobes, subpleural lucencies lying in a single row against the pleura, thin-walled and without distortion of the adjacent vessels. In the lower lobes there are clustered cystic spaces of similar diameter, stacked several layers deep and sharing their walls, with traction bronchiolectasis running into them. Which reading of the lucencies is correct?
choices: Paraseptal emphysema above, honeycombing below
Honeycombing in both upper and lower lobes
Paraseptal emphysema throughout both lungs
Traction bronchiectasis mistaken for cysts
quiz.answer: Paraseptal emphysema above, honeycombing below
quiz.explain: Honeycombing is defined by architecture, not by the presence of holes: clustered cystic airspaces of broadly similar diameter, usually a few millimetres to about a centimetre, subpleural, sharing their walls, and stacked in rows two or more layers deep, in lung that is distorted. Paraseptal emphysema is a single subpleural layer of lucencies separated by intact interlobular septa, upper zone predominant, with no distortion of the surrounding lung and no traction on the airways. Getting the pair the wrong way round is one of the commonest sources of interobserver disagreement in fibrosis reporting, and it is not cosmetic: honeycombing is the single feature that separates a UIP pattern from a probable UIP pattern, so a misread row of emphysematous spaces can promote a scan to definite UIP and start a patient on antifibrotic treatment for a disease they may not have.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with bibasal crackles and restrictive spirometry has HRCT showing reticulation with peripheral traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis, subpleural and basal in distribution, a little superimposed ground glass, and no clustered cystic spaces anywhere. Which category does the 2018 international guideline place this scan in?
choices: A probable UIP pattern
A definite UIP pattern
Indeterminate for UIP
An alternative diagnosis
quiz.answer: A probable UIP pattern
quiz.explain: The guideline sorts a scan into UIP, probable UIP, indeterminate for UIP, or a pattern suggesting an alternative diagnosis. Subpleural and basal predominant reticulation with peripheral traction bronchiectasis or bronchiolectasis, with mild ground glass permitted and honeycombing absent, is probable UIP; honeycombing is what would have made it UIP. Indeterminate is reserved for a scan with subtle subpleural basal fibrosis that will not commit either way, or one whose features are mildly discordant. An alternative diagnosis is called when the scan says something else outright, through upper or mid zone predominance, a peribronchovascular distribution, extensive ground glass, profuse micronodules, discrete cysts, widespread mosaic attenuation and air trapping, or consolidation. The categories matter because they carry management: a UIP pattern in the right clinical setting is accepted as a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without surgical lung biopsy, and a probable UIP pattern, after multidisciplinary discussion in a patient with no exposure and no connective tissue disease, very often is too.

quiz.prompt: A fibrotic HRCT is upper and mid zone predominant with a peribronchovascular distribution, and on the inspiratory images three distinct densities coexist within a single section: normal lung, ground glass, and sharply demarcated lobular lucency. Which reading does the pattern support?
choices: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Fibrotic NSIP from scleroderma
Sarcoid fibrosis of the upper zones
quiz.answer: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis
quiz.explain: Three densities in one section is the sign that hypersensitivity pneumonitis does two things at once: it infiltrates the lung, giving ground glass, and it obstructs bronchioles, giving lobular air trapping, and it leaves normal lung between the two. The 2020 international guideline names this three-density pattern on the inspiratory series as typical of fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which is useful precisely because it does not require an expiratory scan to be recognised. Zonal distribution argues the same way: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is basal and subpleural, and an upper and mid zone peribronchovascular fibrosis is not it. Fibrotic NSIP is basal, is often strikingly subpleural-sparing, and shows ground glass with fine reticulation rather than lobular lucency. Sarcoid fibrosis is also upper zone and peribronchovascular, but it comes with perilymphatic nodules, nodal enlargement and traction of the hila upward.

quiz.prompt: An older HRCT protocol acquires 1 mm axial sections at 10 mm intervals through the chest, rather than a volumetric dataset. What percentage of the lung volume appears in the images? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: One millimetre out of every ten is imaged, so nine tenths of the lung is not represented at all. The technique was designed for diffuse disease, where a sample of the lung answers the question, and it fails for anything focal: a 6 mm nodule lying between two sections does not exist. That is why volumetric thin-section acquisition, reconstructed at about 1 mm with a sharp high-spatial-frequency kernel, has become the default. It gives the same interstitial detail, plus coronal and sagittal reformats that show the craniocaudal gradient on which the UIP categories depend, maximum intensity projections that transform the assessment of nodule profusion and distribution, and minimum intensity projections that make mosaic attenuation and air trapping conspicuous. What volumetric acquisition does not replace are the two supplementary series: prone images, to separate dependent atelectasis from early subpleural fibrosis, and expiratory images, without which air trapping is invisible.

quiz.prompt: A report describes mosaic attenuation and stops there. Set out the three families of cause, the vessel-calibre clue that separates the first from the third, and the extra acquisition that settles the question.
quiz.answer: Mosaic attenuation has three families of cause: small airways disease with air trapping, occlusive vascular disease with mosaic perfusion, and patchy infiltrative disease in which it is the denser lung that is abnormal. In the first two the lucent lung is the diseased lung and its vessels are reduced in calibre relative to those in the denser regions, because ventilation or perfusion is reduced there; in infiltrative disease vessel calibre is equal in the two, because the dense areas are ground glass rather than the lucent areas being underperfused. The acquisition that settles it is an expiratory series. Lobules with air trapping fail to increase in attenuation and fail to reduce in volume, while all normally ventilated lung, including the lung of mosaic perfusion and of infiltrative disease, becomes uniformly denser. Chronic thromboembolic disease is then supported by an enlarged central pulmonary artery, mural or webbed thrombus, and dilated bronchial arteries.
quiz.explain: Mosaic attenuation is a description, and left as a description it is nearly useless to the referrer, because the three causes lead to a bronchodilator, an anticoagulant or an immunosuppressant. Two observations do almost all the work of separating them. The first is deciding which lung is abnormal, and vessel calibre answers it: reduced vessels mark the abnormal lucent lung of airways or vascular disease, equal vessels mark ground glass as the abnormality. The second is the expiratory series, which is the only way to demonstrate air trapping and costs one extra breath-hold at low dose. Two cautions belong with them. Dependent lung in a normal patient is denser and can be mistaken for a mosaic, which prone imaging resolves. And a small amount of air trapping in the dependent lower lobes, particularly in older people and smokers, is a normal finding, so the sign has to be geographic and out of proportion before it is reported as disease.

quiz.prompt: Two thoracic radiologists agree about everything on a fibrotic HRCT except whether one row of subpleural lucencies is honeycombing. Explain concretely what hangs on that single disagreement.
quiz.answer: Honeycombing is the feature that separates a UIP pattern from a probable UIP pattern, given that the rest of the scan is subpleural and basal and nothing suggests an alternative diagnosis. A UIP pattern, in the right clinical context and after multidisciplinary discussion, is accepted as sufficient to diagnose idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without surgical lung biopsy. A probable UIP pattern keeps bronchoalveolar lavage or surgical biopsy on the table for some patients and moves more of the weight of the diagnosis onto the multidisciplinary meeting and the clinical picture. The error in the other direction matters just as much: calling paraseptal emphysema or clustered traction bronchiolectasis honeycombing overdiagnoses UIP, and can commit a patient with a different, potentially treatable fibrosing disease to antifibrotic therapy and to a prognosis that is not theirs. So the disagreement decides an invasive test, a drug and a prognosis, which is why the honest report describes the morphology in detail and takes the case to the meeting rather than asserting the label.
quiz.explain: Interobserver agreement on honeycombing is famously imperfect, and the guideline is built in the knowledge of that, which is why it defines the term by architecture and why the multidisciplinary discussion, not the radiologist alone, makes the diagnosis. Two practical habits reduce the disagreement. The first is to check the morphology against the definition every time rather than by gestalt: stacked layers, shared walls, similar diameters, subpleural, in distorted lung. The second is to look at the coronal reformats and the upper zones before committing, because emphysema declares itself by its zonal distribution and by the absence of traction, and traction bronchiolectasis declares itself by continuity with an airway when it is tracked across contiguous slices.

quiz.prompt: A request asks you to exclude pulmonary fibrosis from a routine contrast-enhanced chest CT reconstructed at 5 mm with a soft tissue kernel. Say why the existing data cannot answer it, and specify what an HRCT protocol adds and what each addition is for.
quiz.answer: Thick sections apply partial volume averaging across a whole secondary lobule, so fine reticulation is smeared into apparent ground glass and small honeycomb cysts are unreadable, and a soft tissue kernel deliberately removes the high spatial frequencies that the fine interstitium is made of. HRCT means thin sections of about 1 mm reconstructed with a sharp kernel, in current practice from a volumetric acquisition so that coronal and sagittal reformats show the craniocaudal gradient on which the pattern categories depend, and maximum intensity projections show nodule profusion and distribution. Prone images are added to distinguish dependent atelectasis in the posterior basal subpleural lung, which disappears when the patient turns over, from early subpleural fibrosis, which does not. Expiratory images are added because air trapping cannot be seen on inspiration at all. Intravenous contrast is unnecessary and can be a nuisance, since dense enhancing vessels obscure fine peripheral detail, and the dose of a dedicated study is spent on the questions the referrer actually asked.
quiz.explain: The two reconstruction parameters are not interchangeable with each other or with anything else, and they are the reason a routine chest CT is not a low-grade HRCT but a different examination. Slice thickness sets how much lung is averaged into a voxel, and the secondary pulmonary lobule is only one to two and a half centimetres across, so a 5 mm section averages structures the diagnosis depends on. The kernel sets which spatial frequencies survive reconstruction, and a soft kernel is chosen for mediastinal soft tissue precisely because it suppresses the frequencies that fine lung detail occupies. Both can be re-reconstructed from raw data if it still exists, which is always worth asking before the patient is recalled. The prone and expiratory series cannot be recovered that way, because they are acquisitions rather than reconstructions, and that is the practical reason to protocol the study properly at the outset.

quiz.prompt: The 2018 international guideline sorts the HRCT appearance in suspected idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis into four categories. Put them in order, from the appearance that argues most strongly for a UIP pattern to the one that argues against it.
quiz.answer: UIP probable-UIP indeterminate alternative-diagnosis
quiz.explain: UIP: subpleural and basal predominant fibrosis, often heterogeneous, with honeycombing, with or without peripheral traction bronchiectasis. Probable UIP: the same distribution with reticulation and peripheral traction bronchiectasis or bronchiolectasis, mild ground glass permitted, but no honeycombing. Indeterminate: subtle subpleural basal fibrosis that will not commit, or fibrosis with a few features that sit awkwardly with UIP. Alternative diagnosis: findings that point elsewhere, such as upper or mid zone predominance, a peribronchovascular or perilymphatic distribution, extensive ground glass, profuse micronodules, discrete cysts, widespread mosaic attenuation with air trapping, or consolidation. The ladder is a statement about diagnostic confidence rather than about disease severity, and the rungs carry different consequences for whether tissue is needed, which is what makes the ordering worth knowing rather than merely worth reciting.

nodes.title: The Incidental Pulmonary Nodule
nodes.goal: Measure an incidental nodule to the Fleischner convention, judge solid from subsolid, and give the follow-up the guidance recommends or say why it does not apply.

quiz.prompt: A 63-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a CT pulmonary angiogram for pleuritic pain, negative for embolus. It shows a single solid nodule in the right lower lobe with a mean diameter of 4 mm, smooth margins and no calcification. There is no known malignancy and no immunosuppression. What does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend?
choices: An optional single CT at 12 months
A CT at 6 months and at 18 months
A CT at 3 months, then PET-CT
Immediate biopsy of the nodule
quiz.answer: An optional single CT at 12 months
quiz.explain: For a single solid nodule under 6 mm, low-risk patients need no routine follow-up, and high-risk patients are offered an optional CT at 12 months. The word optional carries the argument: even in a heavy smoker a nodule this size has under about a one per cent chance of being a cancer, so the recommendation is a discussion rather than an instruction, and features such as an upper lobe location, spiculation, coexisting emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history legitimately tip an individual decision. The 6 to 12 month schedule with a second scan at 18 to 24 months belongs to the 6 to 8 mm band, and going straight to PET-CT or biopsy at 4 mm subjects the patient to tests that cannot answer the question at that size. Note also what the study is: an incidental finding on a scan done for something else, which is the only setting the guidance addresses.

quiz.prompt: A first CT in a 60-year-old shows a solitary part-solid nodule in the left upper lobe, 14 mm overall with a 4 mm solid component. There are no symptoms of infection and no prior imaging exists. What is the next step?
choices: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
PET-CT to assess the solid component
CT-guided biopsy of the solid part
Lobectomy for presumed adenocarcinoma
quiz.answer: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
quiz.explain: The first duty with any subsolid nodule seen once is to establish that it is real and persistent, because a large proportion of subsolid opacities are transient: infection, haemorrhage, focal inflammation and organising pneumonia all look like this and are gone in three months. So a repeat thin-section CT at 3 to 6 months precedes any decision. If it persists with a solid component still under 6 mm, annual CT for five years follows, since a persistent part-solid nodule is often on the adenocarcinoma spectrum but grows slowly and the solid part is the invasive part. PET-CT at a 4 mm solid component is below the useful resolution of the technique and lepidic tumour is poorly avid in any case; percutaneous biopsy of a 4 mm target is unreliable; and resecting before persistence is established treats a proportion of patients for pneumonia they have already recovered from.

quiz.prompt: A persistent 12 mm pure ground-glass nodule is referred with a request for PET-CT to confirm that it is benign. The nodule shows no FDG uptake above background lung. How should that result be used?
choices: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
It confirms the nodule is benign, so discharge
It shows the nodule is inflammatory, repeat in 3 months
It means the nodule should be resected without delay
quiz.answer: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
quiz.explain: FDG uptake tracks glucose metabolism and, in practice, viable cell density. A persistent pure ground-glass nodule is characteristically atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, adenocarcinoma in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, all of which grow along intact alveolar walls with very little cellular bulk, so a negative scan is expected whether the lesion is benign or malignant, and it carries almost no information. Acting on it ends a surveillance programme that the guidance asks to run to five years, and the thing being watched for over those years is the appearance or growth of a solid component. PET-CT earns its place with solid nodules above roughly 8 mm, and even there it has the mirror-image problem of false positives from granulomatous and other inflammatory disease. Small size and low cell density are its two blind spots, and this nodule has both.

quiz.prompt: A CT report flags a new 5 mm nodule. On review it is a smooth, homogeneous, lentiform solid nodule in the right lower zone, in contact with the oblique fissure with its long axis lying along the fissure, and it has a thin linear tail running to the pleura. It was present at the same size on a scan four years earlier. What follow-up is needed?
choices: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
A CT at 12 months for stability
A CT at 3 months, then 12 months
PET-CT to characterise it further
quiz.answer: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
quiz.explain: A typical perifissural nodule is an intrapulmonary lymph node: solid, smooth, homogeneous, oval or triangular, in contact with or within a few millimetres of a fissure or the pleura, usually below the level of the carina, and often with a septal tail running to the pleural surface. In screening cohorts these have proved essentially never to be malignant, and the guidance exempts them from follow-up on morphology alone. Four years of stability settles the matter independently, since two years of unchanged size is the conventional evidence of benignity for a solid nodule. That convention is worth keeping separate in your mind from subsolid disease, where it does not hold: adenocarcinoma in situ can sit unchanged for years, so two years of stability in a ground-glass nodule proves nothing.

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm solid nodule found incidentally contains a focus measuring -70 HU on a region of interest placed on a thin section, together with a coarse central clump of calcification. What follows?
choices: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
The low attenuation indicates a cavity
This appearance requires PET-CT staging
This warrants CT again in 3 to 6 months
quiz.answer: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
quiz.explain: Macroscopic fat inside a pulmonary nodule, conventionally in the region of -40 to -120 HU, is close to diagnostic of a hamartoma, and with coarse popcorn-like calcification the diagnosis is secure and the nodule needs no follow-up at all. The rare exceptions worth knowing are lipoid pneumonia and fat-containing metastases from liposarcoma or renal cell carcinoma, which do not resemble this. Two cautions govern the measurement. It must be made on thin sections, because partial volume averaging with adjacent air can fabricate a fat-like value in a small nodule. And the calcification pattern must be one of the benign ones, which are central, laminated, diffusely solid and popcorn: eccentric or stippled calcium does not exclude malignancy, since a carcinoma can engulf a pre-existing granuloma. Recognising the nodule that needs nothing is as much a part of the algorithm as recognising the one that needs everything.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old two years after renal transplantation, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, has three new solid nodules of 4 to 5 mm on a CT performed for fever. A trainee proposes an optional CT at 12 months, quoting the Fleischner recommendations. What is wrong with that?
choices: The guideline excludes patients like this one
The nodules are multiple, so the interval halves
The nodules are too small to be measured reliably
The patient's age puts her in the low-risk column
quiz.answer: The guideline excludes patients like this one
quiz.explain: The 2017 recommendations apply to incidental nodules in immunocompetent patients aged 35 and over who have no known primary malignancy, and they explicitly do not apply within a lung cancer screening programme, where a structured reporting system takes over. This patient fails on two counts, and each on its own would be enough. Immunosuppressed, new nodules with fever are an infection question until proved otherwise, and invasive fungal disease, nocardia, mycobacteria and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder are answered in days by a repeat scan, bronchoscopy or empirical treatment, not in a year. Under 35, the prior probability of lung cancer is low and the accumulated radiation of surveillance is comparatively costly, so benign and infective causes are managed clinically. Knowing when an algorithm does not apply is the part of it that most often gets skipped.

quiz.prompt: A part-solid nodule under annual surveillance measures 15 mm overall on this year's scan and on last year's, but its solid component has gone from 4 mm to 9 mm over those 12 months. The patient has no new symptoms. What should happen?
choices: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
Continue annual CT to complete five years
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm growth
Treat for infection and rescan in 6 weeks
quiz.answer: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
quiz.explain: In a part-solid nodule the solid component is the invasive component, and it drives both the risk and, if this becomes a cancer diagnosis, the T category. A growing solid component, or one reaching 8 mm, takes the nodule out of surveillance and into PET-CT, sampling or resection. The trap the case is built around is that the overall diameter never changed: had only the total size been recorded, the nodule would have been called stable and left for another year, which is why the solid component is measured separately on every study, on the same thin-section lung-window images. Waiting a further three months to confirm growth repeats a measurement already made over a whole year and delays treatment of a lesion that has declared itself. At 9 mm the solid component is also large enough for PET-CT to be informative, which it was not when the component was 4 mm.

quiz.prompt: On a 1 mm axial section an incidental solid nodule measures 7.0 mm along its long axis and 3.8 mm along the perpendicular short axis on the same image. Applying the Fleischner measurement convention, what size in millimetres is recorded for this nodule? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The convention is the average of the long-axis and short-axis diameters obtained on the same image, rounded to the nearest whole millimetre, measured on thin sections in a lung window. Here 7.0 and 3.8 average to 5.4, which is recorded as 5 mm, and that places an elongated nodule whose longest measurement is 7 mm below the 6 mm threshold, so a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up. Reporting the long axis alone would have committed the same patient to a year of surveillance for the same lesion. The convention exists because it is reproducible rather than because it is the truth about the object: a nodule is not a sphere, and averaging two orthogonal diameters is simply a rule two readers can both follow. Semi-automated volumetry is more reproducible again, and the guidance gives the equivalents, roughly 100 cubic millimetres at 6 mm and 250 at 8 mm, for departments that measure volume instead.

quiz.prompt: A solid nodule has a mean diameter of 6.0 mm. Treating it as a sphere, what mean diameter in millimetres corresponds to exactly one doubling of its volume? Give it to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Volume scales with the cube of diameter, so a doubling needs a diameter multiplied by the cube root of two, that is 1.26: 6.0 becomes 7.56, or 7.6 mm to one decimal place. The lesson is in how small that step is. A whole doubling of tumour volume shows up as 1.6 mm on a ruler, which is inside the interobserver variability of manual measurement of a small nodule, so a solid nodule can double without any reader being able to prove it, and two readers can disagree about growth that never happened. That is the argument for volumetry, which measures the quantity that is actually doubling, and for long enough intervals that real growth outruns the noise. Volume doubling times of roughly 100 to 400 days characterise most solid lung cancers; much faster than that suggests infection or inflammation, and much slower suggests a benign lesion or an indolent subsolid tumour, whose doubling times commonly run to several years.

quiz.prompt: A solitary pure ground-glass nodule of 9 mm is still present and unchanged on the confirmatory CT performed at 9 months. Counting from the first scan, for how many years in total does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend that surveillance continue? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A solitary ground-glass nodule of 6 mm or more gets a CT at 6 to 12 months to confirm that it persists, then CT every two years out to five years in total. Persistence has ruled out infection and haemorrhage; it has emphatically not ruled out tumour, because the lesions that produce a persistent ground-glass nodule grow so slowly that the two-year stability rule used for solid nodules carries no weight here. Five years is not a claim that risk falls to zero afterwards, but a judgement about the yield of continued scanning against its radiation and cost. What the surveillance is watching for is a change in character rather than a change in size: the appearance of a solid component, or the growth of one, is the event that signals invasion and moves the patient from watching to treatment.

quiz.prompt: The 2017 revision moved the threshold below which no routine follow-up is advised from 4 mm up to 6 mm. Justify that change, and say what it implies for a 5 mm solid nodule in a heavy smoker.
quiz.answer: The evidence, largely from screening cohorts, is that a solid nodule under 6 mm carries a risk of malignancy below about one per cent even in high-risk people, and that a year of CT surveillance changes very little for such a nodule, because growth of that magnitude sits inside the measurement noise and because a cancer that small is usually still curable when it later declares itself. Set against that near-zero yield are real costs: the radiation of repeated scans, the financial cost, the anxiety of being under surveillance, and the cascade of further imaging and procedures that follows a followed nodule. Raising the threshold therefore removes surveillance from a very large number of people with little loss of cancer detection. For a 5 mm nodule in a heavy smoker the guidance offers an optional CT at 12 months rather than requiring one: the judgement is handed to the clinician and the patient, and an upper lobe location, spiculation, emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history are legitimate reasons for an individual to take it.
quiz.explain: A threshold in a guideline is a statement about the balance of harms rather than a claim about biology, and reading it that way explains both the change and the hedging around it. Below 6 mm the yield of surveillance is so low that the harms of scanning dominate, so the recommendation is withdrawn; the nodules did not become safer in 2017. It also explains why the high-risk column says optional rather than recommended: at that risk level the decision is genuinely close, and the guideline declines to make it for the patient. The corollary for reporting is to give the referrer what the decision needs, which is the mean diameter measured by the convention, the solid or subsolid character, the location, the margin, and an explicit statement of which follow-up row the nodule falls in, rather than a bare description of a nodule.

quiz.prompt: A nodule reported as 7 mm last year is reported as 9 mm today, and the patient is referred as growing. Before accepting growth, list the conditions that must match between the two measurements, and say which single technique removes most of the remaining disagreement.
quiz.answer: Both measurements should come from thin sections, ideally 1 mm and at most about 1.5 mm, displayed in a lung window with comparable settings, made by the same convention, which is the average of long and short axis on the same image, and read in the same plane; a nodule measured on a 5 mm series last year against a 1 mm series today will appear to change for purely technical reasons, and partial volume averaging in the thicker series usually understates it. Respiratory phase and patient positioning should be comparable, since a nodule in dependent lung can be measured differently in atelectatic surroundings. Above all, the prior images should be re-measured personally rather than the previous report's number being taken on trust, since the two numbers being compared were produced by different readers. Manual diameter carries an interobserver variability of a millimetre or two, which is the same size as the change being argued about, and semi-automated volumetry is substantially more reproducible: it measures the quantity that actually doubles, and expresses change as a volume doubling time.
quiz.explain: Most reported growth in small nodules is measurement, not biology, and the discipline that prevents the error is comparing like with like and doing the comparison yourself. Two habits carry most of the benefit. First, always open the prior study rather than reading its report, because the number in a report is a different reader's judgement on possibly different data. Second, state the technique the measurement came from in your own report, so that whoever compares next year knows what to match. The deeper point is about what growth means once established: a change in diameter is hard to interpret, whereas a volume doubling time places the lesion on a scale where roughly 100 to 400 days is typical of solid malignancy, faster suggests inflammation, and much slower suggests something indolent or benign.

quiz.prompt: An incidental solid nodule is found on a CT performed for another reason. Put these five decisions in the order that gets the follow-up right, beginning with the one that can stop the algorithm before any measurement is made.
quiz.answer: eligibility benign-morphology solid-or-subsolid mean-diameter patient-risk
quiz.explain: First, whether the guidance applies to this patient at all: under 35, immunosuppressed, a known primary malignancy, or a nodule found within a screening programme, and it does not, so any table you consult afterwards gives the wrong answer confidently. Second, whether the nodule is already diagnosed by its morphology, since fat with popcorn calcification makes a hamartoma, a benign calcification pattern makes a granuloma, and a typical perifissural nodule makes an intrapulmonary lymph node, and each of these ends the matter with no follow-up at all. Third, solid or subsolid, because the two run on different tables and different timescales. Fourth, the mean diameter by the averaging convention, which selects the row. And last, the patient's risk category, which chooses between columns and, in the smallest band, between an optional scan and none. Risk comes last because it modifies a recommendation rather than generating one, and applying it first is how a heavy smoker with an obvious hamartoma ends up in five years of surveillance.

nodes.title: Staging Lung Cancer on Imaging
nodes.goal: Assign T, N and M from the images, place a node in its IASLC station, and identify the findings that change the treatment plan.

quiz.prompt: A 3 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma is accompanied by a single FDG-avid node of 12 mm short axis in the left lower paratracheal region, with no other abnormality on PET-CT. The team asks whether lobectomy should still go ahead.
choices: It is N3, so sample it before abandoning surgery
It is N2, so proceed to mediastinoscopy
It is N1, so proceed to lobectomy as planned
It is M1a, so treat as metastatic disease
quiz.answer: It is N3, so sample it before abandoning surgery
quiz.explain: Station 4L is contralateral mediastinum for a right-sided primary, and contralateral mediastinal nodes are N3, which takes a patient off a primary surgical pathway. But avidity is not tissue. Granulomatous disease, anthracosis and nodes reacting downstream of an obstructed bronchus are all FDG-avid, and the positive predictive value of PET in the mediastinum is only moderate, so the single finding that would convert a resectable patient into an unresectable one is exactly the finding that must be proved. Endobronchial ultrasound reaches station 4L, and a negative needle result in a node with this much riding on it is followed by surgical staging rather than accepted. The converse discipline is just as important: normal-sized, PET-negative mediastinal nodes still conceal metastasis in a minority, which is why central tumours, large tumours and N1 disease go to invasive staging even after a clean PET-CT.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a right lower lobe carcinoma has an enlarged pretracheal node. It lies anterior to the trachea, its centre is a little to the left of the midline of the body, but it lies entirely to the right of the left lateral border of the trachea. How is it classified on the IASLC map?
choices: Station 4R, and therefore N2 disease
Station 4L, and therefore N3 disease
Station 3a, and therefore N2 disease
Station 10R, and therefore N1 disease
quiz.answer: Station 4R, and therefore N2 disease
quiz.explain: The IASLC map deliberately does not use the body midline to divide right from left paratracheal nodes. For stations 2 and 4 the boundary is the left lateral border of the trachea, so a node in front of the trachea and to the right of that line is 4R however it looks against the anatomical midline. The consequence is not academic: for a right-sided tumour, 4R is ipsilateral mediastinal, N2, and remains within a multimodality plan that can be given with curative intent, while 4L would be N3. Station 3a is prevascular, anterior to the great vessels and not in contact with the trachea. Station 10R is hilar, beginning below the lower border of the azygos vein where station 4R ends, and hilar nodes are N1. Naming the station rather than describing the node loosely is what lets the next person choose a sampling route.

quiz.prompt: A 4.5 cm left lower lobe squamous carcinoma has a small ipsilateral pleural effusion on CT, with no visible pleural nodularity or thickening. The plan is surgery or chemoradiotherapy depending on stage. What does the effusion require?
choices: Sampling, because it may make the disease M1a
Nothing, because it lacks pleural nodularity
Drainage, because it will limit radiotherapy
Repeat CT, because it may resolve on its own
quiz.answer: Sampling, because it may make the disease M1a
quiz.explain: A malignant pleural or pericardial effusion, and pleural or pericardial nodules, are M1a, which removes curative resection from consideration, so this is one of the highest-consequence findings on a staging CT. Most effusions in lung cancer are malignant, and the absence of visible nodularity does not exclude pleural deposits, which are commonly a few millimetres and below the resolution of the study. The classification is explicit about the exception: where the fluid is not blood-stained, is not an exudate, and repeated cytology is negative, and where clinical judgement attributes it to something else such as obstructive pneumonitis or cardiac failure, the effusion is excluded as a staging element. So cytology decides, not CT, and in an otherwise operable patient with repeatedly negative cytology, thoracoscopy is the next step rather than an assumption in either direction.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT in a patient with a 3.5 cm lung cancer shows a 2.4 cm left adrenal nodule and nothing else outside the chest. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Measure its unenhanced attenuation first
Call it M1b and treat as stage IV disease
Biopsy the adrenal gland under CT guidance
Proceed to surgery and monitor the adrenal
quiz.answer: Measure its unenhanced attenuation first
quiz.explain: Adrenal nodules are common in the general population, and most adrenal nodules in patients with lung cancer are still adenomas. An unenhanced attenuation of 10 HU or less establishes a lipid-rich adenoma; chemical-shift MRI answers the same question when unenhanced CT is unavailable, and contrast washout characterises a lipid-poor adenoma. Getting it right matters more here than in an incidental setting, because a solitary adrenal metastasis is the difference between a treatment given with curative intent and palliative systemic therapy. The M1b category exists because single-lesion, single-organ metastatic disease behaves differently from widespread disease, and an oligometastatic patient may have both sites treated radically. Biopsy is reserved for a lesion that imaging cannot characterise, and phaeochromocytoma should be considered before a needle is put into an adrenal gland.

quiz.prompt: A 2.5 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma is accompanied by a solitary 9 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe, biopsied and shown to be the same tumour type, with no nodal or distant disease. How does the second nodule count?
choices: T4, still within a curative-intent plan
M1a, so systemic treatment is indicated
T3, because it sits in the same lung
N1, because spread is intrapulmonary
quiz.answer: T4, still within a curative-intent plan
quiz.explain: Separate tumour nodules are graded by where they sit relative to the primary: the same lobe is T3, a different ipsilateral lobe is T4, and the contralateral lung is M1a. A T4 arrived at this way is not the same animal as a T4 by invasion of the mediastinum or a great vessel. With N0 disease this configuration is resectable and potentially curable, and it is one of the places where the stage label and the surgical reality diverge, which is a good reason to report the anatomy rather than only the letter. The other trap is assuming the second nodule is a metastasis at all. Synchronous second primaries are common in this population, and comparing histological subtype and molecular profile can turn one T4 tumour into two early-stage tumours, with quite different treatment.

quiz.prompt: A superior sulcus tumour abuts the subclavian artery and the T1 nerve root on CT, with an equivocal fat plane at both sites. Which examination best answers the resectability question, and what is it looking for?
choices: MRI, for brachial plexus and vertebral invasion
PET-CT, for occult nodal and distant disease
CT angiography, for subclavian artery invasion
Bone scan, for invasion of the first two ribs
quiz.answer: MRI, for brachial plexus and vertebral invasion
quiz.explain: At the lung apex the questions that decide the operation are soft-tissue ones: the brachial plexus, the subclavian vessels, the vertebral body, the neural foramina and the spinal canal. MRI with coronal and sagittal planes shows all of them, and CT, whatever its spatial resolution in bone, is poor at the plexus. Tumour reaching the plexus above the T1 root, encasing rather than abutting the subclavian artery, or invading the vertebral body extensively or entering the canal, is generally beyond resection; involvement of the T1 root and below, of the ribs, or of a limited portion of a vertebral body is within the scope of en-bloc resection after induction chemoradiotherapy at experienced centres. PET-CT is still needed, because a superior sulcus tumour is staged for nodal and distant disease like any other, but it does not answer the local question this patient's operability turns on.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a 5 cm tumour and ipsilateral mediastinal nodal disease has a PET-CT that shows no extrathoracic uptake, and has no neurological symptoms. What is still required before treatment is planned?
choices: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain
A repeat PET-CT after chemotherapy
A bone scan for skeletal metastases
No further imaging before treatment
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain
quiz.explain: Normal cerebral cortex takes up FDG avidly, so a metastasis sits against a bright background and PET-CT is unreliable intracranially. Dedicated brain imaging is recommended separately for locally advanced disease and for anyone with neurological symptoms, and contrast-enhanced MRI is substantially more sensitive than CT for small and posterior fossa deposits. The reason to do it before treatment is planned rather than afterwards is that the result changes the plan in either direction: an occult brain metastasis can convert a radical chemoradiotherapy plan into systemic therapy, or, if it is solitary and the thoracic disease is limited, into radical treatment of both sites with stereotactic radiosurgery or resection. A bone scan adds nothing after a PET-CT, which covers the skeleton with better sensitivity and specificity.

quiz.prompt: A peripheral part-solid adenocarcinoma measures 2.4 cm overall on lung windows, with a solid component of 1.8 cm, and there is no nodal or distant disease. Which of those measurements in centimetres is used to assign the clinical T category? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Since the eighth edition, a part-solid tumour is staged on the size of its solid component on CT, and at pathology on the size of the invasive component, because the ground-glass, lepidic part does not carry the same prognosis as invasive tumour of equal size. So 1.8 cm makes this T1b, where the whole-lesion measurement of 2.4 cm would have made it T1c. Both numbers belong in the report, since the referrer needs the total size to follow the lesion and the solid size to stage it. The same logic runs to the bottom of the scale: a pure ground-glass lesion up to 3 cm with no invasive component is staged as in situ disease, and one with an invasive component of 5 mm or less as minimally invasive. It runs upward too, in that growth of the solid component is what constitutes progression in a subsolid lesion.

quiz.prompt: In a patient with a left upper lobe tumour, an enlarged node lies in the space bounded above by the lower border of the aortic arch, below by the upper border of the left main pulmonary artery, and lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Which IASLC station number is that? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: That is station 5, the subaortic or aortopulmonary window node, and left upper lobe tumours drain there characteristically. It is ipsilateral mediastinal for a left-sided primary, so N2. The practical weight of naming it correctly lies in access: neither cervical mediastinoscopy nor endobronchial ultrasound reaches station 5, so tissue requires a parasternal mediastinotomy, a video-assisted thoracoscopic approach or an extended cervical procedure. Station 6, the para-aortic node lying anterior and lateral to the ascending aorta and the arch, is equally out of reach of those routine techniques. This is the concrete reason a report should name the station rather than describe a node loosely as being in the upper mediastinum: the station determines who can biopsy it and how, and a vague description costs the patient an extra clinic visit or the wrong procedure.

quiz.prompt: Explain why an FDG-avid mediastinal node should be sampled before a patient is told that surgery is off, and set out which stations the two standard needle routes reach and which they do not.
quiz.answer: PET is sensitive but only moderately specific in the mediastinum: granulomatous disease, anthracosilicotic nodes, infection, and nodes reacting downstream of an obstructed bronchus are all avid, so an avid node in an otherwise operable patient is a hypothesis rather than a stage. Because upstaging from N1 to N2, or from N2 to N3, removes curative surgery, the finding that changes the plan is precisely the one that has to be proved, and pathological confirmation is the standard of care. Endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspiration, EBUS-TBNA, reaches the paratracheal stations 2R, 2L, 4R and 4L, the subcarinal station 7, and the hilar and interlobar stations 10 and 11. Endoscopic ultrasound from the oesophagus reaches 4L, 7, 8 and 9, and can also sample the left adrenal gland and the left lobe of the liver. Neither reaches the subaortic station 5 or the para-aortic station 6, which need a parasternal mediastinotomy or a thoracoscopic approach. The converse error also matters: a negative needle result in a node with a high pretest probability does not exclude disease, and surgical staging follows.
quiz.explain: The rule underneath all of this is that a finding gets proved in proportion to what it costs the patient if it is wrong. A PET-positive node that merely confirms disease already evident elsewhere changes nothing and needs nothing; a PET-positive node that alone takes away an operation is worth an invasive test. Two extras are worth carrying. First, the two needle routes are complementary rather than alternatives, because they approach the mediastinum from opposite sides, and combining them raises the yield in the posterior and inferior stations that bronchoscopy cannot see. Second, the ninth edition of the classification, in force since 2025, subdivides N2 into single-station and multi-station disease because they carry different prognoses, which raises the value of a report that names each involved station rather than reporting mediastinal nodal disease in aggregate.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT reports no enlarged mediastinal nodes, and the team treats that as N0. Explain the two ways that inference can be wrong, and what determines whether invasive staging is needed anyway.
quiz.answer: The CT criterion is a short-axis diameter of 10 mm or more, and it fails in both directions. Nodes enlarge reactively in obstructive pneumonitis, infection and old granulomatous disease, so a good proportion of enlarged nodes are benign; and metastatic deposits sit inside normal-sized nodes, so a normal CT does not exclude N2 disease, with sensitivity around half. PET-CT improves on both figures without solving either, since deposits below its resolution are missed and lepidic adenocarcinoma and carcinoid tumours are poorly avid, while inflammatory nodes are avid.
