What determines whether invasive staging is done anyway is the pretest probability of mediastinal disease: a central tumour, a large tumour, enlarged or avid N1 nodes, and adenocarcinoma histology all raise it enough that a negative PET-CT is not accepted at face value, and endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) with or without surgical staging is performed before resection. A small peripheral tumour with a clean PET mediastinum carries a low enough residual risk to proceed directly to surgery.
quiz.explain: Size is a poor surrogate for tumour because it measures a consequence that inflammation produces just as readily. That is why nodal staging is a sequence of tests with rising invasiveness and rising accuracy, rather than a single measurement, and why the sequence is entered at the point the pretest probability justifies. The reporting habit that follows is to describe nodes by station, short-axis size and avidity, and to state the pretest features that raise concern, rather than issuing a bare N category from CT alone: the radiologist's job at this step is to set the probability that the next test is chosen against. The same reasoning explains why a positive result is confirmed when it removes an operation, and a negative result is confirmed when the probability was high to begin with.

quiz.prompt: Put these IASLC nodal stations in order of the level at which they are found, from the most cranial to the most caudal.
quiz.answer: station-2R station-4R station-7 station-8 station-9
quiz.explain: Station 2R is the upper paratracheal node, running down to the level where the caudal border of the left brachiocephalic vein crosses the trachea; 4R is the lower paratracheal node below that, down to the lower border of the azygos vein; 7 is subcarinal; 8 is paraoesophageal below the level of the carina; and 9 lies in the inferior pulmonary ligament, the most caudal mediastinal station of all. Two structural facts make the map worth learning rather than looking up each time. Stations 1 to 9 are mediastinal and become N2 when ipsilateral to the tumour and N3 when contralateral or supraclavicular, while stations 10 to 14 are hilar and beyond and are N1. And the boundaries are defined by structures visible on CT, precisely so that a radiologist and a surgeon assigning the same node from the same images arrive at the same number.

quiz.prompt: A single 3 cm peripheral lung cancer is being staged. Taking each site of direct invasion on its own, put them in order of the T category that site alone would confer, from the lowest to the highest.
quiz.answer: visceral-pleura chest-wall vertebral-body
quiz.explain: Invasion of the visceral pleura makes a tumour at least T2 whatever its size. Invasion through it into the parietal pleura or the chest wall makes T3, in company with the phrenic nerve and the parietal pericardium. Invasion of a vertebral body makes T4, in company with the mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus and carina. What is worth carrying is how badly CT performs at each of these boundaries. Contact with the pleura, loss of an extrapleural fat plane, and even a broad interface between tumour and chest wall do not prove invasion; the findings that do are frank rib destruction and an extrapleural soft-tissue mass. The step from T3 to T4 changes the operation and often the intent of treatment, so equivocal cases go to MRI, to careful review of sagittal and coronal reformats, or to assessment at thoracotomy, and the report should say which of those is being asked for.

nodes.title: Acute Stroke Imaging
nodes.goal: Read the hyperacute stroke CT and CT angiogram, and say what in the images selects this patient for thrombectomy.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old presents with sudden dysphasia and right arm weakness. On the unenhanced CT the left middle cerebral artery looks dense - but so do the right middle cerebral artery, the basilar artery and the superior sagittal sinus, and the brain parenchyma looks unremarkable. The haemoglobin is 197 g/L. What best accounts for the dense vessels?
choices: A high haematocrit raising attenuation throughout the vessels
Thrombus filling the left middle cerebral artery trunk
Mural calcification of the intracranial vessel walls
Iodinated contrast retained from a recent study
quiz.answer: A high haematocrit raising attenuation throughout the vessels
quiz.explain: The discriminator is symmetry and company. A thrombus is one clot in one artery, so the sign is unilateral and is judged by comparing the vessel with its fellow on the same slice; a raised haematocrit raises the attenuation of blood itself, so arteries, veins and dural sinuses rise together, and a dense superior sagittal sinus alongside dense arteries is the giveaway that the finding is in the blood rather than in one lumen. Mural calcification is denser still and sits as a rim in the wall, following the vessel rather than filling it, and it is usually bilateral and irregular. Retained contrast would opacify the vessels far more brightly and would come with a history. The trap in the last sentence of the stem is the normal-looking parenchyma: at ninety minutes a normal brain is entirely compatible with a large ischaemic core, so it argues for proceeding to CT angiography rather than for reassurance.

quiz.prompt: An unenhanced CT two hours after onset of a right hemiplegia shows early ischaemic change in the left insular ribbon, the left lentiform nucleus, and the cortical regions M1, M2 and M5. Every other region of the scoring template is normal. What ASPECTS does this study score? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: ASPECTS starts at 10 and subtracts one point for each of ten regions showing early ischaemic change: caudate, lentiform, internal capsule, insular ribbon and the cortical regions M1 to M3 at the ganglionic level, and M4 to M6 at the level just above the ganglia. Five involved regions leaves 5. The score matters because it stands in for core volume when perfusion imaging is unavailable, and the early-window thrombectomy trials enrolled largely at 6 or above, which is still where the guideline recommendation is strongest. Since 2023, SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT and RESCUE-Japan LIMIT have shown benefit in large cores down to an ASPECTS of about 3, so a low score is now a reason for discussion rather than an automatic exclusion. Two cautions in scoring: count established hypoattenuation or focal swelling rather than a subjective impression, and do not count an old infarct as new.

quiz.prompt: Ninety minutes after a middle cerebral artery occlusion the diffusion-weighted images are unmistakably abnormal while the unenhanced CT of the same territory looks close to normal. Account for the difference in terms of where the water is.
quiz.answer: Arterial occlusion causes energy failure within minutes, the sodium-potassium ATPase stops, and sodium and water move from the extracellular space into the intracellular compartment. This is cytotoxic oedema: total tissue water is barely changed, but water has been redistributed into a compartment where its Brownian motion is hindered, so the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) falls and the DWI signal rises. CT attenuation tracks total tissue water content, which has hardly altered at this stage; it falls only later, once ionic oedema and then breakdown of the blood-brain barrier draw new water into the tissue from the vasculature, which is why frank hypoattenuation lags the diffusion change by hours.
quiz.explain: The two studies are sensitive to different physical quantities, and that is the whole answer: diffusion imaging is sensitive to where water is, CT to how much of it there is. Knowing the time course keeps the reader out of two traps. The ADC falls immediately, reaches its nadir over the first days, pseudonormalises at around a week to ten days as cell lysis and vasogenic oedema raise diffusivity again, and then rises above normal; so a bright DWI with a normal or high ADC late on is T2 shine-through rather than new ischaemia, and a subacute infarct can look deceptively unimpressive on diffusion alone. At the front door the corollary is blunter: a normal CT does not exclude infarction and is not a reason to withhold treatment, whereas a normal DWI in the first hours makes infarction unlikely, with small brainstem lesions and profound hypoperfusion imaged before a core has formed as the exceptions worth remembering.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old wakes at 07:00 unable to speak, having been well at 22:00 the night before. MRI at 08:30 shows a left middle cerebral artery territory lesion that is bright on diffusion-weighted imaging with a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and no corresponding signal change on FLAIR. What does the discrepancy between the two sequences allow you to say?
choices: The lesion is probably less than about 4.5 hours old
The lesion is probably more than twelve hours old
The lesion is an artefact of a poor diffusion trace
The lesion is chronic and unrelated to the symptoms
quiz.answer: The lesion is probably less than about 4.5 hours old
quiz.explain: Diffusion turns positive within minutes, while FLAIR signal follows the rise in tissue water and becomes visible at roughly 4.5 to 6 hours; a lesion that is bright on diffusion but invisible on FLAIR therefore dates itself to the first hours. That mismatch is what the WAKE-UP trial used to select patients with an unknown onset time for thrombolysis, and it found benefit. Here the clock reads nine hours since last seen well and the tissue reads under four and a half - the tissue wins. The near-miss is 'more than twelve hours old', which runs the logic backwards: by twelve hours the FLAIR abnormality would be conspicuous, and a DWI lesion with matching FLAIR change is the appearance that argues against a hyperacute onset. A low ADC is what separates a true diffusion lesion from T2 shine-through, so it is quoted in the stem deliberately.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a suspected large-vessel occlusion arrives nine hours after last being seen well, and the hyperacute protocol runs from the scanner to the angiography suite. Put these acquisitions in the order the protocol performs them.
quiz.answer: unenhanced-CT CT-angiography CT-perfusion digital-subtraction-angiography
quiz.explain: The unenhanced study comes first and answers one question - is there blood? - because everything downstream, thrombolysis above all, depends on that answer, and the same images supply the ASPECTS. CT angiography is second, because finding the occlusion, and seeing the aortic arch and cervical vessels the catheter must travel through, decides whether thrombectomy is possible at all. Perfusion is third and is a selection tool rather than a diagnostic one: in the late window it separates a small core with a large penumbra from a completed infarct. Catheter angiography is last and is part of the treatment. Running perfusion before angiography spends contrast and minutes on a question that only matters once a target exists, and leaving the unenhanced study until last is how a haemorrhage gets thrombolysed.

quiz.prompt: CT perfusion nine hours after onset gives an ischaemic core, defined as relative cerebral blood flow below 30 per cent of the contralateral side, of 25 mL, and a Tmax greater than 6 s volume of 90 mL. What is the mismatch ratio? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The mismatch ratio is the whole critically hypoperfused volume divided by the core, 90 over 25, which is 3.6; the mismatch volume - tissue at risk but not yet lost - is the difference, 65 mL. DEFUSE 3 selected patients 6 to 16 hours from last seen well with a core under 70 mL, a ratio of at least 1.8 and a mismatch volume of at least 15 mL, and this patient clears each criterion comfortably. DAWN worked out to 24 hours using a clinical-core mismatch instead, pairing age and NIHSS against core volume. Two cautions travel with these maps: Tmax above 6 s marks critically delayed tissue rather than tissue certain to die, and in very early presentations the core map overstates the damage, so a large core in the first couple of hours deserves scepticism rather than an automatic exclusion.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old is found with weakness of the left leg much worse than the left arm, with the face spared, and is apathetic and incontinent of urine. Before the images are reviewed, which arterial territory should be scrutinised first?
choices: The right anterior cerebral artery territory
The right middle cerebral artery territory
The right posterior cerebral artery territory
The right anterior choroidal artery territory
quiz.answer: The right anterior cerebral artery territory
quiz.explain: The homunculus does the work. Leg and perineum lie on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery; face and hand lie on the convexity, which belongs to the middle cerebral artery. A leg-dominant deficit that spares the face is anterior cerebral until proved otherwise, and the apathy and incontinence fit the same vessel, since the medial frontal cortex and anterior cingulate share its supply. Middle cerebral occlusion gives face-and-arm weakness with aphasia or neglect; posterior cerebral gives a homonymous hemianopia and, when the thalamus goes, hemisensory loss; the anterior choroidal artery gives hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia from the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the optic tract, without cortical signs. One corollary: isolated anterior cerebral infarction is uncommon, and bilateral medial frontal infarction should prompt a look for an azygos anterior cerebral artery or for vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

quiz.prompt: A 69-year-old smoker has repeated brief episodes of right arm weakness, worse on standing up. MRI shows a chain of small acute infarcts in a line through the left corona radiata between the lateral ventricle and the cortex, and CT angiography shows a 90 per cent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Which mechanism does the pattern of the infarcts favour?
choices: Failure of perfusion in the internal borderzone
Artery-to-artery embolism to cortical branches
Lipohyalinosis of a single lenticulostriate vessel
Cardioembolism to the middle cerebral trunk
quiz.answer: Failure of perfusion in the internal borderzone
quiz.explain: Geometry is the argument. The internal borderzone lies in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale, at the far end of the deep perforators and the penetrating pial arterioles - the last field the water reaches. When perfusion pressure falls behind a tight carotid stenosis, infarcts appear there as a rosary of lesions strung in a line, and the postural trigger for the symptoms is the clinical half of the same observation. Embolic infarcts scatter across different territories, sit at the grey-white junction and take wedge or scattered cortical shapes rather than a straight line; a single lacune from lipohyalinosis is one lesion, not a chain. The distinction changes treatment: a haemodynamic pattern behind a symptomatic 90 per cent stenosis argues for prompt revascularisation and for caution about dropping the blood pressure, whereas an embolic pattern shifts attention to the plaque surface and to the heart.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old taking a combined oral contraceptive has had three days of worsening headache and then a seizure. Unenhanced CT shows patchy haemorrhage with disproportionate surrounding oedema in both high parietal lobes, and the superior sagittal sinus looks dense. What does this combination point to?
choices: Venous infarction from dural sinus thrombosis
Bilateral anterior cerebral artery infarction
Haemorrhagic contusions from unwitnessed trauma
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
quiz.answer: Venous infarction from dural sinus thrombosis
quiz.explain: The pattern breaks the rules that arterial infarcts obey. Parasagittal lesions on both sides correspond to no single arterial territory; they are haemorrhagic early rather than late; and the oedema is out of proportion to the lesion because the mechanism is back-pressure rather than absent supply. Add a dense sinus and the diagnosis is venous. Confirm with CT or MR venography, where the empty delta sign is a filling defect within the enhancing sinus wall, and remember that a dense sinus alone can be nothing more than a high haematocrit. Bilateral anterior cerebral infarction, possible with an azygos vessel, would follow the medial surface forward from the genu of the corpus callosum and would not be haemorrhagic at three days. Contusions cluster at the skull base against the orbital roofs and sphenoid ridges. PRES sits posteriorly, parieto-occipital, and is predominantly vasogenic oedema. The management consequence is the striking part: the treatment is anticoagulation, in the presence of intracranial haemorrhage.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a large right middle cerebral artery infarct has a routine CT at sixteen days. The territory that was clearly hypoattenuating on day two now looks close to normal, and the report concludes that the infarct has resolved. Explain what has happened to the tissue, and how you would answer the report.
quiz.answer: This is the fogging phase. Between roughly the second and fourth week, macrophages infiltrate the infarct and new capillaries proliferate within it, so its attenuation rises back towards that of normal brain and the lesion becomes inconspicuous on unenhanced CT. The tissue is not recovering; it is being cleared, and the encephalomalacic cavity will appear later. The report should be answered by saying that a transiently normal-looking CT in this window is not evidence of resolution: the infarct remains demonstrable on MRI, where it stays abnormal on T2 and FLAIR, and it will enhance on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI because the blood-brain barrier is broken.
quiz.explain: Fogging is worth knowing because it appears exactly when the follow-up scan tends to be booked, and because it can hide a subacute infarct in a patient scanned late for the first time: a normal CT two weeks after an event is not evidence that no stroke occurred. The mechanism is the one that also produces gyriform cortical enhancement and, on MRI, cortical T1 hyperintensity from laminar necrosis at around two weeks - reperfused, infarcted cortex packed with macrophages. The trap on the other side is calling that subacute infarct a tumour, since it enhances and can show mass effect. What keeps the reader right is the shape and the history: a wedge that respects a vascular territory and reaches the cortical surface, in a patient whose deficit began on a known day.

quiz.prompt: A 77-year-old with atrial fibrillation was last seen well fourteen hours ago and has an NIHSS of 18. There is no haemorrhage, the ASPECTS is 8, CT angiography shows an occluded left M1 segment, and perfusion gives a core of 12 mL with 95 mL of critically delayed tissue. The on-call team proposes medical management because the six-hour window has passed. What is the strongest response?
choices: Imaging, not the clock, selects patients out to 24 hours
The scan should be repeated after twelve more hours
Intravenous thrombolysis alone is the option left
The core is too large for an endovascular approach
quiz.answer: Imaging, not the clock, selects patients out to 24 hours
quiz.explain: DAWN and DEFUSE 3 replaced the clock with a tissue clock, and guidelines followed: thrombectomy is recommended out to 24 hours from last seen well in patients who meet imaging criteria. This patient meets them with room to spare - an ASPECTS of 8, a 12 mL core and 95 mL of penumbra fourteen hours in, which is the imaging signature of a slow progressor with good collaterals. 'The core is too large' inverts the numbers on the screen. A repeat scan buys nothing except infarct. Intravenous thrombolysis is outside its own window here (4.5 hours, extended to 9 hours only in perfusion-selected patients in trials such as EXTEND), and in any case thrombolysis is not a prerequisite for thrombectomy. The practical lesson is that in the late window the question is never 'how long has it been?' but 'how much brain is still alive?'.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have an occluded M1 segment, an NIHSS of 16, and presented three hours after onset. On multiphase CT angiography the first fills the pial vessels of the affected hemisphere almost as well and almost as fast as the normal side; the second shows sparse and delayed pial filling. Explain what the difference predicts and how it should change what you do next.
quiz.answer: Collateral supply through the pial or leptomeningeal anastomoses determines how fast penumbra converts into core. The first patient is a slow progressor: at three hours the core will still be small and the penumbra large, the chance of a good outcome after successful thrombectomy is high, and there is time to complete the imaging properly and to transfer if the centre cannot treat. The second is a fast progressor whose core is already growing quickly, may already be large despite the short time from onset, and for whom every minute of delay costs tissue, so imaging should be curtailed to what is needed to get the patient onto the angiography table. Collateral status is also why time from onset predicts core volume so poorly, and why a late presenter with good collaterals can be a better candidate than an early one with poor collaterals.
quiz.explain: Collaterals are the variable that makes the same occlusion a different disease in two patients. They are graded on the extent and the timing of pial filling relative to the normal hemisphere, and multiphase CT angiography exists because a single-phase study confuses a slow-filling good collateral bed with an absent one - the phase was simply caught too early. Good collaterals predict a smaller final infarct, a better functional outcome and a lower risk of haemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion; poor collaterals predict the opposite and are the reason some patients arrive early and are already beyond help. Two things follow for practice: report collateral status rather than only the occlusion site, and treat a poor collateral pattern as a reason to compress the workflow rather than as a reason to give up, since the tissue that remains is exactly the tissue that will be lost during any delay.

nodes.title: Intracranial Haemorrhage in Head Trauma
nodes.goal: Assign an intracranial bleed to its compartment from the shape of its margins, and recognise the herniation it threatens.

quiz.prompt: A cyclist struck the top of his head. CT shows a biconvex high-attenuation collection at the vertex that extends from one side of the midline to the other but stops abruptly at the coronal suture on both sides. What is the collection?
choices: An extradural haematoma from the sagittal sinus
An interhemispheric subdural haematoma
Subarachnoid blood filling the vertex sulci
A subgaleal haematoma over the vertex
quiz.answer: An extradural haematoma from the sagittal sinus
quiz.explain: Two boundaries, two different rules, and here both are met by one answer: held at the sutures, free across the midline. A vertex extradural is classically venous, from a torn superior sagittal sinus or a fracture through the sagittal groove, and it behaves differently from the arterial temporal variety - it may accumulate slowly over hours to days, and at operation it bleeds from a sinus rather than from the middle meningeal artery, which is why the neurosurgeon wants to know the diagnosis before the bone flap is raised. It is also the extradural most often missed, because it sits at the top of the stack where axial images contain little brain and the collection is easily dismissed as volume averaging with the vault: coronal reformats are what show it. Subgaleal blood lies outside the skull, crosses sutures with the galea, and expands the scalp rather than indenting the brain.

quiz.prompt: An extradural haematoma measures 6.0 cm in its greatest axial diameter, 4.0 cm perpendicular to that on the same image, and extends over 3.0 cm in the craniocaudal direction. Using the ABC/2 estimate for an ellipsoid, what is its volume in millilitres? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: ABC/2 multiplies the three orthogonal diameters and halves the product: 6 x 4 x 3 / 2 = 36 mL. It approximates the ellipsoid volume, which is four-thirds pi times abc over eight, or about 0.52abc, close enough to the 0.5 the formula uses - and it takes seconds at the workstation, which is why it has survived every attempt to replace it. The number matters because published surgical guidance takes an extradural volume above 30 cm3 as warranting evacuation whatever the GCS, so this measurement decides the content of the phone call rather than merely decorating the report. Two cautions: the estimate overstates volume for irregular or multilobular collections, and the C dimension should be counted from the images - the number of slices containing blood multiplied by the slice thickness - rather than eyeballed from a single plane.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old on warfarin has been drowsy for a week, three weeks after a fall. The CT is reported as showing no haemorrhage. Reviewing it, you find that sulci are absent across the right convexity, the grey-white junction on that side is displaced several millimetres away from the inner table, and there is 4 mm of midline shift to the left. What explains this?
choices: An isodense subdural collection over that convexity
Cortical swelling from a subacute infarction
Diffuse cerebral oedema after a hypoxic insult
Subarachnoid blood layering within the sulci
quiz.answer: An isodense subdural collection over that convexity
quiz.explain: A subdural haematoma passes through an isodense phase at roughly one to three weeks as the clot degrades, and it can match cortex closely enough to disappear. What gives it away is displacement rather than density: effaced sulci over a convexity, a grey-white interface standing off from the inner table, a compressed ventricle, and midline shift with no visible cause. Bilateral isodense collections are the real trap, because the shift cancels and the study looks normal but tight - so look for ventricles that are too small for the age and cortex held away from the vault on both sides. Anaemia lowers clot attenuation as well, so an acute subdural in a profoundly anaemic or coagulopathic patient can be isodense from the outset, and a fluid-fluid level or a swirl of unclotted blood within a collection raises the question of continuing haemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT, which opacifies the displaced cortical veins, or MRI, settles an equivocal study.

quiz.prompt: A 76-year-old with no history of trauma has had several episodes of numbness spreading up the left hand and arm, each lasting a few minutes. CT shows blood confined to three adjacent sulci over the right parietal convexity, with nothing in the basal cisterns or the Sylvian fissures. What should be suspected?
choices: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy of leptomeningeal vessels
Rupture of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction after a headache
A cortical vein thrombosis with local extravasation
quiz.answer: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy of leptomeningeal vessels
quiz.explain: Distribution carries the whole argument. Aneurysmal blood arrives under arterial pressure into the basal cisterns and fills them, and an anterior communicating aneurysm loads the interhemispheric fissure and often the ventricles. Blood confined to a few convexity sulci comes from vessels lying on the surface, and in a patient over about sixty the commonest cause is amyloid angiopathy. The transient spreading sensory episodes are the classic companion - amyloid spells, probably cortical spreading depolarisation over the blood - and they matter because they are routinely mistaken for transient ischaemic attacks and treated with antiplatelets or anticoagulants, which is the worst available move in a brain full of fragile amyloid-laden vessels. Confirm on susceptibility-weighted MRI, looking for lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis that spare the deep grey matter. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction also produces convexity subarachnoid blood and is the right answer in a younger patient with thunderclap headaches, often postpartum or after serotonergic drugs.

quiz.prompt: A patient thrown from a vehicle has blood in five separate spaces on one CT of the head. Put the spaces in order from the scalp inwards.
quiz.answer: subgaleal extradural subdural subarachnoid intraparenchymal
quiz.explain: The order is scalp, skull, dura, arachnoid, brain. Subgaleal blood lies between the galea aponeurotica and the pericranium, outside the skull, and crosses sutures because the galea does - unlike the neonatal subperiosteal cephalhaematoma, which is bounded by them. Extradural blood strips dura from the inner table and is held at the sutures. Subdural blood spreads in the potential space between dura and arachnoid, crossing sutures freely but stopped by the falx and tentorium. Subarachnoid blood follows cerebrospinal fluid into sulci and cisterns and so takes the shape of the space rather than pushing the brain aside. Intraparenchymal blood is within the brain itself. Every shape question a trauma CT asks - biconvex, crescentic, sulcal, rounded - reduces to which of these five spaces the blood is in, and getting the space right is what determines whether the answer is an operation, an observation, or an angiogram.

quiz.prompt: A registrar can recite that an extradural haematoma does not cross a suture while a subdural haematoma does not cross the midline, but cannot say why. Explain both boundaries from the anatomy of the dura, and give the exception you would still be careful about.
quiz.answer: The dura has two layers. The outer periosteal layer is the inner periosteum of the skull and is continuous with the pericranium through the sutures, where it is firmly adherent, so an extradural collection, which forms by stripping dura off the inner table, is halted at sutural lines. The falx and tentorium are reflections of the inner meningeal layer alone and lie deep to the extradural space, so extradural blood crosses the midline without difficulty. Subdural blood collects deep to both layers, between dura and arachnoid, so it spreads under sutures freely but is walled off by the falx and tentorium. The exception to be careful about is a suture that has been fractured through or diastased, which an extradural can cross, and the unfused sutures of an infant, where the rule barely applies.
quiz.explain: Reading the two rules together gives a usable heuristic: a collection that crosses the midline is extradural, and a collection that crosses a suture is subdural. The one refinement is the interhemispheric subdural, which lies along one side of the falx and follows it without crossing to the other side, so it can look like midline blood without breaking the rule. The mechanism also explains the company each keeps. Extradural blood needs enough force to separate an adherent dura, so the great majority in adults have an overlying fracture crossing a vascular groove, most often the middle meningeal artery in the temporoparietal region. Subdural blood needs only a bridging vein to tear, which is why it appears in atrophic, anticoagulated and alcoholic patients after trivial injury, and why its volume tells you less about the force of the impact than its extradural counterpart.

quiz.prompt: A biconvex temporal collection 15 mm thick contains an irregular area of lower attenuation within an otherwise dense clot. The patient's GCS has fallen two points in twenty minutes. What does the low-attenuation area within the clot indicate?
choices: Fresh unclotted blood still entering the collection
Cerebrospinal fluid tracking through a dural tear
Fat from a fracture through the diploic space
An older collection that has begun to liquefy
quiz.answer: Fresh unclotted blood still entering the collection
quiz.explain: This is the swirl sign. Clotted blood is dense because it is retracted and packed with haemoglobin; blood that has not yet clotted attenuates less, so an active bleeding point shows as a swirl or lucency inside a dense haematoma. It means the collection is still growing, it is associated with rapid expansion and worse outcome, and paired with a falling GCS it argues for shortening the interval to theatre rather than repeating the scan in six hours. The near-miss worth thinking through is the older, liquefying collection: that takes days to weeks, is uniform rather than swirled, and does not occur in a patient injured within the hour. Cerebrospinal fluid entering through a dural tear would sit at water attenuation with a sharp margin rather than swirling through the clot. The same sign in an intraparenchymal haematoma carries the same meaning, and its contrast-enhanced relative is the spot sign.

quiz.prompt: An 18-year-old is unconscious with a GCS of 6 after a high-speed collision. The CT shows two punctate dense foci at the grey-white junction of the right frontal lobe, no mass effect and nothing else. The team is reassured by the CT. Explain the discrepancy, and say what imaging you would request and what you would look for.
quiz.answer: The discrepancy is typical of diffuse axonal injury, in which rotational acceleration shears axons where tissues of differing stiffness meet. Most of those lesions are non-haemorrhagic and therefore invisible on CT, so the CT badly underestimates the injury, and a near-normal CT with a very low GCS is evidence of axonal injury rather than grounds for reassurance; the two dense dots are the haemorrhagic minority. MRI is the study. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is the sequence that matters most, since it shows microhaemorrhages that gradient echo and certainly CT miss, and diffusion-weighted imaging shows the non-haemorrhagic lesions as foci of restricted diffusion. Look at the lobar grey-white junction, at the corpus callosum and particularly its splenium, and at the dorsolateral midbrain and upper pons, because depth of involvement grades the injury and carries the prognosis.
quiz.explain: The three depths are the classic staging: grade 1 lobar grey-white junction, grade 2 adding the corpus callosum, grade 3 adding the dorsolateral brainstem, with outcome worsening as the lesions go deeper. The mechanism explains the sites - the callosum is tethered by the falx and the midbrain by the tentorium, so both are shearing planes - and it also explains the company: intraventricular blood near the fornix, and small haemorrhages in the deep grey matter. Timing matters when requesting the study, because susceptibility lesions persist for months while diffusion lesions are most conspicuous in the first week. The final point is medico-legal as much as clinical: documenting axonal injury in a patient whose CT looks bland is often the only objective evidence of why the patient did not wake up.

quiz.prompt: On the axial CT at the level of the foramen of Monro, the distance from inner table to inner table is 140 mm, and the septum pellucidum lies 82 mm from the left inner table. What is the midline shift in millimetres? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The true midline is half the width, 70 mm; the septum sits at 82 mm, so it is displaced 12 mm to the right. Measure at the foramen of Monro, from a line joining the anterior and posterior attachments of the falx, and state where you measured, because shift at the septum, at the third ventricle and at the pineal can differ in a rotated or asymmetric head. The threshold to have in mind is that an acute subdural haematoma more than 10 mm thick, or producing more than 5 mm of midline shift, is generally taken as warranting evacuation whatever the GCS. The most useful thing this measurement does, though, is flag a mismatch: shift far out of proportion to the visible collection means either that swelling is doing the work - in which case evacuating a thin collection will not fix it - or that there is a second collection you have not seen, most often an isodense one on the other side.

quiz.prompt: Three days after evacuation of an acute subdural haematoma that had caused 14 mm of midline shift, a patient develops weakness of the left leg. CT now shows new hypoattenuation along the medial surface of the right frontal lobe. What has happened?
choices: Anterior cerebral artery compression beneath the falx
Posterior cerebral artery compression at the tentorium
Watershed infarction from intraoperative hypotension
Venous infarction from a thrombosed bridging vein
quiz.answer: Anterior cerebral artery compression beneath the falx
quiz.explain: Subfalcine herniation pushes the cingulate gyrus under the free edge of the falx, and the anterior cerebral artery and its callosomarginal branch travel with it, to be compressed against a rigid edge; the medial frontal cortex infarcts and the contralateral leg goes weak. It is the herniation easiest to see on a scan and easiest to leave out of a report, and it is worth naming explicitly because the resulting infarct appears days later and is otherwise attributed to the operation. The mirror image happens one level down: uncal herniation compresses the posterior cerebral artery against the tentorial edge and infarcts the occipital lobe, which is why a homonymous hemianopia after a temporal haematoma is not a coincidence. Watershed infarction from hypotension would be bilateral and in the borderzones rather than confined to one medial frontal lobe, and bridging vein thrombosis would not respect an arterial territory.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a right temporal extradural haematoma develops a dilated right pupil and a left hemiparesis. Over the next hour the left side improves while the right side becomes weak, and the right pupil stays dilated. What accounts for the change of side?
choices: The left cerebral peduncle is pressed on the tentorial edge
A second haematoma has developed on the left side
The left internal carotid artery has dissected acutely
A left middle cerebral artery embolus has occurred
quiz.answer: The left cerebral peduncle is pressed on the tentorial edge
quiz.explain: This is Kernohan's notch phenomenon, the classic false localising sign. Descending transtentorial herniation on the right displaces the whole midbrain across, and the contralateral cerebral peduncle is crushed against the opposite rigid tentorial edge. The corticospinal fibres in that peduncle have not yet decussated, so they serve the right side of the body, and the hemiparesis appears on the same side as the haematoma. The pupil is the honest sign: the third nerve is compressed by the uncus on the side of the mass, so a fixed dilated pupil localises the lesion reliably where the limbs do not. The clinical weight of the sign is that it marks an advanced herniation, and that it must not be read as a new contralateral lesion, because the operation the patient needs is decompression of the right-sided collection. The same mechanism, carried further, tears the perforators from the basilar artery and produces a Duret haemorrhage in the pons and midbrain.

quiz.prompt: A CT one hour after a fall onto the occiput is normal. Eight hours later the patient is confused, and a repeat CT shows haemorrhagic contusions in both inferior frontal lobes and the anterior right temporal lobe. Explain the distribution and the interval, and say what follows for any patient with a normal early CT and a persistent deficit.
quiz.answer: The distribution is contrecoup. An occipital blow accelerates the brain against the irregular anterior skull base, so the inferior frontal surfaces, the gyrus rectus and the temporal poles strike the orbital roofs, the sphenoid ridges and the petrous ridges; contusions concentrate at those sites whatever the point of impact, because it is the roughness of the bone rather than the direction of the blow that determines where the brain is grazed. The interval reflects the blossoming of contusions: what begins as scattered petechial haemorrhage and oedema expands and coalesces over the first six to twenty-four hours, so a very early CT systematically underestimates the injury. It follows that a normal CT in the first hour does not exclude significant contusional injury, and that a patient with a persisting deficit, a falling GCS, coagulopathy or anticoagulation needs a repeat CT rather than reassurance, with MRI if the CT still fails to explain the clinical state.
quiz.explain: The anatomy is why contusions are so predictable: the anterior and middle cranial fossae are ridged and sharp, while the occipital bone and the posterior fossa are smooth, so occipital contusions are comparatively rare and inferior frontal and anterior temporal ones are the default. Two practical consequences follow. First, when a CT of a head injury looks normal, those two sites deserve a deliberate second look on a narrow window, because a small contusion against dense bone is easily lost. Second, expansion is the rule rather than the exception in the first day, so the question after a head injury CT is not only what is on it but when it was done - and in an anticoagulated patient, a normal early scan is the beginning of the observation, not the end of it.

nodes.title: Spine MRI: Degeneration, Compression and Trauma
nodes.goal: Report displaced lumbar disc material in the agreed nomenclature, and separate the spinal emergencies from the incidental findings.

quiz.prompt: On the sagittal T2 image at L5/S1 the displaced disc material behind the vertebral body measures 13 mm craniocaudally at its widest, while its neck where it leaves the disc space measures 7 mm in the same plane. It occupies about 15 per cent of the disc circumference and remains continuous with the parent disc. How should this be reported in the standard lumbar disc nomenclature?
choices: A disc extrusion
A disc protrusion
A broad-based bulge
A sequestered fragment
quiz.answer: A disc extrusion
quiz.explain: The rule is geometric, and it is the only thing separating the first two words. Measure the greatest distance between the edges of the displaced material, then the distance between the edges of its base in the same plane: if the material beyond the disc space is wider than its base - 13 mm against a 7 mm neck - it is an extrusion, and if it is narrower or equal it is a protrusion. Continuity with the parent disc keeps it out of the sequestration category, which is reserved for a fragment that has lost that continuity. A bulge is a different animal altogether: disc tissue extending beyond the ring apophyses around more than a quarter of the circumference, a contour rather than a herniation, and 15 per cent is too little in any case. The words are not interchangeable in a report, because extrusions are more often symptomatic, more likely to migrate, and - counter-intuitively - more likely to resorb spontaneously, since exposed nucleus pulposus provokes a vascularised inflammatory response. Measure in the plane where the ratio is greatest: a herniation that looks contained on the sagittal may be an extrusion on the axial, and one plane is enough to make it one.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old with severe right L5 radiculopathy has an ovoid mass in the right lateral recess at the level of the L4 vertebral body, separate from the L4/5 disc, slightly brighter than that disc on T2, with a thin rim of enhancement after gadolinium and no central enhancement. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A migrated sequestered disc fragment
A synovial cyst from the facet joint
A nerve sheath tumour on the root
An early epidural abscess collection
quiz.answer: A migrated sequestered disc fragment
quiz.explain: Three features do the work. A fragment lying separate from its parent disc, having travelled cranially or caudally in the epidural space, is a sequestration; it is often brighter than the degenerate parent disc on T2 because it is hydrated and inflamed; and it typically shows a thin peripheral rim of enhancement from surrounding granulation tissue with a non-enhancing avascular centre. A nerve sheath tumour enhances solidly and throughout, is centred on the root rather than in the recess, and over time widens the foramen or scallops bone. A synovial cyst arises from a degenerate facet joint, sits posterolaterally against it, and usually has a low-signal rim and a demonstrable connection to the joint. An abscess would come with disc and endplate destruction, marrow oedema and systemic signs. The reporting consequence is practical: a fragment resorbs in a substantial proportion of patients, and if it is to be removed the surgeon needs to be told the parent level and the direction and distance of migration, because a fragment behind a vertebral body is not reached through a standard interlaminar approach to the disc.

quiz.prompt: A patient with recurrent left leg pain nine months after L5/S1 microdiscectomy has soft tissue in the left anterior epidural space at the operated level. Explain how you would use contrast to decide whether this is fibrosis or recurrent disc material, and why the timing of the post-contrast images matters.
quiz.answer: Give gadolinium and image early, within roughly ten to fifteen minutes. Epidural fibrosis is vascularised granulation tissue: it enhances immediately, homogeneously and throughout its substance, and it tends to be retractile rather than mass-like, drawing the thecal sac and root towards it. Recurrent disc material is avascular and does not enhance itself; what enhances is the vascularised tissue around it, so on early images it shows a peripheral rim of enhancement with a non-enhancing centre, and it is polypoid, has mass effect, and is continuous with the disc space. The timing matters because contrast diffuses passively into disc material over time, so on images acquired thirty minutes or more after injection the recurrent disc fills in and becomes indistinguishable from scar, turning a reliable sign into a misleading one.
quiz.explain: The distinction changes management directly, which is why it is worth protocolling properly: recurrent disc material can be re-operated, whereas re-operating on scar tends to make the patient worse and is the classic route into failed back surgery syndrome. Two refinements keep the sign honest. The two often coexist, so the question in practice is which component accounts for the mass effect on the symptomatic root, not which one is present. And mass effect is itself part of the argument - scar retracts and follows the contours of the thecal sac, disc material pushes. If the study cannot be done early after injection, say so in the report rather than calling the appearance for one or the other.

quiz.prompt: CT and MRI of the thoracolumbar junction show a burst fracture of L1 with retropulsion, the patient is neurologically intact, and STIR shows a widened interspinous space with high signal through the interspinous and supraspinous ligaments. What is the TLICS total? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: TLICS adds three components. Morphology: compression 1, burst 2, translation or rotation 3, distraction 4 - here 2. Neurological status: intact 0, nerve root 2, complete cord or conus injury 2, incomplete cord or conus injury 3, cauda equina 3 - here 0. Posterior ligamentous complex: intact 0, indeterminate 2, disrupted 3 - here 3, because interspinous widening with frank ligamentous high signal is disruption rather than suspicion. Total 5. A score of 3 or less is managed non-operatively, 4 is equivocal, and 5 or more points to surgery, so the MRI has just moved a neurologically intact patient into the operative group. That is the reason MRI is added to CT when the CT shows a burst fracture and the posterior elements are in doubt, and it is why the system weights the posterior ligamentous complex so heavily: it is the structure that governs mechanical stability and the one CT judges least well.

quiz.prompt: Put these four descriptions of displaced lumbar disc material in order of increasing displacement from the disc space, as the standard nomenclature grades them.
quiz.answer: bulge protrusion extrusion sequestration
quiz.explain: A bulge is not a herniation at all: it is disc tissue extending beyond the ring apophyses around more than a quarter of the circumference, a generalised change of contour that usually reflects age and degeneration. A protrusion is a localised herniation whose base is at least as wide as any part of the material beyond the disc space. An extrusion is a localised herniation that is wider beyond the disc space than at its base, so its neck is narrower than its dome. A sequestration is an extrusion that has lost continuity with the parent disc altogether. One term is often confused with this last: migration describes displacement away from the site of extrusion, cranially or caudally, and a migrated fragment may or may not be sequestered - the two words answer different questions, one about position and one about continuity.

quiz.prompt: A woman with metastatic breast cancer is referred for lumbar MRI because of two weeks of back pain. The lumbar study shows an epidural soft-tissue mass at T12 indenting the conus, and she has brisk reflexes in the legs and a sensory level. What is the most important next imaging step?
choices: MRI of the whole spine before treatment is planned
CT of the same level to assess the bony detail
Bone scintigraphy to stage the rest of the skeleton
Repeat MRI after dexamethasone has been started
quiz.answer: MRI of the whole spine before treatment is planned
quiz.explain: Roughly a third of patients with metastatic epidural spinal cord compression have compressive disease at more than one level, and the second site is often clinically silent because the first one is producing all the symptoms. Radiotherapy fields and surgical plans are drawn from the full extent of disease, so imaging only the symptomatic level risks treating one deposit and leaving another to compress the cord a fortnight later; national guidance accordingly asks for urgent whole-spine MRI in anyone with suspected metastatic cord compression. The distractors each answer a real but secondary question: CT characterises bone and vertebral body integrity for surgical planning, scintigraphy stages the skeleton, and steroids are started immediately - but none of them changes the immediate decision the way the extent of compressive disease does, and starting steroids is never a reason to delay or repeat the MRI.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have a large central disc extrusion: one at T9/T10 and one at L4/L5. Explain what determines whether the picture is cord compression or cauda equina compression, what each looks like clinically, and how far the MRI must extend.
quiz.answer: The determinant is the level of the conus medullaris, which in adults ends at about T12 to L1, with the lower limit of normal around the L2/L3 disc; a compressive lesion above it presses on the cord, one below it presses on the cauda equina. The T9/T10 extrusion therefore causes cord compression, with upper motor neurone signs below the level: spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, a sensory level, and T2 signal change within the cord if compression has been sustained. The L4/L5 extrusion compresses nerve roots and gives lower motor neurone signs: flaccid weakness, absent reflexes, bilateral radicular pain, saddle anaesthesia, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence. The MRI must cover the whole lumbosacral spine down to the sacrum, because a compressive lesion below the volume scanned is simply missed, and it must extend upwards whenever the signs are of cord rather than root disease, since the true upper level of the lesion may lie well above the symptomatic dermatome.
quiz.explain: Getting the compartment right is what makes the request sensible, because a referral for 'cord compression' at L4/5 asks for something anatomically impossible and often produces a scan that stops too high. Two refinements matter at the bedside. A conus lesion mixes the two pictures - early and severe bladder involvement with a combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs - and is the reason the transition zone is described separately. And retention is a late feature of cauda equina compression rather than an early one, so waiting for it before requesting the scan is how the diagnosis gets made too late; a raised post-void residual and loss of perianal sensation are the findings that should trigger imaging out of hours.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old with back pain after lifting has a collapsed L2 vertebral body. MRI shows a band of low T1 and high STIR signal running parallel to and beneath the superior endplate, with normal fatty marrow preserved through the rest of the body, retropulsion of the posterosuperior corner, normal pedicles and no paravertebral soft tissue. What does this favour?
choices: An acute osteoporotic insufficiency fracture
Metastatic collapse from an occult primary
Vertebral osteomyelitis with early collapse
Myelomatous involvement of the body
quiz.answer: An acute osteoporotic insufficiency fracture
quiz.explain: Five features in the stem point the same way. Band-like oedema parallel to the fractured endplate with normal marrow preserved elsewhere in the body means the marrow has been bruised, not replaced, whereas tumour replaces marrow diffusely and completely. Retropulsion of the posterosuperior corner is a mechanical failure pattern, while a convex bulge of the posterior cortex suggests an expanding tumour. Sparing of the pedicles matters because metastatic disease reaches the vertebra through the vascular supply of the posterior body and commonly takes the pedicle with it. And the absence of paravertebral or epidural soft tissue is decisive: tumour and infection both make soft tissue, mechanical failure does not. A fluid sign - a linear T2-bright cleft within the body - is another benign feature. Infection separates itself on the disc, which it destroys along with both adjacent endplates, whereas a fracture leaves the disc alone. Where the picture is genuinely equivocal, follow-up at six to twelve weeks showing resolving oedema, or a biopsy, settles it; diffusion helps but overlaps.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with chronic mechanical back pain has low T1 and high T2 signal in the marrow on both sides of the L4/5 disc. The disc space is narrowed, the disc itself is dark on T2 with a preserved intranuclear cleft, the endplates are irregular but continuous, and there is no paraspinal or epidural soft tissue. Inflammatory markers are normal. What does this represent?
choices: Type 1 degenerative endplate marrow change
Pyogenic discitis with early osteomyelitis
Metastasis crossing the L4/5 disc space
An acute Schmorl node with marrow oedema
quiz.answer: Type 1 degenerative endplate marrow change
quiz.explain: The marrow signal is identical in the two leading diagnoses - that is the trap, and it is why the disc rather than the marrow decides the case. In degenerative type 1 change the disc is desiccated and dark on T2 and keeps its intranuclear cleft, the endplates are irregular from wear but their cortical line is continuous, and there is no soft tissue. In pyogenic infection the disc is bright on T2 and loses the cleft early, the endplates are eroded with loss of the cortical line, and there is paraspinal or epidural inflammatory tissue that enhances. Type 1 change is vascularised fibrous marrow with oedema, and its natural history is to convert to type 2, fatty (bright on T1, iso to bright on T2), and later to type 3, sclerotic (dark on both). It matters because type 1 is the type most associated with pain and the one most often mistaken for infection. The exception that keeps a reader honest is tuberculous spondylitis, which tends to spare the disc and spread beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament, so a preserved disc does not exclude infection when the clinical picture fits.

quiz.prompt: A restrained front-seat passenger in a frontal collision has a fracture line running horizontally through the spinous process, both pedicles and the posterior body of L2, with anterior wedging, and bruising across the lower abdomen. Beyond the spine, what does this pattern oblige you to look for on the same CT?
choices: Bowel and mesenteric injury in the abdomen
Renal pedicle avulsion at the vascular hilum
Diaphragmatic rupture on the left side
Aortic injury at the level of the isthmus
quiz.answer: Bowel and mesenteric injury in the abdomen
quiz.explain: This is a flexion-distraction, or Chance, injury: the lap belt acts as a fulcrum across the abdomen, the spine hinges over it, the posterior elements fail in tension and the anterior body fails in compression. The same mechanism crushes bowel and mesentery between belt and spine, and the association is strong enough that the fracture should be treated as a marker for visceral injury - small bowel perforation, mesenteric tear and delayed devascularisation being the injuries that get missed on the first pass. Look for free fluid without solid organ injury, mesenteric fat stranding, bowel wall thickening and extraluminal gas. The spinal half of the answer is that this is a distraction morphology with a disrupted posterior ligamentous complex, which places it in the operative range even in a neurologically intact patient. It is also easy to miss on axial images alone, because a horizontal fracture line can run between slices: the sagittal reformats are where it is seen.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral radiograph of the thoracic spine a wedged vertebral body measures 13 mm in anterior height and 24 mm in posterior height, and the vertebrae above and below are of normal shape. Taking the posterior height as the reference, what percentage of the anterior height has been lost? Give the answer to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The loss is (24 - 13) / 24, which is 11/24, or 45.8 per cent, so 46 per cent. The semiquantitative Genant grading reads those bands as roughly 20 to 25 per cent height loss for grade 1 (mild), 25 to 40 per cent for grade 2 (moderate), and more than 40 per cent for grade 3 (severe), applied to anterior height (wedge), middle height (biconcave) or posterior height (crush). This vertebra is a grade 3 wedge deformity. Two practical points travel with the arithmetic. The reference should be the posterior height of the same vertebra when the neighbours are themselves deformed, since comparing with an abnormal neighbour understates the loss. And a vertebral fracture found on any imaging, including one seen incidentally on a CT requested for something else, is an osteoporotic fracture until proved otherwise and is among the strongest predictors of the next one, so it belongs in the conclusion of the report rather than buried in a list of degenerative findings.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows an L1 burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient, and the surgical team asks whether the posterior ligamentous complex is intact. State the sequence you would rely on, the findings that indicate disruption, and why the determination changes the plan.
quiz.answer: Sagittal STIR, or another fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequence; fat suppression is what makes ligamentous and interspinous oedema visible against fatty marrow and epidural fat. Disruption is indicated by high signal within or frank discontinuity of the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and the ligamentum flavum, widening of the interspinous distance compared with the levels above and below, fluid or widening in the facet joints, a perched or dislocated facet, and avulsion at a ligamentous attachment. It changes the plan because the posterior ligamentous complex is the principal restraint against progressive kyphosis and translation: with it intact, a burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient is usually braced, and with it disrupted the same fracture scores into the operative range and is stabilised. CT can only infer the state of the ligaments from bony spacing, which is why MRI is added whenever the answer would change management.
quiz.explain: The reason the classification systems put so much weight here is that the posterior ligamentous complex heals poorly, so a disrupted complex means the deformity will progress even if the bone unites. Two cautions keep the report defensible. MRI over-calls: isolated high signal in the interspinous fat or in the ligamentum flavum alone is common after any injury and is not by itself disruption, which is why the classification offers an 'indeterminate' category worth two points rather than forcing a binary. And the findings should be read together - widened interspinous distance with fluid in the facet joints and discontinuous ligaments is a different report from one equivocal finding in isolation. Say which of the three states you believe the complex is in, because the score, and the operation, follow from that word.

nodes.title: Approach to an Intracranial Mass
nodes.goal: Place an intracranial mass in the intra-axial or extra-axial compartment, then narrow it with enhancement, diffusion and perfusion.

quiz.prompt: A rounded 4 cm mass sits against the right frontal convexity. Between the mass and the brain there is a thin rim of cerebrospinal fluid containing vessels, the cortical grey matter is displaced inwards away from the inner table, and the underlying white matter is buckled rather than expanded. Where has the mass arisen?
choices: Outside the brain, from the dural surface
Within the cortex of the frontal lobe
Within the subcortical white matter
Inside the frontal horn of the ventricle
quiz.answer: Outside the brain, from the dural surface
quiz.explain: The compartment question is answered before any question of histology, because it halves the differential at a stroke. The extra-axial signs are all displacements: a cerebrospinal fluid cleft, pial vessels running between the mass and the brain, grey matter pushed inwards so that the cortical ribbon lies between the mass and the white matter, buckling of the white matter, a widened subarachnoid space, and reaction in the adjacent bone. An intra-axial mass does the opposite - it expands cortex or white matter, effaces the subarachnoid space, and has brain rather than fluid at its margin. Being systematic matters because a large extra-axial mass invaginating deeply can look intra-axial on a single axial image; coronal images and the position of the cortical ribbon resolve it. The differentials then diverge completely: meningioma, dural metastasis, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma and lymphoma outside the brain; glioma, metastasis, abscess and demyelination within it.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old treated for breast cancer three years ago has headache. MRI shows four separate dural-based enhancing masses over both convexities and along the falx, and CT shows lytic destruction of the inner table beneath the largest, with no hyperostosis. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Dural metastatic deposits from the breast primary
Multiple meningiomas in a predisposed patient
Neurosarcoidosis involving the pachymeninges
IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis
quiz.answer: Dural metastatic deposits from the breast primary
quiz.explain: Multiplicity alone does not settle it, since meningiomas are multiple in neurofibromatosis type 2, after cranial radiation, and occasionally sporadically - but the bone does. Meningioma provokes bone: hyperostosis, a thickened sclerotic inner table, sometimes a permeative sclerotic pattern with tumour inside it. Metastasis destroys bone. Add a treated breast primary, the commonest source of dural metastases, and the diagnosis follows. The near-misses are worth holding: sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease thicken the dura in a more sheet-like, less nodular fashion and come with other clues - in sarcoid, leptomeningeal enhancement around the basal cisterns and involvement of the infundibulum and cranial nerves - and neither destroys bone. Solitary fibrous tumour, the entity that absorbed haemangiopericytoma, is the trap for a solitary lesion: narrow dural attachment, prominent internal flow voids, and bone erosion rather than hyperostosis. Saying this out loud in the report matters, because dural metastases change the whole management conversation and 'dural-based masses, likely meningiomas' closes it down.

quiz.prompt: A convexity mass has a tapering rim of thickened enhancing dura extending from each of its margins, and the neurosurgeon takes this as confirming a meningioma. Explain what this sign does and does not establish, and why it still matters to the operation.
quiz.answer: The tapering enhancing dural thickening - the dural tail - establishes that the mass is extra-axial and dural-based, which is genuinely useful, but it does not establish histology. It is seen in most meningiomas and also in dural metastases, lymphoma, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma, sarcoidosis and other pachymeningeal disease, so it is sensitive rather than specific. Histologically the tail may be tumour infiltrating the dura or merely reactive, hypervascular, oedematous dura, and imaging cannot separate the two. It matters to the operation because the tail may contain tumour: completeness of resection of the dural attachment is what the Simpson grading records and what predicts recurrence, so the surgeon plans to excise or coagulate the involved dura rather than the mass alone, and the report should state how far the tail extends and what it runs into, such as a venous sinus.
quiz.explain: What a sign is worth depends on the population it is used in. In a series of convexity masses the dural tail is common in meningiomas and uncommon in gliomas, so it is a good compartment sign; among dural-based masses, where every lesion has one, it discriminates nothing. That is the general lesson: a sign that separates two categories well can be useless one level further down the tree, and the tail is the neuroradiological example. The other half of the lesson is surgical. Simpson grade 1 resection - the mass, its dural attachment and any abnormal bone - carries the lowest recurrence rate, and grades rise as attachment is left behind, so the extent of the tail is an operative planning measurement rather than a descriptive flourish.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old with fever and a recent dental extraction has a 3 cm ring-enhancing left frontal lesion with surrounding oedema. The enhancing rim is smooth, thin, and thinner on the side facing the ventricle, and the centre is markedly bright on diffusion-weighted imaging with an apparent diffusion coefficient well below that of normal white matter. What is the lesion?
choices: A pyogenic abscess containing pus
A metastasis with a necrotic centre
A glioblastoma with central necrosis
A tumefactive demyelinating lesion
quiz.answer: A pyogenic abscess containing pus
quiz.explain: Pus is viscous, cellular and protein-rich, so water motion within it is genuinely restricted: the cavity is bright on diffusion with a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and this is among the most reliable signs in neuroimaging for separating an abscess from a necrotic tumour. Tumour necrosis is liquefied and acellular and has a high coefficient. Two further clues sit in the stem. An abscess rim is smooth and thin and is characteristically thinner along its deep margin, because the deep white matter is less well vascularised than the cortex - which is also why abscesses rupture into the ventricle rather than outwards - and it is often low in signal on T2, sometimes with a dual rim on susceptibility imaging. A glioblastoma rim is thick, irregular and nodular. Cautions: a treated abscess loses its restriction, some tumours restrict after haemorrhage, and spectroscopy adds amino acids, acetate and succinate to the argument, so the clinical trajectory stays in the reasoning rather than being replaced by one sequence.

quiz.prompt: A solitary ring-enhancing mass in the right parietal lobe is surrounded by extensive T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion shows relative cerebral blood volume markedly elevated in the enhancing rim, and moderately elevated in the non-enhancing hyperintense region beyond it. What does the perfusion of the region beyond the enhancement favour?
choices: A glioma infiltrating past the enhancing margin
A solitary metastasis with vasogenic oedema
An abscess with surrounding cerebritis
Radiation necrosis of the white matter
quiz.answer: A glioma infiltrating past the enhancing margin
quiz.explain: Enhancement marks where the blood-brain barrier has failed, which in a high-grade glioma is only the core; the tumour cells themselves extend well beyond it along white matter tracts, into brain that looks merely oedematous. Those infiltrated regions carry neovascularity with them, so relative cerebral blood volume in the peritumoural T2 signal is raised. Around a metastasis the same region is pure vasogenic oedema - plasma driven out through leaky capillaries into the extracellular space, with no tumour cells in it - and its blood volume is low. That difference is one of the few imaging tools that separates a solitary metastasis from a glioblastoma when the conventional images look alike, and it is why the surgical margin and the radiotherapy volume differ so much between the two diagnoses. Caveats worth carrying: the sequence needs preload and leakage correction, because contrast escaping through a broken barrier corrupts the estimate; susceptibility from blood products and from skull base bone degrades the maps; and the finding shifts a probability rather than settling a diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion of a cerebral mass gives a leakage-corrected cerebral blood volume of 5.8 mL per 100 g in the most vascular part of the lesion, while a region of interest in normal-appearing contralateral white matter gives 1.6 mL per 100 g. What is the relative cerebral blood volume ratio? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 5.8 divided by 1.6 is 3.6. The ratio is what gets reported rather than the absolute value, because absolute blood volume from this technique depends on the arterial input function, the injection, the sequence and the vendor, and only the comparison against the patient's own normal white matter is stable across studies. Ratios of roughly 1.75 are commonly used to separate high-grade from low-grade glioma, and 3.6 sits well into the high-grade range - but the threshold shifts with technique and with the leakage correction applied, so it belongs in a report as a supporting argument rather than as a grade. Two traps: sample the most vascular part of the tumour, since a single large region of interest across a heterogeneous mass averages the answer away, and do not sample a vessel, which turns any tumour into a high-grade one instantly. The standing exception is the oligodendroglioma, which often has high blood volume from its dense capillary network despite being low-grade.

quiz.prompt: Rank these five tissues by their typical apparent diffusion coefficient, from the lowest value to the highest.
quiz.answer: abscess-pus lymphoma glioblastoma vasogenic-oedema cerebrospinal-fluid
quiz.explain: The apparent diffusion coefficient measures how freely water moves, so the sequence runs from the most crowded and most viscous compartment to free fluid. Pus is viscous and packed with inflammatory cells, debris and protein and sits at the bottom. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is the most cellular of the common tumours - small round cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and scant extracellular space - so its coefficient is low, generally below that of gliomas and below normal white matter, which is why a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with a low coefficient in an immunocompetent adult is lymphoma until proved otherwise. The solid part of a glioblastoma is cellular but heterogeneously so, and sits in the middle. Vasogenic oedema is extracellular water in a widened extracellular space and diffuses more freely than normal brain. Cerebrospinal fluid is essentially free water and is the highest, which is why it is dark on the high-b image and bright on the map. The practical rule that follows: read the map, not the diffusion-weighted image, because T2 shine-through makes anything T2-bright look restricted.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after completing chemoradiotherapy for an MGMT-methylated glioblastoma, the MRI shows new enhancement at the resection margin with more surrounding FLAIR signal. The patient is clinically well and on a reducing dose of dexamethasone. Explain the two possibilities, what favours each, and what you would do.
quiz.answer: The two possibilities are true progression and pseudoprogression, a treatment effect in which radiation and temozolomide cause endothelial injury, inflammation and increased permeability, producing new or enlarging enhancement without tumour growth. Pseudoprogression is favoured here by the timing, since most cases appear within three months of finishing chemoradiotherapy; by MGMT promoter methylation, which is strongly associated with it; and by a patient who is clinically stable or improving. True progression is favoured by clinical deterioration, by enhancement appearing outside the high-dose radiation field, and by elevated relative cerebral blood volume, whereas pseudoprogression tends to show low blood volume; diffusion, spectroscopy and amino-acid PET add weight but none is definitive. The action is not to declare progression: continue treatment and repeat the MRI at a short interval of about four to eight weeks, since the RANO framework does not call progression within twelve weeks of radiotherapy unless the new enhancement lies outside the high-dose field or there is histological proof.
quiz.explain: The mirror image of this error is worth learning at the same time. Under an antiangiogenic agent such as bevacizumab, the drug restores the blood-brain barrier and the enhancement melts away within days without the tumour having shrunk - pseudoresponse - which is why response on such treatment is judged on the non-enhancing T2 and FLAIR component rather than on the enhancing volume. Both errors have one root: enhancement is a property of the barrier, not of tumour cells, so any drug or injury that changes the barrier changes the picture without changing the disease. The clinical stakes are real in both directions, since calling pseudoprogression as progression stops an effective treatment early, and calling progression as pseudoprogression leaves a growing tumour untreated for two more months.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old presents with a first seizure. MRI shows a non-enhancing, expansile mass in the left frontal lobe that is homogeneously and markedly hyperintense on T2, while on FLAIR the same lesion is suppressed centrally with a bright peripheral rim. What does this appearance favour?
choices: An IDH-mutant astrocytoma, not codeleted
An oligodendroglioma, 1p/19q codeleted
An IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, grade 4
A tumefactive demyelinating plaque
quiz.answer: An IDH-mutant astrocytoma, not codeleted
quiz.explain: The T2-FLAIR mismatch sign - homogeneous high T2 signal with relative FLAIR suppression except at the rim - is among the most specific signs in neuro-oncology, approaching complete specificity for IDH-mutant astrocytoma without 1p/19q codeletion, while its sensitivity is low, so its absence says nothing at all. The likely substrate is the loosely structured, microcystic, water-rich matrix of these tumours: free water is bright on T2 and is nulled by the FLAIR inversion pulse, whereas the rim contains more cellular infiltrated tissue that resists nulling. Oligodendrogliomas, the other IDH-mutant tumour, are heterogeneous, frequently calcified, tend to involve the cortex, and characteristically lack the sign. A glioblastoma in a 32-year-old is possible but would usually enhance and rarely look this homogeneous. Under the 2021 WHO classification these molecular groups are the diagnosis rather than a refinement of it, so a sign that predicts the group changes the conversation before the biopsy. Apply the criteria strictly: the mismatch must involve most of the lesion, and a focal or cystic mismatch does not count.

quiz.prompt: An immunocompetent 68-year-old has a periventricular mass that is hyperattenuating on unenhanced CT, enhances homogeneously and avidly, has a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and shows strikingly little necrosis for its size. Neurosurgery plans a biopsy in four days, and the medical team wants to start dexamethasone now for the surrounding oedema. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Steroids can make the biopsy non-diagnostic
Steroids raise the risk of bleeding at biopsy
Steroids will mask the restricted diffusion
Steroids promote leptomeningeal spread here
quiz.answer: Steroids can make the biopsy non-diagnostic
quiz.explain: The imaging describes primary central nervous system lymphoma: dense on unenhanced CT because the tumour is so cellular, homogeneously enhancing, low in apparent diffusion coefficient for the same reason, periventricular and abutting the ependyma, and with little necrosis in an immunocompetent patient - necrosis and ring enhancement being the rule in the AIDS-related form instead. Lymphoma is exquisitely steroid-sensitive: corticosteroids are lympholytic and can dissolve the enhancing mass within days, the old 'ghost tumour', leaving a biopsy that shows reactive gliosis and debris and forcing either weeks of waiting for the tumour to return or a second procedure. The radiologist's job when this pattern appears is therefore to say in the report that lymphoma leads the differential and that steroids should be withheld until tissue is obtained, unless impending herniation makes them unavoidable. The distractors fail in different ways: steroids do not cause bleeding, do not abolish the low coefficient of the tissue that remains, and do not disseminate the tumour.

quiz.prompt: A diffuse glioma in a young adult does not enhance at all, while the pituitary gland, the choroid plexus and a small meningioma in the same patient enhance intensely. Explain what enhancement is actually measuring, and what follows for judging whether a lesion is benign.
quiz.answer: Gadolinium enhancement measures delivery of contrast into the extracellular space, which requires that contrast can leave the vasculature. It therefore maps where the blood-brain barrier is absent or broken, not where tumour is. The pituitary, choroid plexus, pineal gland, dura and area postrema lie outside the barrier and have fenestrated capillaries, so they enhance normally, as does a meningioma, which is fed by dural vessels that never had a barrier. A diffuse glioma grows through brain whose capillaries retain intact tight junctions, so it can be extensive and still not enhance at all. It follows that absence of enhancement is not evidence that a lesion is benign - a non-enhancing diffuse astrocytoma is still a tumour that infiltrates and eventually progresses, and its grade is set by histology and molecular findings rather than by enhancement - and that enhancement in a treated tumour may reflect a barrier damaged by surgery, radiation or infarction rather than tumour itself.
quiz.explain: The consequences run in both directions and both are common errors.
