Reading enhancement as a proxy for malignancy under-calls the non-enhancing diffuse gliomas, which under the 2021 WHO classification may reach grade 4 on molecular grounds alone - homozygous deletion of CDKN2A/B in an IDH-mutant astrocytoma, for instance, makes it grade 4 without necrosis or microvascular proliferation being present. Reading it the other way over-calls, because a subacute infarct, an area of demyelination, radiation injury and postoperative granulation tissue all enhance briskly. The practical habit is to describe enhancement as a finding about the barrier, then argue about the cause using the company it keeps: territory, diffusion, perfusion, time course and what the patient has already been treated with.

quiz.prompt: An incidental convexity meningioma measured 24 mm in maximum diameter three years ago and measures 31 mm on the current study. Treating the lesion as a sphere, by what factor has its volume increased? Give the answer to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Volume scales with the cube of a linear dimension, so 31 over 24 cubed is 2.2: a 29 per cent increase in diameter is a 116 per cent increase in volume. That is why a surveillance report reading 'minimally increased, 24 to 31 mm' can be so misleading - the tumour has more than doubled. It is also why measurement error deserves respect, since 2 mm of interobserver variation on a 24 mm lesion swings the implied volume by more than a quarter; growth should be judged against the earliest available study rather than the immediately preceding one, and measured on the same plane and sequence each time. For meningiomas specifically, a demonstrable growth rate, T2 hyperintensity, absence of calcification, peritumoural oedema and younger patient age all favour a tumour that will keep growing, and a growing meningioma in an operable location is treated before it becomes a symptomatic one.

nodes.title: The Acute Abdomen
nodes.goal: Read an acute abdominal CT for free gas, obstruction and inflammation, find the transition point, and tell mechanical obstruction from ileus.

quiz.prompt: A supine abdominal radiograph is taken on the intensive care unit for distension. Gas outlines both the inner and the outer surface of a loop of bowel in the right upper quadrant, and a thin vertical line runs to the right of the midline from the liver towards the umbilicus. What do these two findings together indicate?
choices: Free intraperitoneal gas, visible on a supine film
Gas within the portal venous branches of the liver
Gas confined to the wall of the ascending colon
Colon interposed between liver and diaphragm
quiz.answer: Free intraperitoneal gas, visible on a supine film
quiz.explain: Both signs need gas outside the lumen. Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of the bowel wall, which can only happen when free gas lies against the serosa while luminal gas lies against the mucosa; the vertical line is the falciform ligament, visible because free gas has outlined it. That both appear on a supine film matters, because a supine film is often all a ventilated patient can manage and the classic erect view is unavailable. Portal venous gas is branching and lies within the liver, reaching its periphery, rather than tracing a bowel wall. Pneumatosis alone gives a curvilinear lucency in the wall but produces no falciform sign, and it is exactly what Rigler's sign is contrasted against. Colonic interposition, Chilaiditi's appearance, mimics free gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm on an erect film, but haustral folds run through the lucency and it does not outline anything from outside. Where doubt remains, CT settles it, and a left lateral decubitus film is the fallback where CT is not to hand.

quiz.prompt: A CT for abdominal distension measures the small bowel at 2.6 cm, the transverse colon at 7.2 cm and the caecum at 9.4 cm, each outer wall to outer wall. Taking the conventional 3, 6 and 9 cm calibre limits for those three segments, how many of the measurements exceed their own limit? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Small bowel at 2.6 cm is within its 3 cm limit; transverse colon at 7.2 cm exceeds 6; caecum at 9.4 cm exceeds 9. Two of the three. The caecum is the one to watch: it is the widest part of the colon, and by Laplace's law wall tension at a given pressure rises with radius, so it is where a distal large bowel obstruction perforates when the ileocaecal valve stays competent and turns the colon into a closed loop. Treat the numbers as a prompt to look rather than as a diagnosis. Calibre says only that bowel is distended; whether that distension is mechanical depends on finding a point where the calibre changes, and a colon dilated evenly through to the rectum is far more likely to be ileus or acute colonic pseudo-obstruction than a blockage.

quiz.prompt: A CT is reported for a suspected closed-loop small bowel obstruction. Put these steps of the search in the order that first identifies the closed loop and then judges whether it is still viable.
quiz.answer: dilated-loops first-transition second-transition mesenteric-whirl wall-enhancement
quiz.explain: Recognise dilated small bowel; track it distally to the point where calibre drops, which is the first transition; then look immediately around that point for a second transition, because a closed loop is bowel obstructed at two points close together, usually where a band or a hernial neck catches it. The C-shaped or U-shaped loop between them has its own mesentery, and following that mesentery back shows the vessels converging and twisting, the whirl. Only then ask about viability, on wall enhancement, mural thickening, mesenteric fluid and venous engorgement. The order is not arbitrary: viability is judged on the loop you have identified, and a reader who starts by hunting for signs of ischaemia across the whole abdomen finds thickened bowel everywhere and localises nothing. A closed loop is the configuration that strangulates, so finding the second transition is what converts an overnight obstruction into a theatre case.

quiz.prompt: Four days after an open colectomy a patient is distended and not passing flatus. CT shows small bowel loops to 3.4 cm, several air-fluid levels and mildly oedematous folds, and no point at which the bowel calibre changes. Which single further observation would most strongly support ileus rather than mechanical obstruction?
choices: Gas and faecal residue reaching the rectum
Fluid levels at different heights in one loop
Circumferential thickening of the dilated wall
A collapsed segment of distal small bowel
quiz.answer: Gas and faecal residue reaching the rectum
quiz.explain: The absence of a transition point is a negative finding, and negatives are weak: a transition can be subtle, and a low-grade or intermittent obstruction hides one. The positive finding is that content is still moving the whole way through. Gas and residue in a non-dilated rectum say the lumen is patent from duodenum to anus, which no complete mechanical obstruction permits. A collapsed segment of distal small bowel is the opposite observation, and is precisely what a transition point looks like. Differential air-fluid levels within a single loop have been taught for decades as a sign of obstruction; they are neither sensitive nor specific enough to decide a case, but they lean towards a mechanical cause rather than away from it. Wall thickening happens in both and comments on oedema or perfusion, not on mechanism. Postoperative ileus settles with time and correction of electrolytes and opiates; the reason to keep looking is that early postoperative mechanical obstruction, from adhesions or an internal hernia, is indistinguishable at the bedside.

quiz.prompt: CT in a patient with three days of vomiting shows dilated jejunal and proximal ileal loops. In the 20 cm of ileum immediately upstream of a calibre change there is mottled, particulate material mixed with gas that resembles colonic content. What does that material signify?
choices: Stasis in obstructed small bowel, marking the level
Ischaemia of the wall of the obstructed segment
Reflux of colonic content across the ileocaecal valve
Bacterial overgrowth producing a functional ileus
quiz.answer: Stasis in obstructed small bowel, marking the level
quiz.explain: This is the small bowel faeces sign: undigested residue mixed with gas from bacterial fermentation, in a segment where water has been resorbed during prolonged stasis. Its practical value is topographic. It tends to sit just proximal to the transition, so on a study where the calibre change is hard to see, following the mottled material distally leads to it. It says the obstruction has been present for a while rather than that it is severe, and it appears in chronic partial obstruction too. It is not a sign of ischaemia: that question is answered by wall enhancement, mesenteric fluid and vascular engorgement, and a reader who takes the faeces sign as reassurance or as alarm has read it for the wrong thing. Nor is it retrograde colonic content, which does not cross a competent ileocaecal valve in this fashion.

quiz.prompt: A closed-loop small bowel obstruction is confirmed on CT. The loop is thick-walled, there is fluid in the adjacent mesentery, the mesenteric vessels converging on the twist are engorged, and one part of the loop takes up less contrast than the rest of the bowel on the portal venous phase. Which of these observations is the most specific for strangulation?
choices: Enhancement of the wall reduced against other loops
Free fluid tracking through the adjacent mesentery
Circumferential thickening of the obstructed wall
Engorgement of the vessels running to the twist
quiz.answer: Enhancement of the wall reduced against other loops
quiz.explain: Reduced or absent mural enhancement is the sign that speaks directly to perfusion, and it is the most specific of the four for strangulation; where it is unequivocal, the bowel in question is at risk now. The other three are sensitive and unspecific. Mesenteric fluid, mural thickening and vascular engorgement all follow venous congestion, which begins long before arterial supply fails and is present in plenty of obstructions that recover without resection. The trap is the reverse of the usual one: their absence is reassuring, but their presence is not damning, and a report that lists them without commenting on enhancement has answered the easy question. Two cautions on the enhancement itself. Compare like with like, against non-obstructed loops on the same phase, since a hypotensive patient enhances poorly everywhere; and remember that a thin, poorly enhancing wall can look deceptively normal on a single phase, which is why the finding is sought on the portal venous phase where mural enhancement is at its most uniform.

quiz.prompt: A CT in a 26-year-old with right iliac fossa pain shows an appendix of 7 mm outer diameter with a normal thin wall, no periappendiceal fat stranding, no free fluid, and gas throughout its lumen. The registrar wants to report appendicitis on the diameter alone. Set out why the diameter by itself will not carry that report, and say what you would look for instead.
quiz.answer: A diameter above about 6 mm is sensitive but poorly specific: normal appendices are distensible and commonly measure between 6 and 10 mm, particularly when gas-filled, so 7 mm on its own separates nothing. The findings that make the diagnosis are the secondary ones, and they should be sought together: mural thickening with hyperenhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding, free fluid, an appendicolith, thickening of the adjacent caecal apex, and failure of the lumen to fill with gas or with oral contrast. An appendix that is gas-filled along its length, thin-walled and surrounded by clean fat is very unlikely to be inflamed whatever its calibre, and a report should say so rather than hedge.
quiz.explain: The 6 mm figure entered practice from graded-compression ultrasound, where the appendix is compressed and a distended one cannot be flattened. Transposed to CT, where nothing compresses the appendix, the same number keeps its sensitivity and loses much of its specificity, because a normal appendix filled with gas or with a little fluid readily exceeds it. That is why every published CT series reads diameter alongside secondary signs, and why the confident negative report rests on gas through the lumen, a thin wall and clean surrounding fat rather than on a measurement. The corollary matters for the report a surgeon can act on: hedging over a normal-looking appendix at 7 mm generates observation, repeat imaging and sometimes an operation, all of which cost more than a clear statement supported by the findings actually present.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with free gas remote from the colon and free fluid across the peritoneum; at laparoscopy there is generalised purulent contamination with no faeculent soiling. Which modified Hinchey stage does that describe? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The modified, imaging-based Hinchey scheme runs: stage I, inflammation confined to the pericolic tissues, with Ia a phlegmon and Ib a pericolic abscess; stage II, a pelvic, distant intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal abscess; stage III, generalised purulent peritonitis; stage IV, generalised faecal peritonitis. Purulent contamination without faecal soiling is III. The grades are not a taxonomy for its own sake. I and II are usually managed with antibiotics and, where the collection is large enough to warrant it, percutaneous drainage; III and IV go to theatre, and whether the peritoneum contains pus or faeces separates the two operative grades and tracks with mortality. Free gas by itself does not fix the stage: a small locule beside an inflamed segment sits comfortably within stage I, and it is the distribution of gas and fluid, read against the state of the patient, that says how far the perforation has spread.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has left iliac fossa pain. CT shows sigmoid wall thickening with numerous diverticula and pericolic fat stranding. Which additional finding would shift the reading furthest towards carcinoma rather than diverticulitis?
choices: Enlarged pericolic nodes beside a short thick segment
Fluid tracking at the root of the sigmoid mesentery
Engorged vasa recta feeding the thickened segment
Inflammation out of proportion to the wall thickening
quiz.answer: Enlarged pericolic nodes beside a short thick segment
quiz.explain: The two diseases share the sigmoid, the wall thickening and, often enough, the diverticula, and a carcinoma can perforate and inflame exactly as diverticulitis does. The features that discriminate are the length of the abnormal segment and the company it keeps. A short segment with shouldered, abrupt margins and enlarged pericolic nodes is the carcinoma pattern; a long segment, more than about 10 cm, with fat stranding out of proportion to the degree of mural thickening, engorged vasa recta and fluid at the root of the sigmoid mesentery is the diverticulitis pattern. The three distractors are all diverticulitis findings, which is what makes them tempting to a reader who has already settled on the diagnosis. Carry away the limit of the exercise: none of these signs is decisive, CT cannot exclude a carcinoma hidden in an inflamed segment, and that is why an episode of complicated diverticulitis is followed by colonoscopy once the inflammation has resolved.

quiz.prompt: Five days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy a well, afebrile patient with a soft abdomen has an erect chest radiograph for a cough, and gas is seen beneath both hemidiaphragms. Explain how you would interpret that film, and what would make you treat the same finding as a leak.
quiz.answer: Gas introduced at surgery is absorbed over days, and how long it takes varies with the volume left behind, with the route of surgery and with the patient's build, so the interval alone cannot separate residual gas from a fresh perforation. In a patient who is well, afebrile and has a soft abdomen, a small volume at this stage is expected, and the useful next step is comparison with earlier films rather than an intervention. What changes the reading is the trend and the company the gas keeps: a volume that is increasing rather than shrinking across serial films, a new or unexpectedly large collection of gas, free fluid, a collection with an enteric or biliary character, or any of pain, fever, tachycardia and rising inflammatory markers. Then the study to do is CT, and the object is to find the leak itself rather than to count the gas.
quiz.explain: This is a question about what a finding means rather than about what it is, and the answer is that free gas after an operation is uninterpretable in isolation. The single most useful piece of information is the previous film, because a shrinking volume of gas in a patient who is improving needs nothing at all, while the same volume growing in a patient who is not is an anastomotic leak until proved otherwise. Note which way the error runs in practice: the common mistake is not calling a leak free gas, but calling a leak nothing because the patient has recently been operated on. The clinical state carries most of the weight, and radiology's job is to say whether the gas is accompanied by fluid, by a collection, or by a defect, and to compare it with what was there yesterday.

quiz.prompt: An abdominal CT in a hypotensive septic patient shows branching lucencies within the liver that extend to within 2 cm of the capsule, together with curvilinear gas in the wall of a segment of small bowel. Which reading of the hepatic gas fits its distribution, and why?
choices: Portal venous gas, since portal flow runs outward
Biliary gas, since bile drains towards the hilum
Abscess gas, since abscesses form peripherally
Arterial gas, injected during line insertion
quiz.answer: Portal venous gas, since portal flow runs outward
quiz.explain: Distribution settles it. Portal venous flow is centrifugal, from the hilum outwards, so gas carried in it reaches the subcapsular branches and appears within 2 cm of the liver edge. Bile flows the other way, towards the hilum, so pneumobilia collects centrally and characteristically stops short of the periphery; that 2 cm rule is the discriminator, and it is worth having, because the two look otherwise identical. An abscess produces a focal collection of gas with a wall, not branching lucencies following vessels. Read the finding with its companion: gas in the bowel wall together with portal venous gas in a hypotensive septic patient is bowel ischaemia until proved otherwise, and the pair is what earns an urgent surgical conversation. The caution is that either finding alone can be benign. Pneumatosis occurs with chronic obstructive lung disease, steroids, chemotherapy and after endoscopy, and portal venous gas after instrumentation or in a patient with none of the clinical picture. It is the physiology, not the gas, that decides.

quiz.prompt: Appendicitis is usually described as an obstructed appendix failing in stages. Put these events in the order in which they occur.
quiz.answer: luminal-obstruction appendiceal-distension mural-hyperenhancement periappendiceal-stranding extraluminal-abscess
quiz.explain: An appendicolith, lymphoid hyperplasia or, in older patients, a tumour obstructs the lumen; continued mucus secretion distends it past 6 mm; rising intraluminal pressure inflames the wall, which thickens and hyperenhances; transmural inflammation spreads into the periappendiceal fat and produces free fluid; and finally the wall gives way, with extraluminal gas, a phlegmon or a walled-off abscess. The reason to hold the sequence is that the findings appear in that order on imaging. A distended appendix with a normal wall and clean fat is either very early or not appendicitis at all, while stranding without an enlarged appendix should send you looking for another cause, such as right-sided diverticulitis, epiploic appendagitis, terminal ileitis or a perforated caecal tumour. One inversion is worth expecting: hyperenhancement is lost rather than gained once a segment becomes gangrenous, so a focal defect in an otherwise enhancing wall is a late and serious finding, not a reassuring one.

nodes.title: The Liver Lesion
nodes.goal: Characterise a hepatic lesion from its behaviour across contrast phases, and apply LI-RADS correctly in a patient at risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

quiz.prompt: A 38 mm liver lesion is found on a staging CT in a woman with breast cancer. On the late arterial phase there are two discrete peripheral nodules of enhancement whose attenuation matches the aorta; on the portal venous phase the enhancement has extended inward; at five minutes the lesion is almost uniformly filled and still dense. Which reading does this pattern support?
choices: A haemangioma, from the blood-pool enhancement
A hypervascular metastasis from the breast
A hepatocellular carcinoma with a capsule
An abscess with a rim of enhancement
quiz.answer: A haemangioma, from the blood-pool enhancement
quiz.explain: The discriminator is not that the lesion enhances at its edge but that the enhancing parts track the blood pool. Discontinuous globular nodules matching the aorta in the arterial phase, then matching the portal vein and the blood pool later, filling centripetally and staying dense at five minutes, is the behaviour of a lesion whose contents are blood in wide vascular spaces. A hypervascular metastasis is the near miss and it fails on three counts: its rim is continuous rather than nodular, its enhancement is not isodense to the aorta, and it washes out relative to liver on the delayed phase rather than staying dense. A hepatocellular carcinoma in a non-cirrhotic liver is improbable to begin with, and it enhances diffusely then washes out with a late-enhancing capsule. An abscess has a continuous enhancing wall around fluid that does not fill in, usually with a zone of transient perilesional enhancement. Two haemangioma variants to keep in mind: the small flash-filling lesion, which enhances uniformly in the arterial phase and then simply follows the blood pool, and the giant lesion with a central fibrous scar that stays unfilled at five minutes.

quiz.prompt: An observation in a cirrhotic liver measured 14 mm on a CT five months ago and measures 21 mm today, on comparable phases and in the same plane. Express the increase in diameter as a percentage of the earlier diameter. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 21 minus 14 is 7, and 7 over 14 is 50 per cent. That figure is the LI-RADS v2018 definition of threshold growth: an increase in diameter of 50 per cent or more within six months or less. Threshold growth ranks with nonrim arterial phase hyperenhancement, nonperipheral washout and an enhancing capsule as a major feature, so on its own it can lift an observation a category. Two disciplines go with it. Growth that is real but slower, or measured across a longer interval, is not threshold growth; it is an ancillary feature favouring malignancy, which can raise a category but can never take an observation to LR-5. And a diameter comparison is worth no more than the two measurements in it, since a different phase, a different plane or a different observer will shift a 14 mm lesion by a couple of millimetres with no biology involved at all, which is why the comparison is made on the same phase and, where possible, by the same method.

quiz.prompt: A 63-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has a surveillance multiphase CT with an extracellular contrast agent. A 15 mm observation in segment 8 shows nonrim arterial phase hyperenhancement and nonperipheral washout on the portal venous phase. There is no enhancing capsule, no targetoid feature and no prior imaging for comparison. Which LI-RADS v2018 category does the diagnostic table give?
choices: LR-3, intermediate probability of malignancy
LR-4, probably hepatocellular carcinoma
LR-5, definitely hepatocellular carcinoma
LR-M, probably malignant but not specific
quiz.answer: LR-4, probably hepatocellular carcinoma
quiz.explain: The table is read on three things: whether there is nonrim arterial phase hyperenhancement, the size, and how many of the three additional major features are present, those being nonperipheral washout, an enhancing capsule and threshold growth. With arterial hyperenhancement and a diameter under 20 mm, one additional feature gives LR-4 and two are needed for LR-5. Washout is the only one here. Move the identical lesion to 25 mm and arterial hyperenhancement plus washout is LR-5, and that is the cell most readers remember, which is why this one is so often misassigned. The size threshold is not bureaucracy. LR-5 is the category on which hepatocellular carcinoma is diagnosed and treated without tissue, and its near-total specificity is what makes that safe; a small observation with a single additional feature is not specific enough to carry a diagnosis of that weight. LR-M is unavailable because targetoid features are stated to be absent. LR-4 is not a dead end either: it goes to the multidisciplinary meeting for short-interval follow-up, imaging with a different agent or modality, or biopsy.

quiz.prompt: A liver MRI using gadoxetate disodium acquires a dynamic multiphase series and a late series. Put these acquisitions in the order in which they are obtained.
quiz.answer: unenhanced late-arterial portal-venous transitional hepatobiliary
quiz.explain: The unenhanced series is the baseline against which enhancement is judged and the only one that shows intrinsic T1 hyperintensity, from fat, blood or copper. The late arterial phase, some fifteen to twenty seconds after contrast reaches the aorta, is defined by the portal vein being enhanced while the hepatic veins are not yet, and it is where arterial phase hyperenhancement is assessed. The portal venous phase, at roughly a minute, is where washout and the capsule are judged with this agent. The transitional phase, at around two to five minutes, is neither one thing nor the other: the extracellular contribution is falling while hepatocyte uptake is rising. The hepatobiliary phase, at about twenty minutes and later in a dysfunctional liver, shows which lesions contain working hepatocytes. Gadoxetate buys that last phase at a price, since its lower gadolinium dose and the arterial-phase transient dyspnoea some patients get make the arterial phase harder to obtain cleanly than with an extracellular agent.

quiz.prompt: A cirrhotic patient's MRI uses gadoxetate disodium. A 22 mm observation in segment 6 shows nonrim arterial phase hyperenhancement and is hypointense to the surrounding liver on the three-minute images. The trainee records nonperipheral washout and assigns LR-5. Explain what is wrong with that reasoning, and where washout may legitimately be judged with this agent.
quiz.answer: The three-minute images are the transitional phase, in which hepatocytes have already begun to take up the agent, so the signal of the background liver is rising while the signal of the lesion is not. Almost any lesion without functioning hepatocytes therefore looks relatively hypointense at that time, whether or not it truly washes out; this is pseudo-washout, a property of the background rather than of the lesion. With a hepatobiliary agent, LI-RADS confines the assessment of washout, and of the enhancing capsule, to the portal venous phase; the transitional and hepatobiliary phases contribute ancillary features only, and low signal on either favours malignancy without being a major feature. Read properly, this observation has arterial phase hyperenhancement and no confirmed additional major feature.
quiz.explain: Everything here follows from what the agent does. Gadoxetate behaves like an extracellular agent early and like a hepatocyte-specific agent late, and the transitional phase is the crossover where the two behaviours are mixed. Since washout is defined as a lesion becoming hypo-enhancing relative to liver, and the liver's own enhancement is climbing during the transitional phase for reasons that have nothing to do with the lesion, the observation is confounded by design. That is the whole reason LI-RADS narrows the window with this agent. The practical cost of getting it wrong is asymmetric: pseudo-washout upgrades benign and indeterminate nodules towards LR-5, and LR-5 is the category that ends investigation and starts treatment. An observation with arterial phase hyperenhancement and nothing else confirmed is LR-3 or LR-4 depending on size, and the honest report says which phase each feature was judged on.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive has a 5 cm liver lesion found incidentally. On gadoxetate MRI it enhances avidly and homogeneously in the late arterial phase, becomes isointense to liver on the portal venous phase, has a central area bright on T2-weighted images that enhances on the delayed phase, and is iso- to hyperintense to liver at twenty minutes. Which feature does most to separate focal nodular hyperplasia from hepatocellular adenoma?
choices: Iso- to hyperintensity on the hepatobiliary phase
Homogeneous hyperenhancement in the late arterial
A central scar bright on the T2-weighted series
Loss of signal on the opposed-phase gradient echo
quiz.answer: Iso- to hyperintensity on the hepatobiliary phase
quiz.explain: Focal nodular hyperplasia is made of hepatocytes with disorganised biliary drainage, so it takes up a hepatobiliary agent much as liver does and then excretes it poorly, and stays iso- or hyperintense at twenty minutes. Most adenoma subtypes lack that behaviour and are hypointense at the same time point. The other three features are shared or unreliable. Both lesions hyperenhance in the arterial phase. A T2-bright centre suggests the fibrous scar of focal nodular hyperplasia, but adenomas contain necrosis and old haemorrhage that also look bright, and a true scar is present in a minority of small lesions anyway. Opposed-phase signal drop indicates intracellular fat and points to the HNF1A-inactivated adenoma, but only a subset of adenomas is steatotic. The exception worth knowing is that some inflammatory adenomas retain a hepatobiliary agent, so the call is made on the whole picture and not on one image. It matters because the paths diverge: focal nodular hyperplasia is left alone, while an adenoma over about 5 cm, any adenoma in a man, and the beta-catenin-activated subtype carry risks of haemorrhage and malignant change that lead to resection.

quiz.prompt: A dual-echo gradient echo series through the liver gives a mean signal of 300 arbitrary units on the in-phase image and 180 on the opposed-phase image in the same region. Using the signal fat fraction, that is the difference between the two divided by twice the in-phase signal, what fat fraction does this give as a percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 300 minus 180 is 120, and 120 divided by 600 is 0.20, so 20 per cent. Water and fat protons precess at slightly different frequencies, so at the opposed-phase echo time their signals subtract and at the in-phase echo they add; the difference between the two images is therefore twice the fat signal and dividing by twice the total gives the fraction. Above roughly 5 per cent the liver is steatotic. Two limitations travel with the arithmetic. The two-point calculation is ambiguous above 50 per cent fat, because it cannot tell which species dominates and returns the same value either side of the mirror. And it is biased by iron, which shortens T2* and preferentially attenuates whichever echo is acquired later, which at 1.5 T is the in-phase one, so a siderotic liver reads as less fatty than it is, and in severe iron overload the calculated fraction can fall to zero or spuriously negative; that is why quantitative work uses multi-echo proton density fat fraction rather than this sum. Fat matters for lesions as well as for the parenchyma: fat in the background erases the contrast that makes a metastasis conspicuous, while fat inside a lesion is a clue in adenoma and in well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old with no liver disease and normal liver function has a 2 cm lesion with arterial phase hyperenhancement and portal venous washout on a staging CT, and the report assigns LR-5. Say why applying LI-RADS here is a mistake, and what the mistake costs the patient.
quiz.answer: LI-RADS is defined for a population at high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma: adults with cirrhosis, with chronic hepatitis B, or with a current or prior hepatocellular carcinoma. It is not for patients without those risks, nor for cirrhosis arising from congenital hepatic fibrosis or from vascular disorders, nor for children. The categories carry the probabilities they do because the prevalence of hepatocellular carcinoma in that population is high; the same two imaging features in an otherwise normal liver are far more likely to belong to a hypervascular metastasis, an adenoma or an atypical focal nodular hyperplasia. Assigning LR-5 imports a diagnosis that would otherwise require a biopsy, and the cost is a patient treated, or listed for transplantation, for the wrong tumour while the true primary goes unsought.
quiz.explain: This is Bayes wearing a reporting system as a disguise. Arterial phase hyperenhancement with washout has a positive predictive value approaching certainty in a cirrhotic liver and a mediocre one in a healthy liver, and the imaging features are identical in both; only the prior has changed. That is why the eligible population is written into the first line of the algorithm rather than left as a footnote, and why the exclusions are specific: in congenital hepatic fibrosis and in vascular disorders such as Budd-Chiari syndrome or cardiac congestion the liver is nodular without carrying the same risk, and hypervascular benign nodules are common, so the criteria misfire. The general lesson generalises past the liver: a structured reporting system encodes a probability that belongs to the population it was built on, and lifting it out of that population keeps the vocabulary while silently discarding the statistics.

quiz.prompt: In a patient with hepatitis C cirrhosis a 32 mm mass in segment 7 shows rim arterial phase hyperenhancement, peripheral washout on the portal venous phase and progressive central enhancement at five minutes. The multidisciplinary meeting proposes listing for transplantation on the imaging alone. What should happen instead?
choices: Biopsy the mass before any oncological decision
Repeat the multiphase study in three months
Treat with transarterial chemoembolisation
Ablate the mass and follow the response
quiz.answer: Biopsy the mass before any oncological decision
quiz.explain: The three findings together are the targetoid appearance, and LI-RADS categorises a targetoid mass as LR-M: probably or definitely malignant, but not specific for hepatocellular carcinoma. Most LR-M lesions turn out to be intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma or combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma, and a substantial minority are hepatocellular carcinomas that happen to look targetoid, which is exactly why imaging cannot settle it. The consequences diverge sharply. Cholangiocarcinoma and combined tumours recur early after transplantation and are excluded by most programmes, so a listing decision taken on these images risks committing a scarce organ to a tumour that will fail. Repeating in three months treats a mass that is already probably malignant as though it were indeterminate. Chemoembolisation and ablation both commit to a diagnosis nobody has made, and ablation destroys the tissue that would have made it. Tissue is the answer, and LR-M is the category whose whole function is to say so.

quiz.prompt: Hepatocellular carcinoma in a cirrhotic liver develops through a recognised sequence of nodules. Put these lesions in the order in which they arise.
quiz.answer: regenerative-nodule low-grade-dysplastic high-grade-dysplastic early-HCC progressed-HCC
quiz.explain: The imaging follows the blood supply, and the blood supply follows the biology. A regenerative nodule is fed like the rest of the liver, predominantly portal, and is effectively invisible. As dysplasia advances the normal portal supply is lost before the new arterial supply is built, which is why a high-grade dysplastic nodule or an early carcinoma can be hypovascular on every phase, and why LI-RADS needs intermediate categories at all. Only once unpaired arteries have grown does the lesion hyperenhance in the arterial phase, and washout with an enhancing capsule belongs to the progressed lesion, whose sinusoids have capillarised. Two practical consequences. A hypovascular nodule in a cirrhotic liver is followed rather than dismissed, because a proportion of them are partway along this road. And ancillary features that track the same biology, such as restricted diffusion, mild T2 hyperintensity, fat sparing within a fatty nodule and hypointensity on the hepatobiliary phase, are what let a reader raise a category before the arterial phase catches up.

quiz.prompt: On surveillance CT in a cirrhotic patient there is an 8 mm wedge-shaped focus of arterial phase hyperenhancement abutting the capsule in segment 6. It is isodense to liver on the portal venous and delayed phases, invisible on the unenhanced series, and looks identical on studies from two years ago and one year ago. How should it be reported?
choices: An arterioportal shunt, categorised as benign
A hepatocellular carcinoma, LR-5 on its features
An indeterminate observation for close follow-up
A confluent fibrosis band with delayed uptake
quiz.answer: An arterioportal shunt, categorised as benign
quiz.explain: Four things say perfusion rather than lesion: the wedge or triangular shape, the subcapsular position, invisibility on every phase except the arterial one, and stability across two years. Perfusion alterations of this kind are common in cirrhosis, and LI-RADS names them among the observations that may be assigned LR-1. The near miss is LR-3, and it is the expensive one, because calling a stable shunt indeterminate commits the patient to years of scans and the anxiety that goes with them. LR-5 is not even available, since it requires at least 10 mm together with additional major features, and this lesion has neither. Confluent fibrosis is a different creature: wedge-shaped too, but running from the hilum to the capsule with volume loss and capsular retraction, low on T1, high on T2 and enhancing late. What would overturn the reading is any of a mass-like shape, a correlate on another phase, new appearance since a previous study, or growth.

quiz.prompt: A multiphase liver CT in a patient with a known neuroendocrine primary is triggered on the aorta with a short delay. On the earliest post-contrast series the aorta is dense, the portal vein contains no contrast, and the metastases that were obvious on a previous study are barely visible. What went wrong?
choices: The series was taken in the early arterial phase
The injection rate was too low for the volume
The scan was triggered from the portal vein
The contrast dose was small for the patient
quiz.answer: The series was taken in the early arterial phase
quiz.explain: A portal vein containing no contrast dates the acquisition precisely: this is the early arterial phase, some fifteen seconds too soon. Hypervascular lesions are most conspicuous in the late arterial phase, defined by an enhanced portal vein with hepatic veins not yet opacified, because that is when the lesion has taken up its arterial supply while the background parenchyma, which draws three-quarters of its blood from the portal vein, is still relatively unenhanced. Earlier than that, neither the lesion nor the liver has much contrast in it and the difference between them, which is the whole signal, is small. The fix is a longer diagnostic delay after the aortic trigger, not more contrast and not a faster injection, both of which would deliver the same badly timed picture. Getting this right is the difference between finding and missing neuroendocrine, renal and thyroid metastases, and it is why LI-RADS specifies the late arterial phase rather than simply the arterial phase.

nodes.title: The Renal Mass
nodes.goal: Sort a renal mass into cystic or solid, assign a Bosniak class and say what it implies for management, and avoid the pseudo-enhancement trap.

quiz.prompt: A 13 mm rounded lesion lies entirely within the renal parenchyma. On the unenhanced series it measures 42 HU and on the nephrographic phase 58 HU, with the region of interest the same size and in the same place on both. By how many Hounsfield units has the measured attenuation risen? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 58 minus 42 is 16. The convention is that a rise of 20 HU or more is true enhancement, 10 HU or less is none, and everything between is equivocal, so 16 lands in the gap. It lands there for a reason. A small lesion surrounded on all sides by densely enhancing cortex is the classic setting for pseudo-enhancement, in which beam hardening and the scanner's correction for the surrounding iodine raise the measured value of a lesion that contains no iodine at all. The effect is largest below about 15 mm and for completely intrarenal rather than exophytic lesions, which describes this one exactly, and it can add 10 to 20 HU or occasionally more. The number therefore does not settle the case. Ultrasound, MRI with subtraction, or a dual-energy iodine map does, and the alternative of simply repeating the CT reproduces the same artefact.

quiz.prompt: A 5 cm cystic lesion in the left kidney has several thin septa and, arising from one of them, a 6 mm rounded projection with obtuse margins that measures 30 HU before contrast and 78 HU on the nephrographic phase. What does that projection mean for management?
choices: Bosniak IV: treat it as a cystic renal cancer
Bosniak IIF: image again at six and twelve months
Bosniak III: repeat the study in three months
Bosniak II: no further imaging is warranted
quiz.answer: Bosniak IV: treat it as a cystic renal cancer
quiz.explain: An enhancing nodule is the finding that defines the top Bosniak class, and 48 HU of enhancement in a convex protrusion with obtuse margins of this size is unambiguous. The great majority of such lesions are malignant, usually a cystic clear cell carcinoma, and they are managed as cancer with surgery or ablation rather than watched. Each near miss fails on a specific point. Class III describes thick or irregular enhancing walls and septa without a nodule, carries a risk of roughly one in two, and is a genuine dilemma, but it is not this lesion. Class IIF describes numerous thin enhancing septa, or smooth minimal thickening, and is followed rather than treated. Class II ends the imaging altogether. Two habits protect the classification from misuse: the class rests on measured enhancement rather than an impression of brightness, and septa and nodularity are assessed on the phase and the plane where they are best seen, since a nodule seen on one image and not sought on the others is how a class IV lesion gets called class II.

quiz.prompt: A colleague asks how a lesion that contains no iodine can measure 15 HU higher after contrast. Explain the mechanism, say which lesions are most vulnerable to it, and give two ways of settling whether the lesion truly enhances.
quiz.answer: The mechanism is pseudo-enhancement. Densely enhancing renal parenchyma around a small lesion hardens the beam, and the scanner's beam-hardening correction, which assumes a smoother distribution of attenuation than is actually present, over-corrects within the lesion; partial volume averaging of adjacent enhancing cortex adds to the error. The vulnerable lesions are the small ones, below about 15 mm, that sit entirely within the parenchyma rather than exophytically, and the effect grows as the surrounding cortex enhances more strongly. To settle it: ultrasound, on which a simple cyst is anechoic and thin-walled with posterior acoustic enhancement, or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, which shows microbubbles or their absence directly; MRI with subtraction of the pre-contrast from the post-contrast images, which is not subject to beam hardening; or dual-energy CT, whose iodine map and virtual unenhanced images measure iodine rather than infer it from a difference.
quiz.explain: The instructive part is that the artefact is not noise but bias: it pushes measurements in one direction, upward, and it does so most reliably in exactly the lesions where a wrong answer matters, the small intrarenal ones that are otherwise indistinguishable from a small carcinoma. Repeating the CT therefore reproduces the error rather than averaging it away, which is the intuition to unlearn. Each solution works by removing the assumption the artefact exploits. Ultrasound and contrast-enhanced ultrasound do not use an attenuation measurement at all. MRI subtraction compares the same voxel with itself, and its own failure mode is misregistration between breath-holds rather than beam hardening. Dual-energy CT separates iodine from soft tissue by their different behaviour at two energies, which is a measurement of material rather than of density.

quiz.prompt: Put these Bosniak classes of a cystic renal lesion in order, from the lowest probability of malignancy to the highest.
quiz.answer: Bosniak-I Bosniak-II Bosniak-IIF Bosniak-III Bosniak-IV
quiz.explain: Class I is a simple cyst: a hairline-thin smooth wall, homogeneous fluid attenuation, no septa, no calcification and no enhancement. Class II covers minimally complex cysts that need no follow-up, including a few thin septa, fine calcification, and the homogeneous lesion measuring 70 HU or more on the unenhanced series, which is a haemorrhagic or proteinaceous cyst. Class IIF is the follow-up class, malignant in a small percentage, watched rather than treated. Class III, with thick or irregular enhancing walls or septa, is malignant about half the time and is resected, ablated or biopsied. Class IV, with an enhancing nodule, is malignant in the great majority. The value of the ladder is that it turns an appearance into a decision, and its permanent weakness is class III, which sits in the middle by design; no revision of the classification has removed the fact that half of those patients have an operation they did not need.

quiz.prompt: A 1.8 cm mass in the renal medulla was reported as absent on a CT angiogram acquired 30 seconds after injection, and is obvious on a dedicated study a week later. Which acquisition shows a mass in that position most reliably, and why?
choices: The nephrographic phase, when parenchyma is uniform
The corticomedullary phase, when cortex is brightest
The excretory phase, when the collecting system fills
The unenhanced series, before iodine obscures things
quiz.answer: The nephrographic phase, when parenchyma is uniform
quiz.explain: In the corticomedullary phase the cortex is brilliant and the medulla is not, so a medullary mass has much the same attenuation as the medulla around it and vanishes into it. That phase is worth having for vascular anatomy and for demonstrating the avid enhancement of a clear cell carcinoma, but it is the wrong phase on which to declare a mass absent, and reporting a CT angiogram as excluding a renal mass is a recurring error. By the nephrographic phase, once contrast has filtered into the tubules, cortex and medulla enhance to the same degree, and any mass enhancing less than that uniform background stands out; this is the detection phase and it is also where enhancement is measured. The excretory phase belongs to the collecting system and the urothelium, and the unenhanced series to fat, calcification and the baseline from which enhancement is calculated. A dedicated renal mass protocol exists because no single acquisition answers all of those questions.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old with significant comorbidity has a solid enhancing renal mass on active surveillance. It measured 24 mm at diagnosis and measures 30 mm on a scan two years later. What is the linear growth rate in millimetres per year? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 30 minus 24 is 6 mm over two years, which is 3 mm per year. Most small renal masses grow slowly, of that order, and a proportion do not grow at all, which is what makes surveillance a reasonable offer to an older or comorbid patient with a mass under 4 cm. The figure that matters at the meeting is not this year's diameter but the trajectory across several studies measured the same way, together with the size threshold: 4 cm is the boundary between T1a and T1b, and crossing it is one of the triggers to move from watching to treating. Rapid growth, a change in morphology, and new venous or nodal disease are the others. The measurement discipline is the whole exercise, since 6 mm is comfortably within the disagreement between two observers working on different phases and different planes, so the same axis is measured on the same phase each time, and where possible by the same reader.

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm exophytic right renal mass contains a 6 mm focus measuring minus 58 HU on the unenhanced series, and also two punctate calcifications at its margin. Which reading does the combination support?
choices: Renal cell carcinoma engulfing perirenal fat
Angiomyolipoma, which may be watched by size
A capsular lipoma, of no clinical consequence
A retroperitoneal liposarcoma invading inward
quiz.answer: Renal cell carcinoma engulfing perirenal fat
quiz.explain: Macroscopic fat in a renal mass is close to diagnostic of angiomyolipoma, and calcification is the observation that breaks the rule. Angiomyolipomas essentially do not calcify, whereas renal cell carcinomas calcify readily and can engulf perirenal or sinus fat, or undergo osseous or fatty metaplasia. Fat together with calcification in one renal mass is therefore read as carcinoma until proved otherwise, and this lesion belongs to a surgeon rather than to a follow-up list. Two related traps sit either side of it. The fat-poor angiomyolipoma, some five per cent of them, has no measurable fat at all and is homogeneously hyperdense before contrast, low on T2 and avidly enhancing, and it is regularly resected as a presumed carcinoma. And a large angiomyolipoma is watched, embolised or treated with an mTOR inhibitor on the basis of its size and its aneurysms, because of the risk of haemorrhage, not because the diagnosis was ever in doubt.

quiz.prompt: A cystic renal lesion has been called Bosniak II on CT. The urology meeting asks whether MRI would add anything before the patient is discharged. Say what MRI shows better, what it shows worse, and how that changes the class in practice.
quiz.answer: MRI shows internal architecture better: more septa are seen and thin ones are resolved, septal and wall enhancement is demonstrated more sensitively using subtraction of the pre-contrast from the post-contrast images, and haemorrhagic or proteinaceous contents are characterised by their T1 and T2 signal. It shows calcification worse, which matters little, because calcification carries no independent malignant risk in the current classification. Because MRI sees more, the same lesion is often upgraded relative to its CT class: a class II lesion may become IIF once four thin septa are counted rather than two. So the modality has to be stated in the report, follow-up should compare like with like rather than alternating between the two, and the honest answer to the meeting is that MRI may create a follow-up commitment rather than end one.
quiz.explain: The lesson generalises beyond the kidney: a classification calibrated on one modality does not transfer intact to a more sensitive one. Every number in the Bosniak scheme, the thickness of a septum, the count of septa, the presence of enhancement, was derived from what CT can resolve, and MRI resolves more of all three, so identical biology lands a class higher. The 2019 revision addressed this by writing MRI-specific criteria and by defining thicknesses and nodules in millimetres, but it could not abolish the effect. Two practical consequences. Choosing the modality is a management decision, not a technical one, and it should be made with the question in mind. And when comparing with a previous study, compare on the same modality wherever possible; a lesion that appears to have progressed from II to IIF between a CT and an MRI has probably not changed at all.

quiz.prompt: A department acquires unenhanced renal series at 120 kVp and the nephrographic phase at 80 kVp to save contrast. A small lesion measures 20 HU unenhanced and 47 HU on the nephrographic phase, and the report states that it enhances by 27 HU. What is the flaw in that statement?
choices: Iodine attenuates more strongly at the lower voltage
Noise at eighty kilovolts widens the measured value
Beam hardening from the ribs raises the lesion value
The nephrographic phase was timed too late to judge
quiz.answer: Iodine attenuates more strongly at the lower voltage
quiz.explain: Attenuation in Hounsfield units is a property of the tissue and of the beam together, not of the tissue alone. Iodine's K-edge sits at 33 keV, so as the mean photon energy falls the photoelectric contribution rises steeply and the same concentration of iodine measures substantially more at 80 kVp than at 120, commonly around half as much again. A low-kilovoltage series is therefore excellent for detecting enhancement and useless for measuring it against a 120 kVp baseline: part of the 27 HU is iodine and part is the tube. The published thresholds of 10 and 20 HU were derived at around 120 kVp, so either the two series must match or the comparison must be made on virtual monoenergetic or virtual unenhanced images from a dual-energy acquisition, which normalise the beam. The distractors each name a real effect that does not fit: noise widens the scatter of a measurement without shifting its mean, streak and hardening from bone are local and would not systematically inflate a lesion this way, and the timing given is correct for a nephrographic phase.

quiz.prompt: A 7 cm right renal mass extends into a right renal vein that is expanded to twice the calibre of the left. The intraluminal material enhances to a similar degree as the primary tumour on the corticomedullary phase, and small tortuous vessels surround the vein. What does this establish?
choices: Tumour thrombus, which changes the operation
Bland thrombus, for anticoagulation instead
Extrinsic compression of the vein by tumour
A flow artefact from unopacified vein blood
quiz.answer: Tumour thrombus, which changes the operation
quiz.explain: Three findings separate tumour from bland thrombus and all three are here: the vein is expanded, the intraluminal material enhances, and neovascular collaterals surround it. Bland thrombus does not enhance and usually leaves the calibre of the vein alone. The distinction is operative rather than academic. Venous invasion makes the tumour at least T3a, and how far the thrombus reaches decides the procedure: renal vein or infradiaphragmatic inferior vena cava is one operation, thrombus reaching above the diaphragm or invading the caval wall is another, sometimes requiring bypass, so the report must state the cranial extent and whether the wall itself is involved. Extrinsic compression narrows a vein rather than expanding it. A flow artefact, unopacified blood entering an opacified vein, is the mimic worth excluding deliberately, and a later phase excludes it, because the artefact disappears and thrombus does not.

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm solid renal mass is homogeneous and markedly low in signal on T2-weighted images. It measures 38 HU before contrast, 62 HU in the corticomedullary phase and 74 HU in the nephrographic phase, while the adjacent cortex reaches 220 HU. Which reading does this support?
choices: Papillary renal cell carcinoma, weakly vascular
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, richly vascular
A fat-poor angiomyolipoma, which enhances avidly
An oncocytoma, whose central scar fills in late
quiz.answer: Papillary renal cell carcinoma, weakly vascular
quiz.explain: Two features point the same way: low signal on T2 and weak, slowly progressive enhancement far below the cortex. Papillary carcinoma is the hypovascular renal cancer, typically homogeneous when small, low on T2, and enhancing to well under half the cortical value. Clear cell carcinoma is its opposite, enhancing avidly in the corticomedullary phase and often heterogeneous with necrosis. The fat-poor angiomyolipoma is the near miss and it shares the low T2 signal, which is why signal alone does not separate them; it enhances strongly rather than weakly, so it is the enhancement curve that decides. Oncocytoma also enhances avidly, and its central scar and spoke-wheel arteries overlap so completely with clear cell carcinoma that it is not a diagnosis to be made on imaging. Recognising the papillary pattern is prognostically and operatively useful rather than a licence to skip histology: it is generally the less aggressive tumour and the subtype most likely to be multifocal and bilateral, which is worth saying before a partial nephrectomy is planned.

quiz.prompt: A dedicated renal mass protocol CT acquires several series through the kidneys. Put them in the order in which they are acquired.
quiz.answer: unenhanced corticomedullary nephrographic excretory
quiz.explain: The unenhanced series sets the baseline attenuation from which enhancement is measured, and it is the only one on which fat and calcification can be judged. The corticomedullary phase, at roughly thirty to forty seconds, shows the arterial anatomy and the avid enhancement of a clear cell carcinoma, and hides medullary masses. The nephrographic phase, at roughly ninety to a hundred seconds, enhances cortex and medulla equally, and is where masses are detected and enhancement measured. The excretory phase, several minutes later, opacifies the collecting system and is where a urothelial tumour is found. Which of the four are actually acquired should follow the question asked: the unenhanced and nephrographic pair is the minimum for characterising a mass, the excretory phase is added for haematuria, and each additional phase is dose spent, so a protocol that runs all four by habit is a protocol nobody has thought about.

nodes.title: Pancreas and Biliary Tree
nodes.goal: Read acute pancreatitis and its complications in the revised Atlanta terms, locate and explain a biliary obstruction, and stage a pancreatic cancer for resectability.

quiz.prompt: Six weeks after an episode of necrotising pancreatitis a patient is febrile and unable to eat. CT shows a 12 cm encapsulated collection in the lesser sac containing heterogeneous non-liquid material and areas of fat attenuation. The team books a small-bore percutaneous pigtail drain. What is the collection, and what does that mean for the plan?
choices: Walled-off necrosis, which a small drain will block
A pseudocyst, which a small drain should empty
An acute necrotic collection, too early to drain
A pancreatic abscess, for antibiotics by themselves
quiz.answer: Walled-off necrosis, which a small drain will block
quiz.explain: The revised Atlanta terminology turns on two questions: is there necrosis, and is it more or less than four weeks since onset. Fluid only, under four weeks, is an acute peripancreatic fluid collection; fluid only, encapsulated, after four weeks, is a pseudocyst. With necrosis the same two boxes are an acute necrotic collection and, once encapsulated after four weeks, walled-off necrosis. Solid debris and fat attenuation say necrosis; the interval and the capsule say walled-off. It matters because solid necrotic material does not pass through a small catheter, and the drain that was booked will block and leave an infected collection undrained. The modern approach is a step-up: drainage first, usually endoscopic transmural into the stomach or percutaneous by a retroperitoneal route, escalating to endoscopic or minimally invasive necrosectomy if the patient does not improve. Pancreatic abscess is a term the revised classification deliberately abandoned, because it blurred infected fluid with infected necrosis, and the two need different operations.

quiz.prompt: A pancreatic head adenocarcinoma abuts the superior mesenteric vein. On thin-section images the tumour touches the vessel wall around one quarter of its circumference, and the vein keeps a normal contour. How many degrees of contact is that? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A quarter of 360 degrees is 90. The number matters because resectability is written in degrees of circumferential contact rather than in impressions of invasion. For the veins, contact of 180 degrees or less with a normal contour is resectable; more than 180 degrees, or contour irregularity or thrombus with a suitable vessel above and below to reconstruct to, is borderline; and venous involvement that cannot be reconstructed is unresectable. The arterial thresholds are stricter, because arterial reconstruction is rarely worth doing: any contact with the superior mesenteric artery or the coeliac axis takes the tumour out of the resectable group, with 180 degrees or less making it borderline and more than 180 degrees locally advanced. Two disciplines make the measurement worth anything. Measure on a thin-section pancreatic protocol study with multiplanar reformats rather than on axial images alone, since an obliquely running vessel exaggerates contact on an axial image. And report contact rather than asserting invasion: the two are not the same thing, and only the pathologist sees the second.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with painless jaundice and weight loss has a portal venous phase CT. The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct are both dilated and both stop abruptly in the pancreatic head, but no mass is visible and the head looks normal in attenuation. What should happen next?
choices: A pancreatic protocol CT with a parenchymal phase
A portal venous phase repeated with more contrast
An ultrasound of the liver to confirm the level
Reassurance, as no mass has been demonstrated
quiz.answer: A pancreatic protocol CT with a parenchymal phase
quiz.explain: Two dilated ducts cut off in the head, the double duct sign, in an adult with painless jaundice is pancreatic head carcinoma until something else is proved, and a normal-looking head does not overturn it. A minority of ductal adenocarcinomas are isoattenuating to pancreas on a single portal venous acquisition, and those are precisely the ones that get missed. The study that finds them is a dedicated pancreatic protocol: thin sections through the gland in a pancreatic parenchymal phase at roughly forty to fifty seconds, when normal parenchyma is at its brightest and the poorly vascularised fibrous tumour is at its darkest, followed by a portal venous phase for the veins and the liver. Look also for the secondary signs that betray an invisible tumour, which are the duct cut-off itself, upstream parenchymal atrophy, a subtle contour bulge and loss of the fatty lobulation of the gland. If a protocol study is still negative, endoscopic ultrasound is next. The differential is genuine, and includes ampullary and distal bile duct carcinoma, an impacted stone, chronic pancreatitis and autoimmune pancreatitis, but none of them is excluded by reassurance.

quiz.prompt: A jaundiced 70-year-old has an ultrasound showing dilated intrahepatic ducts, a common bile duct of 14 mm and a distended, thin-walled gallbladder. Say where the obstruction must lie and why, what the distended gallbladder adds, and what MRCP is being asked to distinguish.
quiz.answer: Dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts and of the common bile duct together places the obstruction below the cystic duct insertion, that is, distal; a hilar lesion dilates the intrahepatic ducts and leaves the common duct and the gallbladder collapsed. The distended, thin-walled gallbladder is the Courvoisier observation: a gallbladder chronically scarred by stones does not distend, so painless distension leans towards a malignant distal obstruction rather than a stone, as a lean rather than a rule. MRCP is asked to separate a stone, which appears as a rounded filling defect with a signal void, dependent within the duct and often with a meniscus of bile around it, from a stricture, which narrows the duct abruptly or with shouldering and may show wall thickening and enhancement; and to define how far the abnormality extends, for whoever must drain or resect it.
quiz.explain: Localising the level is the whole job, because the level names the differential and dictates the drainage. The logic is plumbing: the gallbladder fills and empties through the cystic duct, so a blockage above that junction cannot distend it while a blockage below it can, and the calibre of the common duct then reports on which side of the junction the problem lies. Two cautions on the numbers and the eponym. A common bile duct of 14 mm is dilated by any standard, but the upper limit drifts upward with age and after cholecystectomy, so a mildly dilated duct in an elderly patient without jaundice is a much weaker finding than this one. And Courvoisier's law fails in both directions, since about a tenth of malignant distal obstructions occur in patients who also have gallstones, and a stone impacted in the distal duct with a healthy gallbladder produces exactly this picture. It is a probabilistic argument, and MRCP is what converts it into a diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: Bile passes from the liver towards the duodenum through a sequence of levels at which an obstruction may sit. Put these levels in the order in which bile reaches them.
quiz.answer: hilar-confluence common-hepatic-duct cystic-duct-insertion intrapancreatic-duct ampulla
quiz.explain: Each level carries its own differential. At the confluence, hilar cholangiocarcinoma, nodal disease or iatrogenic injury; along the common hepatic duct, a node or Mirizzi syndrome, where a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann's pouch compresses the duct from outside; at and below the cystic duct insertion the duct becomes the common bile duct, and it is that junction that decides whether the gallbladder distends; through the intrapancreatic segment, pancreatic head carcinoma and chronic pancreatitis; at the ampulla, an impacted stone, ampullary carcinoma or benign papillary stenosis. Naming the level also chooses the drainage. Endoscopic stenting reaches a distal obstruction easily and a hilar one poorly and incompletely, since a stent in one sectoral duct leaves the other undrained and at risk of cholangitis, which is why the endoscopist's first question is always how high the block sits.

quiz.prompt: Put these categories of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in order, from the one most likely to be removed at operation to the one least likely.
quiz.answer: resectable borderline-resectable locally-advanced metastatic
quiz.explain: The ladder describes what the vessels and the distant sites permit. Resectable means no arterial contact and venous contact of 180 degrees or less with a normal contour. Borderline means venous involvement that can still be reconstructed, or arterial contact of 180 degrees or less with the superior mesenteric or coeliac artery, or contact with the common hepatic artery that spares the coeliac axis. Locally advanced means arterial contact beyond that, or venous occlusion that cannot be reconstructed, and it is treated with chemotherapy rather than surgery. Metastatic means disease beyond the pancreas and its regional nodes, which the report must hunt for actively: small hypodense hepatic lesions, peritoneal and omental deposits, ascites in an anicteric patient. Two things keep the ladder honest. The categories are not fixed, since borderline and increasingly locally advanced disease is offered neoadjuvant chemotherapy and then reassessed. And a category is a prediction about an operation, not a description of a tumour, so the report should give the measurements the surgeon needs rather than only the label.

quiz.prompt: A patient with necrotising pancreatitis has a peripancreatic collection first seen on day 6. On the revised Atlanta terminology, how many weeks after the onset of symptoms must pass before that collection, once it has encapsulated, is walled-off necrosis rather than an acute necrotic collection? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Four weeks is the interval the revised Atlanta classification applies to both encapsulated collections: after four weeks, a purely fluid collection with a defined wall is a pseudocyst and an encapsulated collection containing necrotic material is walled-off necrosis. Before four weeks the same two are an acute peripancreatic fluid collection and an acute necrotic collection. The interval is a convention rather than a biological switch, since some collections wall off sooner and some later, but it is a useful one, because a wall is what allows a collection to be drained without spilling its contents into the free peritoneum. Delaying intervention beyond four weeks wherever the patient can wait is the single change that most improved outcomes in necrotising pancreatitis, which is why the terminology encodes the clock. Note that the clock runs from the onset of symptoms rather than from admission or from the first scan, so the history has to be taken before the CT is described.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after severe pancreatitis a patient's haemoglobin falls abruptly. CT shows a 15 mm rounded structure within a peripancreatic collection that is as dense as the aorta on the arterial phase and follows the aorta on the later phases. What is it, and what should be done?
choices: A pseudoaneurysm, for urgent embolisation
An infected collection, for drainage today
A splenic vein thrombus, for anticoagulation
A pseudocyst with debris, for reassessment
quiz.answer: A pseudoaneurysm, for urgent embolisation
quiz.explain: Attenuation that matches the aorta on every phase means the structure contains circulating blood, and inside a peripancreatic collection that means a pseudoaneurysm: pancreatic enzymes have eroded the wall of an adjacent artery, most often the splenic, less often the gastroduodenal or the pancreaticoduodenal arcade. It is the complication that kills without warning, and the treatment is angiographic embolisation rather than an operation on a hostile abdomen. The reason to name it quickly is the trap sitting in the alternatives: a drain placed into a collection that contains a pseudoaneurysm can open it, so the arterial phase is examined before any peripancreatic collection is drained, and a sudden fall in haemoglobin after pancreatitis is a vascular question until proved otherwise. Splenic vein thrombosis is the other vascular complication, common and usually silent, and it produces left-sided portal hypertension with gastric varices rather than acute bleeding, which is a reason to look at the fundus rather than to anticoagulate on sight.

quiz.prompt: A patient admitted eight hours ago has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a serum lipase five times the upper limit of normal. A contrast CT requested to grade severity shows a normal-looking pancreas, and the team concludes that the attack is mild. What is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: Necrosis takes days to declare itself on imaging
The scan was acquired in the wrong contrast phase
Lipase must be tenfold raised to be diagnostic
The reconstruction is too smooth to show the gland
quiz.answer: Necrosis takes days to declare itself on imaging
quiz.explain: Two errors compound here. First, the scan was not needed: the revised Atlanta classification diagnoses acute pancreatitis on any two of characteristic pain, amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging, so pain with a fivefold lipase has already made the diagnosis, and imaging at presentation adds nothing unless the diagnosis is genuinely in doubt or another cause of an acute abdomen has to be excluded. Second, and worse, a negative early scan is being treated as information. Perfusion failure evolves over days and necrosis is frequently invisible within the first seventy-two hours, so an early study understates severity and reads as falsely reassuring. Where severity has to be assessed on imaging, the study is best done at seventy-two to ninety-six hours; in the meantime severity is a clinical and physiological judgement, and the early markers that matter are organ failure and its persistence beyond forty-eight hours. Early CT does have indications: a deteriorating patient, a suspected complication such as bleeding or perforation, and real diagnostic uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: A 3 cm pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is in contact with the superior mesenteric artery over 90 degrees, and with the superior mesenteric vein over 200 degrees with a teardrop deformity of the vein but a patent lumen above and below. There is no distant disease. Say how the tumour should be categorised, what each vessel finding contributes, and what you would expect of the restaging scan.
quiz.answer: This is borderline resectable. The arterial finding decides the category: contact with the superior mesenteric artery of 180 degrees or less takes the tumour out of the resectable group and into the borderline group, and contact of more than 180 degrees would have made it locally advanced. The venous finding, contact beyond 180 degrees with contour deformity, is also borderline rather than unresectable, because there is a patent segment above and below for a venous resection and reconstruction. The plan is therefore neoadjuvant chemotherapy with restaging rather than an upfront operation. The restaging scan should be read cautiously: soft tissue around a vessel persists as fibrosis after the tumour has responded, so CT systematically understates response, and a study that looks unchanged does not preclude exploration in a patient who is otherwise fit and whose tumour markers have fallen.
quiz.explain: The item turns on the asymmetry between arteries and veins. Venous involvement is a technical problem, since the superior mesenteric and portal veins can be resected and reconstructed with acceptable results provided there is healthy vessel at both ends, so venous contact does not by itself put a tumour beyond surgery. Arterial involvement is a biological statement as much as a technical one, since tumour tracking along the perineural and lymphatic tissue around the superior mesenteric artery is what leaves positive margins, and arterial resection has not been shown to pay for itself outside trials. That is why the artery decides the category even when the vein looks worse on the images. The restaging caveat is the second half of the lesson and the one most often forgotten: after chemotherapy, CT cannot distinguish viable tumour from the fibrosis that replaces it, so the decision to explore rests on the whole picture, performance status, CA 19-9 and the absence of new metastases, rather than on the degree of vessel contact alone.

quiz.prompt: Surveillance MRI of a 2.5 cm branch-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm in a fit 68-year-old now shows a 7 mm mural projection that enhances after gadolinium. The main pancreatic duct measures 4 mm and there is no jaundice. What does the new finding call for?
choices: Referral for resection, as the nodule enhances
A repeat scan in six months to see if it grows
Endoscopic ultrasound once the cyst enlarges
A return to annual surveillance as before now
quiz.answer: Referral for resection, as the nodule enhances
quiz.explain: An enhancing mural nodule of 5 mm or more is one of the high-risk stigmata in the international consensus guidelines, alongside obstructive jaundice in a patient with a cystic lesion of the head and a main pancreatic duct of 10 mm or more. In a fit patient a high-risk stigma means surgical referral rather than more imaging. The features that would instead have justified endoscopic ultrasound are the worrisome ones: a cyst of 3 cm or more, a thickened or enhancing cyst wall, a main duct of 5 to 9 mm, a non-enhancing mural nodule, an abrupt change in duct calibre with upstream atrophy, lymphadenopathy, a rising CA 19-9, or an episode of pancreatitis. The distinction that must be got right on the images is enhancement itself, because mucin globules and debris sit inside these cysts and mimic nodules exactly; they do not enhance, and they move when the patient moves, so subtraction images and a change of position settle it. The reason not to temporise is that mural nodularity and main-duct involvement are what carry the risk of invasive carcinoma, while a small branch-duct cyst with none of these features is safely watched for years.

quiz.prompt: A 3 cm hypoenhancing mass in the pancreatic head is found in a man with fifteen years of heavy alcohol use. There are coarse calcifications through the rest of the gland, and MRCP shows the main pancreatic duct running through the mass, smoothly narrowed over its length but not interrupted. Which reading does the appearance support?
choices: Chronic inflammation, from the duct traversing it
Carcinoma, from the poorly enhancing head mass
Carcinoma, from the dilated duct upstream of it
Chronic inflammation, from the gland calcification
quiz.answer: Chronic inflammation, from the duct traversing it
quiz.explain: The duct-penetrating sign, a main pancreatic duct that passes through a mass and is smoothly narrowed rather than obstructed, favours mass-forming chronic pancreatitis, because inflammation encases the duct while adenocarcinoma destroys and interrupts it, giving an abrupt cut-off with upstream dilatation. It is the most useful single MRCP discriminator between the two, and it is the reason the ducts are examined before the mass. Each alternative fails on a specific point. Poor enhancement is shared, since mass-forming pancreatitis is as hypoenhancing as adenocarcinoma, so it separates nothing. Calcification is a feature of chronic pancreatitis, but chronic pancreatitis is itself a risk factor for carcinoma, so calcification cannot exclude a tumour arising within a scarred gland; that is the trap which runs the wrong way. And the duct here is not the abruptly interrupted, dilated duct that carcinoma produces. None of this is sufficient on its own. Autoimmune pancreatitis is the other great mimic, with a diffusely sausage-shaped gland, a capsule-like rim, a long irregularly narrowed duct and raised IgG4, and where doubt persists after imaging, endoscopic ultrasound with sampling is what settles it.

nodes.title: Describing a Fracture
nodes.goal: Turn a radiograph of a broken bone into a description a surgeon can act on, and know where the first film hides an injury.

quiz.prompt: A report on a mid-shaft femoral fracture states that the proximal fragment is displaced laterally by half a shaft width. The surgeon reads it, reaches for the films, and asks the radiologist to rewrite the sentence. What is wrong with it?
choices: Displacement is stated for the distal fragment, not the proximal
Displacement should be given in millimetres, not in shaft widths
Displacement needs a true lateral before it can be judged
Displacement and angulation are the same measurement here
quiz.answer: Displacement is stated for the distal fragment, not the proximal
quiz.explain: The convention exists because of what the surgeon does with it.
