The proximal fragment is held by the trunk and cannot be moved; the distal fragment is the one reduced onto it, so every element of the description is stated for the distal fragment relative to the proximal. Written the other way round the sentence inverts the direction of the correction, and a team acting on it plans to push the limb the wrong way. Translation expressed as a fraction or percentage of the shaft width is in fact the standard, so the millimetre option corrects something that is not broken; and while two orthogonal projections are needed before displacement can be described at all, this report already has them and would still be wrong.

quiz.prompt: On the lateral view of a distal radius fracture in an elderly woman who fell on the outstretched hand, the articular surface of the distal fragment tilts towards the dorsum, and the fragment is displaced dorsally. How should the angulation be recorded?
choices: Dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, apex volar
Volar angulation of the distal fragment, apex dorsal
Dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, apex dorsal
Dorsal tilt of the proximal fragment, apex volar
quiz.answer: Dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, apex volar
quiz.explain: Two fragments meeting at an angle make a wedge, and the apex points away from the side the distal fragment tilts towards: a distal fragment tilted dorsally opens the angle dorsally, so the apex lies volar. That is the Colles pattern, and both halves of the phrase are in circulation, which is exactly why a report should give the direction the distal fragment tilts and let the apex follow rather than leaving the reader to guess which convention was used. Recording the apex on the same side as the tilt describes a deformity that cannot exist, and stating the tilt of the proximal fragment repeats the error of describing the piece the surgeon cannot move.

quiz.prompt: Take the normal palmar tilt of the distal radial articular surface as 11 degrees. On the injured lateral the surface is tilted 15 degrees towards the dorsum. Through how many degrees must the distal fragment be rotated to restore the normal tilt? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Tilt is signed about a neutral surface that faces straight along the shaft. Fifteen degrees of dorsal tilt is minus fifteen on a scale where palmar tilt counts as positive, so reaching plus eleven means turning the fragment through twenty-six degrees, not through the four you get by subtracting one figure from the other. The sign error is the common one and it halves the correction the surgeon plans for. The same arithmetic applies to radial inclination on the posteroanterior view and to radial height, and it is the reason a report gives numbers rather than adjectives: how much residual dorsal tilt is acceptable depends on the patient's age and demands, and that judgement is not the radiologist's to make on the reader's behalf.

quiz.prompt: A tibial shaft fracture treated in a cast is followed with radiographs from the day of injury to a year later. Put these radiographic appearances in the order they appear on the films.
quiz.answer: crisp-lucency margin-resorption soft-callus bridging-callus remodelling
quiz.explain: On the day of injury the fracture is a sharply defined lucency between two crisp cortical edges. Over the following one to two weeks osteoclasts resorb the dead bone at the fracture margins, so the line becomes wider and less distinct, and a fracture invisible on the first film can declare itself here — which is the whole basis of the ten-to-fourteen-day repeat radiograph. Ill-defined periosteal new bone, the soft callus, follows at around two to three weeks; it mineralises and bridges the cortices over the next several weeks; and remodelling then reshapes the bone along its lines of loading over months to years, in a child to the point that the fracture becomes untraceable. The clinically useful trap is the middle step: a line that looks worse at two weeks than at presentation is usually healing normally, not displacing.

quiz.prompt: An adult falls on the outstretched hand. The lateral elbow radiograph, taken correctly at 90 degrees of flexion, shows a lucency lifted off the posterior aspect of the distal humerus and a raised triangular lucency anteriorly. No cortical break is visible on either projection. What should be done?
choices: Treat as an occult radial head fracture and immobilise
Report a normal elbow, since no cortical break is seen
Attribute the appearance to the flexed position of the arm
Proceed to CT of the elbow before any immobilisation
quiz.answer: Treat as an occult radial head fracture and immobilise
quiz.explain: The posterior fat pad sits deep in the olecranon fossa and is invisible on a normal elbow; anything that distends the joint lifts it into view. On a properly positioned lateral, a visible posterior fat pad therefore means a haemarthrosis, and in an adult who has fallen on the hand the commonest cause by far is an undisplaced radial head fracture. The anterior fat pad is visible normally and becomes a sail only when displaced, so it is the less specific of the two. Management is a sling or collar and cuff with early movement and a repeat film at seven to ten days; CT is reserved for a fracture already known to be displaced or comminuted, where it changes the operation. A lateral taken away from 90 degrees can lift the fat pads without an effusion, which is why the positioning is stated before the sign is trusted — and in a child the same finding points to a supracondylar fracture instead.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial loading of the thumb after falling on the outstretched hand. Four-view scaphoid radiographs are reported as normal. Set out how the wrist should be managed and justify each step.
quiz.answer: Treat the wrist as fractured until it is proved otherwise: immobilise it and arrange definitive imaging rather than discharging on the strength of a normal radiograph, because a substantial minority of scaphoid fractures are invisible on the first films. MRI is the most accurate second-line test and can be done within days; it shows the fracture line and the surrounding marrow oedema on the day of injury, and a normal MRI allows the splint to come off and the patient to be discharged. Where MRI is not available, CT displays cortical detail well but is less sensitive for the undisplaced fracture, and repeat radiographs at ten to fourteen days depend on resorption widening the line, which works but delays the diagnosis by a fortnight. The effort is justified by the blood supply: the scaphoid is perfused retrogradely through its distal pole, so a missed waist or proximal pole fracture risks non-union and avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment, with wrist collapse and secondary arthritis to follow.
quiz.explain: Everything here follows from a single anatomical fact and a single statistical one. The statistical fact is that normal initial radiographs do not exclude a scaphoid fracture, so the negative film changes nothing about the immediate management of a clinically suspicious wrist. The anatomical fact is the retrograde blood supply, which makes the cost of a missed fracture disproportionate: the proximal fragment is fed through the fracture, and immobilisation is what protects it. MRI has displaced the traditional repeat radiograph in most units on cost-effectiveness grounds as much as accuracy — an early definitive answer releases the many patients who have no fracture from weeks of unnecessary immobilisation and time off work.

quiz.prompt: A horizontal-beam lateral radiograph of the knee, taken after a fall from a ladder, shows a fluid-fluid level in the suprapatellar recess with the upper layer less dense than the lower. No fracture line is visible on the anteroposterior or lateral projection. What follows from the level?
choices: Marrow fat is in the joint, so a fracture enters it
Blood alone has layered, which follows a ligament tear
The level is an artefact of the horizontal beam technique
Synovial fluid has separated, which suggests an effusion
quiz.answer: Marrow fat is in the joint, so a fracture enters it
quiz.explain: Fat floats on blood, and the fat in question is marrow fat, which can reach the joint cavity by one route: a fracture that crosses the cortex within the capsular attachment. A fat-fluid level is therefore proof of an intra-articular fracture even when no line is visible, and the usual culprit at the knee is a depressed lateral tibial plateau fracture; CT is the next step, and MRI where the ligaments and menisci also need assessing. A pure haemarthrosis after a twisting injury does suggest an anterior cruciate tear, but blood does not separate into two layers of different density. The horizontal beam is what makes the level visible rather than what creates it — a level cannot form on a film shot with the beam vertical, which is why the technique is specified in the trauma series.

quiz.prompt: The elbow radiographs of a six-year-old are checked against the sequence in which the ossification centres appear, so that a displaced medial epicondyle is not mistaken for a trochlear centre. Put the centres in the order they ossify.
quiz.answer: capitellum radial-head medial-epicondyle trochlea olecranon lateral-epicondyle
quiz.explain: The centres appear at roughly one, three, five, seven, nine and eleven years, earlier in girls, and the ages matter far less than the order, which is reliable. The order is a diagnostic tool rather than a piece of trivia: a fragment of bone at the trochlea in a child whose medial epicondyle is not visible is an avulsed medial epicondyle that has migrated, sometimes into the joint after a transient dislocation, and calling it a trochlear centre leaves an intra-articular fragment in a growing elbow. The corollary is that the medial epicondyle should be identified before the trochlea is accepted, on every paediatric elbow. The centres fuse in a different order from the one in which they appear, so this sequence applies to appearance only.

quiz.prompt: After a generalised seizure a man cannot externally rotate his shoulder. The anteroposterior radiograph shows the humeral head overlapping the glenoid, and the head is rounded and symmetrical rather than showing its usual greater tuberosity profile. What is the next step?
choices: Obtain an axillary or scapular-Y view of the same shoulder
Report an anterior dislocation and reduce it in the department
Report a normal shoulder and treat the pain conservatively
Request MRI to look for a rotator cuff tear before reduction
quiz.answer: Obtain an axillary or scapular-Y view of the same shoulder
quiz.explain: A posterior dislocation locks the humerus in internal rotation, so the head presents its smooth articular surface to the beam and loses the tuberosity step, and the joint can look almost congruent on the frontal view alone. That is why the diagnosis is missed: the single view is unreliable, and the fix is a projection orthogonal to it — an axillary, a modified Velpeau axillary if the arm will not abduct, or a scapular-Y — with CT if the patient cannot be positioned at all. Seizures and electric shock are the classic mechanisms, and both can produce bilateral dislocations, so the other shoulder is examined too. Reducing what is assumed to be an anterior dislocation without a second view risks manoeuvring the wrong way against a locked head and an impaction fracture of its anteromedial surface.

quiz.prompt: A registrar telephones the orthopaedic team with 'a fracture of the distal radius'. Give four further elements the description must carry before the team can choose between a cast and theatre, and say what each one changes.
quiz.answer: Whether the fracture line enters the radiocarpal or distal radioulnar joint, and if so the size of the articular step or gap, because an articular step is what pushes the decision towards fixation rather than casting. The displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, given as translation as a fraction of the shaft width and as the direction in which the distal fragment tilts, in degrees, because that is the deformity the surgeon has to reverse and the figures determine whether it can be held. Whether the metaphysis is comminuted, particularly dorsally, because a comminuted metaphysis loses its buttress and collapses again after a closed reduction, which argues for fixation from the start. Whether the skin is broken over the fracture, and the state of the median nerve and the radial pulse, because an open fracture or an acute carpal tunnel syndrome goes to theatre whatever the alignment. Radial height, radial inclination and palmar tilt, the state of the ulnar styloid and any associated carpal injury complete the description.
quiz.explain: The four elements map onto the four questions the surgeon is actually asking: does this joint need to be rebuilt, how far out is it, will it stay where I put it, and does it need to go to theatre tonight. Naming the bone and saying 'fracture' answers none of them. The habit worth acquiring is to describe every fracture in the same fixed sequence — which bone and which part of it, whether it is open, the pattern of the line, the position of the distal fragment in translation, angulation, rotation and shortening, whether it reaches an articular surface, and what the adjacent joints and soft tissues show — because a fixed sequence is what stops the rotational deformity, or the second fracture at the joint above, from being the one thing left out.

quiz.prompt: A workman falls from a height and lands on his heels. On the lateral calcaneal radiograph the angle is measured between a line from the superior margin of the posterior tuberosity to the posterior facet and a line from that facet to the superior aspect of the anterior process. Below how many degrees is this angle regarded as reduced, indicating depression of the posterior facet? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The tuber joint angle described by Boehler measures 20 to 40 degrees in the intact calcaneus; flattening below 20 degrees means the posterior facet has been driven downwards into the body of the bone, and the angle can go negative in a severe injury. It is worth measuring precisely because the fracture line in an axial loading injury runs obliquely and can be genuinely invisible until the facet is seen to have dropped, and because the uninjured side gives a within-patient control. Two further habits belong with the finding: CT in the coronal plane through the posterior facet is what grades the fracture and plans the operation, and axial loading injuries travel up the body, so the other calcaneus, both tibial plateaus and the thoracolumbar junction are examined in the same patient.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old woman cannot bear weight after a fall onto her hip. An anteroposterior pelvis and a lateral of the hip are reported as showing no fracture, and she remains unable to stand the next morning. Which test resolves the question, and why?
choices: MRI, which shows the marrow oedema of an undisplaced line
CT, which is as sensitive as MRI for an undisplaced line
Repeat radiographs in ten days, once resorption widens it
Bone scintigraphy, which is positive within the first hours
quiz.answer: MRI, which shows the marrow oedema of an undisplaced line
quiz.explain: MRI is the reference standard for the radiographically occult hip fracture. It shows the low-signal line on T1 and the surrounding oedema on a fluid-sensitive sequence from the day of injury, and a limited two-sequence coronal protocol takes only a few minutes. CT misses a proportion of undisplaced femoral neck fractures, particularly in osteoporotic bone where the trabecular detail it depends on has already been lost, so a negative CT does not exclude the diagnosis — though CT is the reasonable substitute where MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. Scintigraphy needs a day or more in an elderly patient before it becomes reliable. Waiting ten days is the worst option of the four: it leaves an undisplaced intracapsular fracture to displace in a patient who is immobile in the meantime, and displacement is what converts a fixable fracture into an arthroplasty.

nodes.title: The Radiographic Pattern of Arthritis
nodes.goal: Read a hand, a knee or a pelvis and separate the arthritides by distribution, erosion, joint space, bone density and new bone.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old woman has six weeks of hand stiffness worst in the morning. Radiographs show fusiform soft-tissue swelling around the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints on both sides, reduced bone density around those joints, and small erosions at the radial margins of the metacarpal heads. The distal interphalangeal joints are normal and there is no new bone. What does the film support, and what should follow?
choices: Early rheumatoid arthritis; request MRI or ultrasound of the hands
Psoriatic arthritis; look for nail pitting and hidden skin plaques
Erosive osteoarthritis; treat symptomatically and repeat the film
Gouty arthropathy; aspirate the joint for crystal analysis
quiz.answer: Early rheumatoid arthritis; request MRI or ultrasound of the hands
quiz.explain: Four features move together here. The distribution is bilateral, symmetric and proximal — metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists — with the distal interphalangeal joints spared, which is close to the opposite of psoriatic disease. The density is reduced periarticularly, because hyperaemic synovitis resorbs the adjacent trabecular bone. The erosions sit at the margin, at the bare area between the edge of the articular cartilage and the capsular insertion, where synovium lies against unprotected bone. And there is no new bone at all, which is what separates rheumatoid arthritis from every spondyloarthritis. The action matters as much as the label: a visible radiographic erosion is already a late finding, so ultrasound or MRI, which show synovitis and bone marrow oedema before the cortex is breached, is what changes treatment inside the window in which treatment works best.

quiz.prompt: A 39-year-old man has one swollen, sausage-shaped fourth finger. The radiograph shows erosion at the fourth distal interphalangeal joint with irregular, ill-defined new bone along the adjacent phalangeal shaft and resorption of the terminal tuft. Bone density is normal, the other fingers are unaffected and the wrist is normal. What does the combination indicate?
choices: Psoriatic arthritis, with erosion and proliferation in one ray
Rheumatoid arthritis presenting atypically in a single finger
Erosive osteoarthritis, which favours the distal finger joints
Chronic tophaceous gout eroding the terminal phalanx
quiz.answer: Psoriatic arthritis, with erosion and proliferation in one ray
quiz.explain: Psoriatic arthritis destroys and builds at the same time, and the coexistence of erosion with fluffy periosteal new bone beside it is close to diagnostic; rheumatoid arthritis erodes without ever laying down new bone. The distribution is the second half of the argument: disease running along one digit through all its joints, asymmetrically, is a ray pattern, whereas rheumatoid disease picks out the same row of joints on both hands. Preserved bone density, distal rather than proximal predominance, tuft resorption and the swollen whole digit all belong to the same picture, and the advanced form gives the pencil-in-cup deformity and arthritis mutilans. Erosive osteoarthritis does favour the distal joints but erodes centrally and appears in an older patient alongside osteophytes; gout would preserve the joint space and produce a corticated erosion with an overhanging edge next to a soft-tissue tophus, not periostitis.

quiz.prompt: An untreated seropositive rheumatoid wrist and hand are radiographed at intervals over fifteen years. Put these radiographic changes in the order in which they first appear.
quiz.answer: soft-tissue-swelling periarticular-osteopenia marginal-erosion joint-space-narrowing carpal-ankylosis
quiz.explain: Synovitis comes first and shows as fusiform periarticular soft-tissue swelling; the hyperaemia that accompanies it resorbs trabecular bone next to the joint, giving periarticular osteopenia. Pannus then reaches the bare area at the joint margin, where no cartilage protects the bone, and erodes it. Only after that does the pannus thin the cartilage across the whole joint, which is why the narrowing of rheumatoid arthritis is uniform rather than confined to a loaded compartment as in osteoarthritis. Deformity, subluxation and finally bony ankylosis — commonest in the carpus — end the sequence. The order is the argument for imaging early with a modality that sees synovium: by the time the radiograph shows the third step, the damage that treatment was meant to prevent has happened.

quiz.prompt: A woman with twenty years of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is listed for a general anaesthetic, and the anaesthetist asks for flexion and extension lateral cervical radiographs before intubation. On the flexion view the distance is measured between the posterior cortex of the anterior arch of the atlas and the anterior cortex of the odontoid peg. Above how many millimetres is this distance abnormal in an adult? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres is the upper limit of the anterior atlanto-dental interval in an adult; up to five is accepted in a child, whose ligaments are laxer and whose odontoid is incompletely ossified. Beyond the adult limit the transverse ligament has been destroyed by pannus and the atlas slides forward on the axis in flexion, which is precisely what happens when an anaesthetist positions a head for laryngoscopy. The interval that predicts neurological injury, though, is the one behind the peg — the space left for the cord between the odontoid and the posterior arch — because as the anterior gap opens, that posterior space closes. Radiographs answer the question of movement; MRI is what shows pannus, cord compression and cord signal change, and vertical migration of the peg through the foramen magnum is the more dangerous and easily missed second pattern.

quiz.prompt: A hand radiograph in a 58-year-old woman shows erosions at several distal interphalangeal joints. Set out the features that separate erosive osteoarthritis from psoriatic arthritis on the radiograph alone.
quiz.answer: Erosive osteoarthritis erodes centrally. The subchondral plate collapses in the middle of the joint while osteophytes hold up the margins, producing the gull-wing outline on the frontal view, and sometimes a saw-tooth appearance where the opposing surface is remodelled. It sits in a hand that shows osteoarthritis elsewhere — first carpometacarpal and proximal interphalangeal involvement, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts — with normal bone density and no periosteal reaction. Psoriatic arthritis erodes at the margins, where the bare area lies, and then lays down new bone: ill-defined fluffy periosteal reaction along the shaft next to the erosion, ossification at entheses, and in advanced disease pencil-in-cup deformity and acro-osteolysis of the tuft. Its distribution is asymmetric and follows a whole ray rather than a row of equivalent joints, the soft tissues may show a uniformly swollen digit rather than a joint-centred swelling, and bone density is preserved. Neither shows the periarticular osteopenia of rheumatoid arthritis, and neither spares new bone the way rheumatoid arthritis does.
quiz.explain: The two questions that settle almost every eroding hand are where in the joint the erosion sits and whether the bone is reacting. Central erosion with marginal osteophytes is a degenerative process eating through a thinned subchondral plate; marginal erosion with adjacent proliferation is an enthesis-driven inflammatory one. Distribution is the cross-check: osteoarthritis, erosive or not, picks out the same joints on both hands in a recognisable pattern, whereas psoriatic disease is asymmetric and runs down a ray. Where the film is genuinely equivocal, the clinical examination — nail pitting and onycholysis, a scalp or natal cleft plaque, dactylitis, enthesitis at the heel — usually decides it faster than more imaging will.

quiz.prompt: A 72-year-old has wrist pain and swelling. The radiograph shows a thin band of calcification in the triangular fibrocartilage and in the intercarpal cartilage, narrowing of the radiocarpal joint with subchondral cysts, and widening of the scapholunate interval with proximal migration of the capitate. The metacarpophalangeal joints are normal and bone density is preserved. What does the pattern indicate?
choices: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition with scapholunate collapse
Rheumatoid arthritis with carpal collapse and ligament failure
Primary osteoarthritis of the wrist following an old injury
Haemochromatosis arthropathy of the second and third heads
quiz.answer: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition with scapholunate collapse
quiz.explain: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposit in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, and the triangular fibrocartilage is one of the four places worth looking for them, with the knee menisci, the symphysis pubis and the acetabular labrum. Their arthropathy is degenerative in character — narrowing, sclerosis and prominent subchondral cysts — but it appears in joints that primary osteoarthritis has little reason to visit, and the radiocarpal joint is the classic one: crystal-driven failure of the scapholunate ligament lets the interval widen and the capitate migrate proximally between scaphoid and lunate. Rheumatoid disease also destroys the carpus, but with periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions and erosion of the ulnar styloid rather than chondrocalcinosis. Haemochromatosis is the important companion diagnosis and produces chondrocalcinosis too, but its signature is hook-like osteophytes on the radial aspect of the second and third metacarpal heads, and those joints are stated to be normal here.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old man has had inflammatory back pain for two years. The anteroposterior pelvis shows erosion and sclerosis on the iliac side of the right sacroiliac joint with irregular widening of the joint space, and a normal left joint. Under the modified New York criteria, a unilateral abnormality must reach at least which sacroiliitis grade to satisfy the radiographic criterion? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The grading runs from 0 for a normal joint, through 1 for suspicious change, 2 for minimal sclerosis or small erosions without any alteration of joint width, 3 for unequivocal abnormality with erosion, sclerosis, widening, narrowing or partial ankylosis, to 4 for total ankylosis. The radiographic criterion is met by grade 2 or more on both sides, or grade 3 or 4 on one side alone, which is why a convincing unilateral change has to reach grade 3 while a milder bilateral change need only reach grade 2. The reason the whole exercise has been overtaken clinically is worth knowing: radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear, and MRI showing bone marrow oedema in the subchondral bone of the sacroiliac joints identifies active inflammation long before, which is what allows a diagnosis of non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis to be made at all. Grading a plain film also has poor interobserver agreement, and oblique or dedicated views add little over a good frontal view.

quiz.prompt: The lumbar spine of a man with ankylosing spondylitis is followed on lateral radiographs from his twenties into his fifties. Put these vertebral appearances in the order in which they develop.
quiz.answer: shiny-corner vertebral-squaring syndesmophyte bridging-ankylosis
quiz.explain: Inflammation begins at the enthesis where the outer annulus inserts into the vertebral corner. Erosion there provokes reactive sclerosis, and the dense corner against a normal body is the shiny corner of the Romanus lesion. Continued erosion of the anterior corners flattens the normal anterior concavity of the body, which is squaring. Ossification then advances vertically through the outer fibres of the annulus as a thin, marginal syndesmophyte, and successive syndesmophytes meet to bridge the disc, ending in the fused bamboo spine. The whole sequence is the argument for the distinction that matters on a spine film: the syndesmophyte of ankylosing spondylitis is thin, vertical and marginal because it follows the annulus, while the bulky, asymmetric, non-marginal paravertebral ossification of psoriatic and reactive arthritis does not, and the flowing anterior ossification of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis spares the sacroiliac joints and the disc heights altogether. A fused spine also fractures like a long bone, which is why new pain in this patient means CT rather than reassurance.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has medial knee pain. Weight-bearing radiographs show loss of the medial tibiofemoral joint space with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes on the medial tibial plateau, a normal lateral compartment, and no erosion or periarticular osteopenia. A supine film taken a year earlier had been reported as normal. What accounts for the difference between the two studies?
choices: Load is needed to bring the worn compartment surfaces together
The earlier film was taken before any of the cartilage was lost
The osteophytes had not yet formed when the first film was taken
Sclerosis obscured the joint space on the earlier projection
quiz.answer: Load is needed to bring the worn compartment surfaces together
quiz.explain: Cartilage is radiolucent, so joint space is inferred from the gap between two cortical surfaces, and that gap closes to its true minimum in a worn compartment only when the joint is loaded. A supine knee film can therefore show a preserved space in a knee with advanced cartilage loss, which is why the standing anteroposterior view is the standard, and why a flexed posteroanterior weight-bearing view is added when the posterior femoral condyles are the suspected site, since that is where cartilage wears first. The rest of the description is a compact statement of osteoarthritis and its difference from an inflammatory arthritis: one compartment rather than the whole joint, new bone in the form of osteophytes and sclerosis, normal bone density, and no erosions.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old man has pain at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The radiograph shows a well-corticated erosion on the medial aspect of the metatarsal head with a thin spur of bone overhanging an adjacent soft-tissue mass, a preserved joint space and normal bone density. Argue from the film why this is gout rather than rheumatoid arthritis, and say what would confirm it.
quiz.answer: Three features argue against rheumatoid arthritis. The erosion is punched out with a sclerotic rim and an overhanging edge of bone, because a tophus enlarges slowly enough for the adjacent bone to react and to be lifted rather than simply destroyed, whereas the rheumatoid marginal erosion has neither a sclerotic margin nor an overhanging edge. The joint space is preserved, because urate deposits in and beside the joint and erodes bone long before it destroys cartilage, while rheumatoid pannus thins cartilage across the whole joint and narrows it early and uniformly. Bone density is normal, whereas periarticular osteopenia is an early rheumatoid sign. The soft-tissue mass is the tophus itself, occasionally containing dense internal calcification, particularly in renal impairment. Confirmation: ultrasound shows the double contour sign of urate deposited on the surface of the hyaline cartilage and hyperechoic aggregates within a tophus, dual-energy CT colour-codes urate deposits volumetrically, and aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light remains the definitive test.
quiz.explain: Gout is the arthritis that breaks the usual coupling between erosion and joint destruction, and that dissociation — substantial erosion with a joint space that still looks reasonable and bone that is still dense — is what should bring it to mind on any hand or foot film. The distribution helps: the first metatarsophalangeal joint, the midfoot, the olecranon bursa, the knee and the hands in longstanding disease, characteristically asymmetric. Two cautions on confirmation: the double contour sign and dual-energy CT are much less sensitive in the first attack than in established disease, so a negative study does not exclude gout in an acute joint, and an eroded joint with a soft-tissue mass that turns out to have no urate needs a different explanation, including infection.

quiz.prompt: Two men in their thirties have inflammatory back pain. The first has thin vertical ossifications running from the corner of one vertebral body to the corner of the next, with symmetric erosion and sclerosis of both sacroiliac joints. The second has bulky coarse ossification bridging vertebrae away from the disc margin, skipping levels, with sacroiliitis on one side. What separates them?
choices: The first is ankylosing spondylitis; the second, psoriatic disease
The first is psoriatic disease; the second, ankylosing spondylitis
Both are ankylosing spondylitis at different stages of the disease
Both are diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not inflammation
quiz.answer: The first is ankylosing spondylitis; the second, psoriatic disease
quiz.explain: Where the ossification runs tells you which structure is ossifying. In ankylosing spondylitis it is the outer fibres of the annulus fibrosus, which run vertically from one vertebral corner to the next, so the syndesmophyte is thin, vertical and marginal, and the disease is symmetric — including its sacroiliitis, which is bilateral and equal. In psoriatic and reactive arthritis the ossification forms in the paravertebral tissues away from the disc margin, so it is bulky, coarse, asymmetric and often skips levels, matching an asymmetric or unilateral sacroiliitis. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is the third pattern and the one most often confused with the second: flowing ossification along the anterior longitudinal ligament across four or more contiguous vertebrae, with the disc heights preserved and the sacroiliac joints and facet joints uninvolved, which is why the sacroiliitis described here excludes it.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a hot, swollen, painful knee for ten days. The radiograph shows loss of the entire joint space compared with a film taken three weeks earlier, ill-defined erosion of both articular surfaces, a large effusion, and no osteophytes. What must be excluded before anything else?
choices: Septic arthritis; aspirate the joint before treatment is started
Rheumatoid arthritis; start disease-modifying therapy promptly
Rapidly progressive osteoarthritis of the femorotibial joint
Neuropathic arthropathy from long-standing diabetic neuropathy
quiz.answer: Septic arthritis; aspirate the joint before treatment is started
quiz.explain: The tempo is the diagnosis. Bacterial enzymes and the host response destroy cartilage over days, so the whole joint space disappears at once and both articular surfaces erode, with no time for the new bone that any chronic arthropathy would have produced. Nothing else on the list moves that fast: rheumatoid arthritis does not destroy a knee in three weeks and is rarely monoarticular at onset, rapidly progressive osteoarthritis is a real but slower entity and a diagnosis of exclusion, and a neuropathic joint shows the triad of increased density, debris and dislocation with abundant fragmentation, in a patient whose pain is characteristically less than the film suggests. Aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals comes before antibiotics wherever possible, since an aspirate taken afterwards may not grow the organism — and crystals and infection can coexist, so finding crystals does not close the question.

nodes.title: Reading the Mammogram
nodes.goal: Work up a mammographic finding, assign the BI-RADS category that names the next action, and say when ultrasound or MRI adds something.

quiz.prompt: A screening mammogram in a 54-year-old shows a new group of calcifications in the upper outer left breast that were not present two years ago. The reader is tempted to call them probably benign and repeat the study in six months. Explain what must happen first, and how the category is then chosen.
quiz.answer: The screening study is incomplete, so the correct assessment is category 0 and a recall for further imaging rather than a probably-benign category assigned from a screening film. The further imaging is magnification views in the craniocaudal and true lateral projections, which resolve the morphology of individual particles and let milk of calcium layer into teacup shapes on the horizontal-beam lateral, with ultrasound if an underlying mass is suspected. Probably-benign is an assessment made after a complete diagnostic workup, precisely because magnification so often reclassifies a group in one direction or the other. Once the morphology and distribution are seen, typically benign forms such as vascular, coarse popcorn-like, large rod-like, round, rim, dystrophic, milk of calcium and suture calcifications take category 2 and routine screening. A group of round or punctate calcifications with no suspicious feature may take category 3 with the six-month follow-up protocol. Amorphous, coarse heterogeneous, fine pleomorphic and fine linear or fine-linear branching morphologies are suspicious and take category 4, rising through the subcategories with more suspicious morphology and with a linear or segmental rather than grouped distribution, and are sampled by stereotactic or tomosynthesis-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy, with a specimen radiograph to prove the calcifications were retrieved and a marker clip left at the site.
quiz.explain: Category 0 exists because the screening examination and the diagnostic examination are different tests with different purposes, and a suspicion level cannot honestly be assigned until the second one has been done. The workup is not a formality: magnification changes the apparent morphology of calcifications more than any other manoeuvre in mammography, turning apparently grouped amorphous particles into either unmistakable milk of calcium or unmistakable fine pleomorphic ones. The specimen radiograph and the marker clip are the two steps most often forgotten and the two that determine whether the pathology result can be trusted and whether the surgeon can find the site again.

quiz.prompt: The BI-RADS lexicon lists the distribution descriptors for calcifications in a deliberate sequence. Put these distributions in order of increasing suspicion of malignancy.
quiz.answer: diffuse regional grouped linear segmental
quiz.explain: The order follows how closely the arrangement of the particles imitates the anatomy of a duct system. Diffuse calcifications scattered randomly through both breasts are essentially always benign. Regional calcifications occupy a large volume of tissue that does not correspond to a duct distribution and are usually benign, though the volume alone means they warrant a look. Grouped calcifications occupy a small volume — the lexicon defines this by number within a defined distance — and can be either. Linear calcifications lie along a line, with or without branching, because they are sitting in a duct. Segmental calcifications occupy a duct and its branches, which is why they raise the possibility of extensive or multicentric disease in one lobe. Distribution and morphology are always read together: benign-morphology particles in a segmental distribution stay benign, while fine pleomorphic particles in a segmental distribution are as suspicious as calcifications get.

quiz.prompt: At diagnostic workup a woman has a solitary, circumscribed, oval, non-calcified mass that is not palpable, and the radiologist assigns BI-RADS 3 with a six-month follow-up rather than a biopsy. That category carries an agreed ceiling on the likelihood of malignancy. What is that ceiling, as a percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Probably benign means a likelihood of malignancy greater than zero but no more than two per cent — low enough that surveillance is safer than biopsying every such lesion, but not low enough to ignore. The obligation the category carries is a protocol, not a vague plan: a unilateral study at six months, then bilateral at twelve and twenty-four months, and stability across two to three years permits a downgrade to benign. Three constraints go with it. The category should be assigned after a complete diagnostic workup rather than from a screening study, it is not appropriate for a palpable finding or where the patient cannot or will not comply with follow-up, and the findings for which the evidence supports it are few: a solitary circumscribed non-calcified mass, a focal asymmetry that effaces on spot compression, and a group of round or punctate calcifications. A finding that enlarges or changes during surveillance is biopsied.

quiz.prompt: On the mediolateral oblique view a small mass sits in the upper half of the breast; the craniocaudal view places it laterally. A true lateral mediolateral view is then taken to establish its position for biopsy. Compared with the oblique, where should the mass lie if the craniocaudal reading is correct?
choices: Lower on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
Higher on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
At the same height, since both are lateral projections
Further from the nipple on the true lateral projection
quiz.answer: Lower on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
quiz.explain: Rotating the tube from the oblique to a true lateral swings the lateral part of the breast downwards and the medial part upwards, so a lateral lesion drops and a medial lesion rises — the aide-memoire is that lead sinks and muffins rise. Watching the lesion move in the predicted direction is how you prove that the two views show the same object rather than two different ones, which is the whole point of triangulation and the reason a mass seen on one view alone gets a second projection before anything else. The true lateral also supplies the vertical coordinate a biopsy or wire localisation needs, and it is the projection on which milk of calcium layers into teacup shapes that the craniocaudal view shows only as smudges.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old presents with a palpable lump. Targeted ultrasound at the site of the lump shows a 15 mm anechoic structure with a circumscribed margin, an imperceptible wall, posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal vascularity or mural nodule. What follows?
choices: Assess as benign and reassure; no biopsy or imaging follow-up
Assess as probably benign and repeat the scan in six months
Aspirate the lesion and send the fluid for cytological study
Take a core biopsy, since a palpable lump requires tissue
quiz.answer: Assess as benign and reassure; no biopsy or imaging follow-up
quiz.explain: A structure meeting every criterion for a simple cyst is a category 2 finding, and imaging follow-up adds nothing; the criteria have to be met in full, though, because it is the combination of anechoic contents, an imperceptible wall, a circumscribed margin and posterior enhancement that gives the near-perfect negative predictive value. Aspiration is a treatment for a symptomatic cyst rather than a diagnostic step, and clear or greenish fluid from a simple cyst is discarded rather than sent for cytology, which has a poor yield and a real false-positive rate. The categories that do require action are the neighbours: a complicated cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes is followed or aspirated, and a complex cystic and solid mass with a thick septation or a vascularised mural nodule is biopsied. In a woman of this age ultrasound is the right first test for a palpable lump, with mammography added when the ultrasound is suspicious or the clinical concern persists.

quiz.prompt: A spiculated irregular mass with associated fine-linear branching calcifications and overlying skin retraction is worked up, and the radiologist must decide between category 4C and category 5 before the multidisciplinary meeting. For a finding to be placed in category 5, the likelihood of malignancy must be at least what percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Category 4C runs from above fifty per cent to below ninety-five; category 5 begins at ninety-five per cent and means the imaging alone is close to diagnostic. The distinction is not cosmetic, because the category changes what happens after the biopsy. A benign core biopsy result against a category 5 finding is by definition discordant and obliges repeat sampling or surgical excision, whereas a benign result against a 4A finding may reasonably be accepted with imaging follow-up. Category 5 is also the level of confidence at which definitive surgical and oncological management can be planned around the biopsy result before it returns. Category 6 sits outside this scale altogether: it is reserved for a malignancy already proved by biopsy and awaiting definitive treatment, and it is not a way of expressing very high suspicion.

quiz.prompt: A spiculated mass with an irregular margin in the upper outer quadrant is assessed as category 5. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy returns fibrocystic change with no atypia, and the pathologist confirms that representative breast tissue was sampled. What should be done?
choices: Treat the result as discordant and proceed to excision biopsy
Accept the benign result and return her to routine screening
Accept the result but repeat the mammogram in six months
Repeat the core biopsy under stereotactic guidance instead
quiz.answer: Treat the result as discordant and proceed to excision biopsy
quiz.explain: Radiological-pathological concordance is the last step of every image-guided biopsy and the one that catches the sampling error. A finding carrying at least a ninety-five per cent likelihood of malignancy cannot be explained by fibrocystic change, so the benign result is discordant whether or not the pathologist is confident about what is on the slide, and the pathway is repeat sampling or, more usually at this level of suspicion, surgical excision. Accepting it and returning the patient to screening is the failure mode this check exists to prevent. Repeating the biopsy stereotactically is the wrong technique for a mass that ultrasound can see, and short-interval mammography leaves a probable cancer in place. The same discipline governs the lesions that are excised despite a benign core result because of their upgrade rate at excision — atypical ductal hyperplasia, a radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion, papillary lesions, and a discordant result of any kind.

quiz.prompt: A multidisciplinary meeting reviews six mammograms, each assigned a different BI-RADS assessment category. Put the categories in order of increasing likelihood of malignancy.
quiz.answer: category-2 category-3 category-4A category-4B category-4C category-5
quiz.explain: Each category is a probability band, and each band names an action. Category 1 and category 2 both carry an essentially zero likelihood and both mean routine screening; category 2 differs only in that a benign finding has been described. Category 3 is above zero but no more than two per cent and means short-interval surveillance. The three category 4 subdivisions run above two to ten, above ten to fifty, and above fifty to below ninety-five per cent, and all three mean tissue diagnosis — the subdivision guides how the result is then handled rather than whether to biopsy. Category 5 is ninety-five per cent or more. Two categories deliberately sit outside this ladder: category 0 is not a suspicion level at all but a statement that the workup is incomplete, and category 6 is a cancer already proved by biopsy.

quiz.prompt: Comparison with prior mammograms shows a focal asymmetry in the right breast that is larger and denser than on the study two years earlier, visible on both projections, containing no mass and no calcification. Spot compression shows it persists rather than effacing, and targeted ultrasound of the area is normal. What should be done?
choices: Biopsy it, because a developing asymmetry carries real risk
Return to routine screening, since ultrasound was normal here
Assess as probably benign and reimage the area in six months
Report it as summation of normal tissue on both projections
quiz.answer: Biopsy it, because a developing asymmetry carries real risk
quiz.explain: An asymmetry that is new or has increased, is visible on both projections and persists on spot compression has a positive predictive value high enough to demand tissue, and it is one of the presentations of invasive lobular carcinoma, the type that most often grows without forming a mass. A normal ultrasound does not overturn that, because a lesion with no discrete mass frequently has no sonographic correlate; it changes only the technique used to sample it, which becomes stereotactic or tomosynthesis-guided rather than ultrasound-guided, or MRI-guided if MRI is used to localise. Tomosynthesis is the tool that separates a true asymmetry from summation of overlapping normal tissue, and summation is precisely what a finding that persists on spot compression is not.

quiz.prompt: Five years after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a mammogram shows a spiculated density at the upper outer quadrant with overlying skin thickening. It lies exactly at the surgical site with surgical clips within it, and it has been unchanged over four annual studies, having been denser on the earliest of them. What should be done?
choices: Report the postsurgical scar and continue annual surveillance
Assess as suspicious and take a core biopsy from the density
Request MRI, since a scar and a recurrence look the same
Assess as probably benign and reimage the breast in six months
quiz.answer: Report the postsurgical scar and continue annual surveillance
quiz.explain: Four things identify a scar: it is at the operative site, marked by clips; it changes shape markedly between the two projections, because it is a plane of fibrosis rather than a mass; it has no central density; and above all it becomes less conspicuous or stays stable over successive studies, since scar tissue and post-radiotherapy oedema regress. Recurrence does the opposite — a scar that becomes denser, develops a central mass, or acquires new calcifications is the finding that triggers biopsy. MRI is genuinely useful where the mammogram is equivocal, because mature scar beyond about a year typically enhances little while recurrence enhances, but ordering it against a four-year stable appearance buys false positives rather than information. Comparison with the previous films is the whole of the argument here, which is why the prior studies are part of the examination and not an optional extra.

quiz.prompt: A 47-year-old has a biopsy-proven invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast, and the mammogram shows only a subtle architectural distortion, so the extent of disease is uncertain. Separately, a 30-year-old whose mother and sister had premenopausal breast cancer asks whether she should be screened by MRI instead of mammography. Give the reasoning in each case.
quiz.answer: In the first case MRI earns its place. Lobular carcinoma grows in single-file strands without forming a discrete mass or a desmoplastic reaction, so it is the type that mammography most often misses or underestimates, particularly in dense tissue; MRI has the highest sensitivity of any breast technique for invasive disease and is used here to measure the extent of the tumour, to look for multifocal or multicentric disease and for a contralateral cancer that would change the operation. The condition attached is that MRI also finds lesions that prove benign, so any additional finding that would alter surgery is biopsied first, usually under ultrasound after a targeted second-look scan, rather than acted on directly. In the second case supplemental MRI is offered to women at high lifetime risk — carriers of a pathogenic BRCA1, BRCA2 or comparable variant and their untested first-degree relatives, women whose family history puts their lifetime risk above roughly a fifth on a model that accounts for it, and women irradiated to the chest in adolescence or early adulthood — but it is an addition to mammography rather than a replacement, because MRI is poor at showing calcifications, which is how a large share of ductal carcinoma in situ presents. In a premenopausal woman the study is booked for the second week of the menstrual cycle to limit background parenchymal enhancement, which otherwise obscures small lesions and generates recalls.
quiz.explain: The two halves are the same argument used in opposite directions. MRI's strength is sensitivity to enhancing invasive tumour, so it is worth doing where the question is how much invasive disease there is and mammography cannot answer it, and where a woman's prior risk is high enough that the extra cancers found outweigh the extra benign biopsies. Its weakness is calcification, which is why it supplements rather than replaces mammography in screening, and why an MRI-detected finding is a hypothesis to be tested rather than a diagnosis. The cycle timing and the second-look ultrasound are the two practical steps that make the difference between an MRI service that adds cancers and one that mainly adds recalls.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old whose screening mammogram was reported as normal, with the density assessed as extremely dense, presents nine months later with a 2 cm palpable invasive cancer. On review of the earlier film the unit finds nothing to see even in retrospect. What does the case say about mammographic density?
choices: Dense tissue masks cancer, and it also raises the risk itself
Dense tissue masks cancer but carries no risk of its own
Dense tissue is a reader effect and not a property of tissue
Dense tissue lowers sensitivity but raises specificity to match
quiz.answer: Dense tissue masks cancer, and it also raises the risk itself
quiz.explain: Fibroglandular tissue attenuates x-rays much as a tumour does, so a cancer surrounded by it has little contrast against its background and mammographic sensitivity falls with increasing density — the masking effect that produced this interval cancer. Separately and independently, high breast density is itself a risk factor for developing breast cancer, so the two effects compound rather than offset. That is the argument for supplemental imaging in dense breasts: tomosynthesis raises cancer detection and lowers recall by separating overlapping tissue, and supplemental ultrasound, contrast-enhanced mammography and MRI each find additional cancers, with MRI shown to reduce the interval cancer rate in extremely dense breasts. The honest caveat is that a mortality benefit from supplemental screening has not been demonstrated, and every additional test brings false positives with it. Density is a qualitative judgement made on the current study and can change over time, with hormonal status and with weight.

nodes.title: Imaging the Child
nodes.goal: Read the neonatal chest and abdomen, image the infant hip at the right age with the right test, and recognise the injuries that oblige a safeguarding referral.

quiz.prompt: Two infants are tachypnoeic in the first hours of life. The first, born at term by caesarean section without labour, has a film showing fluid in the horizontal fissure, prominent perihilar streaking and normal to slightly increased lung volumes. The second, born at 29 weeks, has uniformly low volumes, a fine granular pattern throughout both lungs and air bronchograms extending to the periphery. Interpret each film and say how the next 48 hours should differ.
quiz.answer: The first is transient tachypnoea of the newborn: fetal lung fluid that would normally be cleared during labour and the first breaths is still in the interstitium and the lymphatics, so it collects in the fissures and around the hila while the alveoli remain aerated, which is why the lung volumes are preserved or even increased. It is managed supportively, with oxygen if needed, and it clears as the fluid is absorbed, typically within 24 to 48 hours, so the follow-up film should look better rather than worse. The second is surfactant deficiency: without surfactant the alveoli collapse at end-expiration, so the volumes are low, the fine granularity is the summation of countless airless acini, and the air bronchograms are conspicuous because aerated bronchi stand out against airless lung. Untreated it worsens over the first day or two rather than clearing, and it is treated with exogenous surfactant and respiratory support, after which the film can clear strikingly and sometimes asymmetrically. Two cautions belong with the pair: group B streptococcal pneumonia can be radiographically indistinguishable from surfactant deficiency, so antibiotics are started while cultures are awaited, and a sudden deterioration on a ventilator should prompt a search for pulmonary interstitial emphysema or a pneumothorax rather than a change in the underlying diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Lung volume is the discriminator that does most of the work on a neonatal chest film, because it follows directly from where the abnormality sits. Fluid in the interstitium leaves the air spaces open and the lungs large; absent surfactant collapses the air spaces and makes the lungs small. Everything else — gestation, mode of delivery, the tempo over the following two days, and the response to surfactant — is confirmatory. The pair also illustrates why the neonatal film is read alongside the gestational age and the clinical course rather than in isolation: the same granular pattern in a term infant should raise pneumonia, and coarse patchy shadowing with hyperinflation in a term or post-term infant with a history of stained liquor points instead to meconium aspiration.

quiz.prompt: A radiograph of a preterm infant shows one umbilical catheter that dips into the pelvis, turns and ascends to the left of the vertebral bodies, with its tip at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra. A second catheter runs directly cephalad from the umbilicus with its tip at the level of the ninth thoracic vertebra. How should the lines be reported?
choices: Both are well sited; the descending course marks the artery
Both need withdrawal; the tips lie within the heart itself
The lines are swapped; the ascending one is the arterial line
The venous line is in the portal vein and must be pulled back
quiz.answer: Both are well sited; the descending course marks the artery
quiz.explain: The course identifies the vessel before the tip is judged. The umbilical artery runs caudally to the internal iliac artery before turning up the aorta, so an initial dip into the pelvis is the signature of an arterial catheter; the umbilical vein runs straight up through the falciform ligament and the left portal vein into the ductus venosus, so a catheter that only ascends is venous. Acceptable arterial tip positions are high, between the sixth and ninth thoracic vertebrae — above the coeliac axis and below the ductus arteriosus — or low, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, below the renal arteries; the intervening stretch is avoided because it lies across the origins of the visceral vessels. The venous tip should sit at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium, around the eighth or ninth thoracic level. The two failures worth knowing are a venous tip that stops short in the liver, which risks portal vein thrombosis and extravasation of hypertonic infusate into the parenchyma, and a tip advanced into the right atrium, which risks arrhythmia, thrombus and pericardial tamponade.

quiz.prompt: A preterm infant on the neonatal unit has serial abdominal radiographs during an episode of necrotising enterocolitis. Put these radiographic findings in order of increasing severity.
quiz.answer: dilated-loops pneumatosis portal-venous-gas pneumoperitoneum
quiz.explain: Dilated, separated loops with a loss of the normal polygonal gas pattern are the earliest and least specific finding, and by themselves they support only a suspicion. Intramural gas — a bubbly or curvilinear lucency within the bowel wall, produced by gas-forming organisms in a damaged mucosa — is the finding that establishes the diagnosis. Branching lucencies over the liver are that gas carried back in the portal venous system, and they mark more extensive disease and a worse prognosis. Free intraperitoneal gas means the bowel has perforated and is the one finding that is an absolute indication for surgery; it appears as gas outlining the falciform ligament on the supine film, as both sides of the bowel wall becoming visible, or as a lucency over the liver on a left lateral decubitus view, which is the projection to request in an infant too unwell to be sat up. A loop that stays in the same position and the same shape across serial films is a further sign of a segment that is no longer viable, and ultrasound adds bowel wall thickness, perfusion and free fluid that the radiograph cannot show.

quiz.prompt: A term neonate aged three days vomits bile. Put the steps of the emergency pathway in the order in which they are carried out.
quiz.answer: nasogastric-decompression abdominal-radiograph upper-GI-contrast laparotomy
quiz.explain: Bile-stained vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proved otherwise, and the whole pathway is built around how quickly the midgut dies once its vascular pedicle twists. Resuscitation and a nasogastric tube come first, both to decompress the stomach and to confirm the character of the aspirate. The plain film is quick and can show a double bubble, a gasless abdomen or dilated loops — but it is very often normal, so it can raise the suspicion and cannot lower it. The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the reference standard: it shows where the duodenojejunal flexure lies, which should be to the left of the left-sided pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb, and in volvulus it shows a corkscrew or beaked duodenum. A twisted midgut then goes straight to a Ladd procedure. Ultrasound showing the superior mesenteric vein lying anterior or to the left of the artery, or a whirlpool of vessels wrapping the pedicle, is increasingly used and can make the diagnosis quickly, but in most units a normal ultrasound does not by itself exclude malrotation.

quiz.prompt: A 5-week-old boy has non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and a palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium. Ultrasound of the pylorus is performed in the right lateral decubitus position with a high-frequency linear probe. At or above what single-wall muscle thickness, in millimetres, is the pylorus regarded as hypertrophied? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres of single muscle wall thickness, measured on the short-axis image away from the near-field, together with a pyloric channel length of about fifteen to seventeen millimetres or more, defines the hypertrophied pylorus. The measurements matter less than the dynamic observation that accompanies them: the study is watched for several minutes, and in true hypertrophic pyloric stenosis vigorous gastric peristalsis fails to drive fluid through the channel, whereas pylorospasm relaxes and lets fluid pass. A borderline pylorus in a young infant is rescanned rather than operated on. The surgical point is that this is not a surgical emergency but a medical one: the persistent vomiting of gastric contents produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and that must be corrected before an anaesthetic, because alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea. Ultrasound has replaced the contrast meal, and no ionising radiation is involved at all.

quiz.prompt: A neonate with trisomy 21 vomits in the first hours of life. The supine abdominal radiograph shows two gas-filled structures in the upper abdomen, one under the left hemidiaphragm and one to its right, with no gas anywhere beyond them. What does the absence of distal gas indicate?
choices: Complete duodenal obstruction, most likely an atresia
Midgut volvulus twisting a patent duodenum shut
A duodenal web with a central perforation in it
Annular pancreas causing a partial obstruction
quiz.answer: Complete duodenal obstruction, most likely an atresia
quiz.explain: The two bubbles are the distended stomach and the dilated duodenal cap proximal to the obstruction, and what discriminates among the causes is whether any gas has passed beyond them. Complete absence of distal gas means a complete obstruction, and in a neonate with trisomy 21 that is duodenal atresia, which needs no contrast study before surgery. Gas beyond the second bubble means the obstruction is incomplete — a fenestrated web, an annular pancreas, or malrotation with Ladd bands — and those do need a contrast study, both to define the anatomy and because malrotation carries the risk of volvulus. The trap to hold on to is the converse: a neonate vomiting bile whose film is normal or near-normal still needs an urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because a midgut volvulus can produce very little to see on a plain film and is the one diagnosis here that cannot wait.

quiz.prompt: A previously well 9-month-old has episodes of screaming with drawing up of the legs, and a sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm structure with concentric rings in the transverse plane. The abdomen is soft, there is no peritonism and the child is well perfused. What should follow?
choices: Fluoroscopically guided air enema reduction, with surgery on standby
Immediate laparotomy, since ultrasound has already made the diagnosis
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to search for a lead point
Observation with intravenous fluids, since most reduce spontaneously
quiz.answer: Fluoroscopically guided air enema reduction, with surgery on standby
quiz.explain: Ileocolic intussusception at this age is usually idiopathic, following lymphoid hypertrophy after a viral illness, and ultrasound is both sensitive and specific enough to be the diagnostic test — the target on the transverse image and the pseudo-kidney on the longitudinal one. Reduction by air, or by fluid under ultrasound guidance, is the treatment, and it succeeds in the large majority. It is done with a surgeon informed and theatre available, because of the small risk of perforation during the procedure and because a failed reduction goes on to operation. The contraindications are perforation, peritonitis and shock, none of which is present here. CT adds radiation to a child and delays a treatment that is already available; a lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, a duplication cyst, lymphoma or the bowel wall haematoma of Henoch-Schoenlein purpura is looked for in children outside the typical age range or after repeated recurrence. A short small-bowel-only intussusception found incidentally is usually transient and needs no intervention.

quiz.prompt: A girl born in the breech position at term has a normal hip examination at birth, and is referred for imaging because of the breech presentation alone. Coronal hip ultrasound is performed by the Graf method. At or above what alpha angle, in degrees, is the bony acetabular roof regarded as normal? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The alpha angle lies between the vertical line of the iliac wing and the slope of the bony acetabular roof, and sixty degrees or more is a mature hip. Between fifty and fifty-nine the roof is deficient, which may be physiological immaturity in the first weeks or genuine dysplasia depending on the infant's age; below fifty the hip is dysplastic and the femoral head is subluxed or dislocated. Two points about timing follow. Ultrasound is the technique before the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months, because the cartilaginous head and roof are invisible on a radiograph; after that an anteroposterior pelvis takes over, read with Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines, with the ossific nucleus expected in the lower inner quadrant, together with Shenton's line and the acetabular index. And a risk-factor scan of this kind is deferred to about six weeks of age, because physiological laxity in the first weeks produces findings that resolve on their own and would lead to over-treatment. An infant with an abnormal clinical examination is a different matter and is imaged and referred sooner.

quiz.prompt: A girl born at term in the breech position has a normal hip examination at birth. At two weeks of age the department receives a request for an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph to screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip. What should the department do?
choices: Perform hip ultrasound instead, and book it at about six weeks
Perform the radiograph, which shows the cartilage well enough
Perform hip ultrasound at once, before the laxity settles down
Perform MRI of the hips under sedation to assess the labrum
quiz.answer: Perform hip ultrasound instead, and book it at about six weeks
quiz.explain: Both halves of the answer matter. The modality is wrong because the femoral head is entirely cartilaginous until around four to six months, so a neonatal radiograph shows an empty acetabulum and unreliable landmarks, while ultrasound images the cartilaginous head and the acetabular roof directly and adds a dynamic assessment of stability under stress. The timing is wrong because physiological ligamentous laxity in the first weeks of life produces immature-looking hips that resolve spontaneously, so scanning too early converts normal newborns into patients; a scan at around six weeks is the compromise that finds the hips that need treating without treating the ones that do not. This applies to screening on the basis of a risk factor — breech presentation, a first-degree family history, oligohydramnios — in an infant whose examination is normal. An infant with a positive Ortolani or Barlow test is imaged and referred to orthopaedics sooner, and a frankly dislocated irreducible hip is discussed immediately.

quiz.prompt: A term neonate has not passed meconium by 48 hours and the abdomen is distended. The radiograph shows many dilated bowel loops throughout the abdomen. A water-soluble contrast enema shows a small-calibre colon with a change in calibre at the rectosigmoid junction, and the rectum narrower than the sigmoid above it. What does the enema indicate?
choices: Hirschsprung disease; the aganglionic rectum stays narrow
Meconium ileus; inspissated pellets fill an unused colon
Ileal atresia; the colon is unused and small along its length
Functional immaturity of the colon in an infant of a diabetic
quiz.answer: Hirschsprung disease; the aganglionic rectum stays narrow
quiz.explain: In a normal neonate the rectum is the widest part of the large bowel, so a rectum narrower than the sigmoid — a rectosigmoid index below one — is abnormal in itself, and a transition in calibre above it marks the boundary between the aganglionic distal segment, which cannot relax, and the dilated ganglionic bowel proximal to it. Suction rectal biopsy is what confirms the diagnosis; the enema shows where to expect the transition and how much bowel is involved. Two technical points determine whether the study works: it is done without a preceding rectal examination or washout, either of which can decompress the transition zone and hide it, and delayed films are taken, since retention of contrast beyond 24 hours supports the diagnosis. The alternatives differ in the calibre of the colon along its whole length: meconium ileus gives a microcolon with filling defects in the terminal ileum and points to cystic fibrosis, ileal atresia gives an unused microcolon with no pellets, and small left colon syndrome shows an abrupt calibre change at the splenic flexure in an infant of a diabetic mother and resolves without surgery.

quiz.prompt: A five-month-old who is not yet crawling is brought in with a swollen thigh, and the radiograph shows a transverse mid-shaft femoral fracture. The parents describe a roll from a sofa onto a carpeted floor. Set out the imaging that should follow and the findings that would raise the concern further.
quiz.answer: The starting point is that the injury is not explained by the history: a femoral shaft fracture requires substantial force, and in an infant who cannot yet crawl, cruise or weight-bear, a short fall of this kind is an inadequate mechanism. The mismatch between the injury, the mechanism offered and the child's motor development is itself the concerning feature. A full skeletal survey to a national standard is indicated in any child under two years with suspected physical abuse: a defined set of collimated, coned, high-detail views of the whole skeleton rather than a single film of the entire baby, reported by a radiologist experienced in the work, and a limited follow-up survey at about eleven to fourteen days shows healing periosteal reaction at sites that were invisible acutely. Neuroimaging is added in an infant, because occult abusive head trauma is common at this age and clinical signs are unreliable. The findings carrying the highest specificity are classic metaphyseal lesions at the ends of the long bones, posterior and posteromedial rib fractures, and scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures; fractures of clearly different ages, multiple fractures, and any fracture whose mechanism does not match the history or the developmental stage add further weight. The imaging is one contribution to a multi-agency safeguarding assessment made with the clinical team, and is not a verdict on its own.
quiz.explain: The single most useful question in this area is whether the injury fits what the child is physically capable of doing. Fractures in non-ambulant infants are uncommon and are the group in which inflicted injury is most frequent, which is why the developmental history is recorded before the film is reported. The survey is a protocol rather than an ad hoc set of films because its purpose is to find fractures that are clinically silent, and the follow-up survey exists because callus makes visible what the acute study could not — particularly rib and metaphyseal injuries. The last sentence is the one that is easiest to get wrong in either direction: imaging can describe the injuries and their probable ages and mechanisms, and it can say whether the account offered fits, but the determination is made by the safeguarding process rather than by the radiologist alone.

quiz.prompt: A skeletal survey in an 8-month-old, carried out after a reported fall from a bed, shows a healing fracture of the posterior sixth left rib near the costovertebral junction, a linear parietal skull fracture and a mid-clavicular fracture. The parents point out that the child was resuscitated by a paramedic at the scene. How should the rib fracture be weighed?
choices: Highly specific for abuse; chest compressions seldom fracture there
Adequately explained by the chest compressions given at the scene
A common birth injury at this age, and of no further concern
Of no more weight than the skull fracture in the same survey
quiz.answer: Highly specific for abuse; chest compressions seldom fracture there
quiz.explain: Posterior and posteromedial rib fractures arise when an infant is gripped around the chest and squeezed front to back, levering the rib over the transverse process, and they are among the findings with the highest specificity for inflicted injury. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation does fracture ribs in a small minority of infants, and the fractures it produces are predominantly anterior or anterolateral, although posterior fractures after resuscitation have been reported with the two-thumb technique; a documented resuscitation is therefore weighed as a possible contributor rather than accepted as a complete explanation, and it does not on its own dispose of the finding. The other two fractures illustrate the difference between specificity and presence. A linear parietal skull fracture is common and non-specific, follows an ordinary household impact as readily as an inflicted one, and cannot be dated, because the skull heals without callus. A clavicular fracture is the commonest birth injury but would have remodelled long before eight months, and in any case is non-specific. Classic metaphyseal lesions carry specificity comparable to posterior rib fractures and are the other finding to hunt for on the survey.

nodes.title: Structured Reporting
nodes.goal: Write a report to a standard template, assign a RADS category that carries its own recommendation, and close the loop on a finding that needs acting on.

quiz.prompt: A department rewrites its CT reports to follow the standard section headings used in structured reporting. Put those five headings in the order they appear, from the top of the report.
quiz.answer: indication technique comparison findings impression
quiz.explain: The order is not decorative; each section exists so that a later reader can tell what question was asked, what was done to answer it, and what the answer was. The indication frames the study and is what makes an incidental finding incidental. The technique records contrast, phases and reconstruction, so that a reader in six months knows what the study could and could not have shown - a non-contrast scan reported as showing no liver lesion means something different from a portal-venous one. The comparison names the prior studies actually reviewed, and naming them is a claim that they were opened. The findings are the observation, and the impression is the answer. The impression is the part that is read, quoted in the notes and acted on, which is why it goes last and why it has to stand alone.

quiz.prompt: A CT report on a patient with weight loss runs to eleven lines of findings, one of which records a 3 cm hypoenhancing pancreatic mass with upstream duct dilatation. The impression reads, in full: 'Abnormal appearances as described above. Clinical correlation advised.' The surgeon telephones the next day to ask whether the scan showed anything to explain the symptoms. What is the substantive failure in this report?
choices: The impression did not answer the clinical question asked
The findings should have opened with the pancreatic mass
The mass needed a stated differential in the findings
The report should have advised a repeat scan at 3 months
quiz.answer: The impression did not answer the clinical question asked
quiz.explain: The mass was seen, measured and recorded, and still the report failed, because the section the referrer reads contained nothing. 'As described above' asks a clinician who has not seen the images to do the synthesis, and 'clinical correlation advised' hands back the decision the study was requested to inform. A usable impression names the finding, gives the most likely explanation, ranks the alternative worth acting on, and states the next step with a modality and an interval. The near-miss about ordering the findings is a real point of style - leading with the abnormality that matters does help - but a perfectly ordered findings section under an empty impression still leaves the surgeon telephoning.
